question: For nearly a thousand years, the largest cathedral in the Christian world was a domed church in Constantinople, built in 537 AD by Emperor Justinian. It is called:
context: The dome was a feat of engineering — pendentives let a round dome sit on a square base. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

question: Istanbul straddles a narrow strait that separates Europe from Asia. That strait is called:
context: About 31 km long, the Bosphorus links the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara. Two suspension bridges and a rail tunnel cross it today.

question: On Croatia's Adriatic coast, a walled medieval city with marble streets and orange-tiled roofs juts into the sea. It is called:
context: The Republic of Ragusa (Dubrovnik's medieval name) was a wealthy maritime rival to Venice. The walls, up to 25 m high, still circle the old town.

question: The city of Petra in southern Jordan, carved into rose-pink sandstone cliffs by the Nabataean Arabs around 300 BC, contains a famous facade at the end of a narrow gorge. The facade is called:
context: Al-Khazneh was carved in the 1st century AD, probably as a royal tomb; its name comes from Bedouin legends of pirate gold hidden in the urn at its top.

question: At the heart of Marrakech in Morocco lies a vast covered market of narrow lanes selling spices, leather, and lanterns. This kind of old-city market is called a:
context: The medina of Marrakech (founded 1070 by the Almoravids) is UNESCO heritage; its central square, Jemaa el-Fnaa, hosts storytellers and snake charmers at dusk.

question: In central Mali stands the world's largest mud-brick building, replastered every year in a community festival. It is the Great Mosque of:
context: Built in 1907 in the Sudano-Sahelian style on the site of a 13th-century original. The annual replastering keeps the rains from washing it away.

question: In the Ethiopian highlands, eleven churches are carved downward from solid rock, connected by tunnels and trenches. The town is:
context: Built in the 12th-13th centuries by King Lalibela as a 'New Jerusalem' after Saladin made pilgrimage hard. They are still active churches.

question: Behind Cape Town in South Africa rises a flat-topped mountain whose 'tablecloth' of cloud spills down the cliffs on summer days. It is called:
context: One of the oldest mountains on Earth (520 million years), with over 2,200 plant species — more than the British Isles. A cableway has run since 1929.

question: Damascus, capital of Syria, often appears in lists of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth. Its known occupation goes back at least:
context: Tell Ramad, just outside the city, dates to about 9,000 BC. The Old City has been continuously settled since at least 6,300 BC.

question: In central Isfahan, Iran, lies one of the largest city squares on Earth, ringed by a Safavid-era royal palace, a grand mosque, and a private mosque. It is called:
context: Built by Shah Abbas the Great around 1602. 'Naqsh-e Jahan' means 'Image of the World.' The Persian proverb 'Isfahan is half the world' refers partly to it.

question: In the desert city of Yazd, Iran, traditional houses have tall ventilation towers that catch breezes and cool the rooms below. They are called:
context: Yazd is one of the oldest centers of Zoroastrianism; its badgirs ('wind catchers') predate electric air conditioning by a thousand years.

question: Since 2010, the world's tallest building has stood in the desert city of Dubai. It is named for a UAE ruler and reaches:
context: The Burj Khalifa has 163 floors and a Y-shaped plan inspired by a desert flower. It surpassed Taipei 101 in 2010.

question: In the heart of Samarkand, Uzbekistan, three blue-tiled Islamic colleges face each other across a public square. The square is called:
context: The three madrasahs (Ulugh Beg, Sher-Dor, Tilya-Kori) were built between 1417 and 1660. Samarkand was a great Silk Road hub under Timur (Tamerlane).

question: The old city of Jaipur, India, is painted a uniform terracotta pink under an 1876 decree issued to welcome a royal visitor. That visitor was:
context: Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh ordered the city painted pink, the traditional color of hospitality, for the visit of the future Edward VII. Made permanent in 1877.

question: On the Ganges in northern India, the holy city of Varanasi has more than 80 stepped riverbank platforms where Hindus bathe and cremate the dead. These platforms are called:
context: Varanasi is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth. Dying there is believed to grant moksha — liberation from rebirth.

question: At the center of Beijing sits the world's largest palace complex, with 980 buildings under yellow glazed-tile roofs. It is called:
context: Home to 24 Ming and Qing emperors from 1420 to 1912. Yellow roof tiles were reserved for the emperor; commoners could not use them.

question: South of Beijing's Forbidden City lies a circular blue-tiled temple where Ming and Qing emperors performed annual rituals praying for good harvests. It is called:
context: The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests was built in 1420 without nails, on three marble terraces. The complex is laid out as a symbolic square (earth) within circles (heaven).

question: Hong Kong's mountain ridge, served by the world's oldest funicular tram (1888), offers the famous skyline view from the top. It is called:
context: Locally just 'The Peak.' The tram climbs 396 m on a 27-degree gradient; the upper terminus is at 396 m altitude.

question: Just north of Seoul, South Korea, runs a 4-km-wide buffer strip — one of the most heavily militarized borders on Earth — separating two countries since 1953. It is called:
context: Created by the Korean War armistice in 1953. Wildlife thrives inside the DMZ because humans cannot enter.

question: In central Tokyo, an intersection famous worldwide stops traffic in all directions every couple of minutes so up to 3,000 pedestrians can cross at once. It is called:
context: Nicknamed 'the scramble.' Featured in 'Lost in Translation' and 'The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift.'

question: A three-story Zen temple in Kyoto, its upper two floors covered in pure gold leaf, reflects in a pond at its base. It is called:
context: Built in 1397 as a retirement villa for shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. Burned by a novice monk in 1950; the present building was reconstructed in 1955.

question: Behind a shrine in southern Kyoto, thousands of bright orange wooden gates form tunnels snaking up a forested mountain. The shrine is:
context: Dedicated to Inari, the kami of rice and prosperity. Each torii is donated by a business; over 10,000 line the mountain paths.

question: In Nara, Japan's first permanent capital, sits the world's largest bronze Buddha — 15 meters tall, in a wooden hall that was once the world's largest wooden building. The temple is:
context: The Daibutsu was cast in 752 AD; the current hall (rebuilt 1709) is only two-thirds the original size and still vast.

question: The skeletal dome of one bombed-out building near ground zero was left standing in Hiroshima as a memorial. The bomb fell on:
context: The Genbaku Dome, a former exhibition hall, was almost directly under the burst. UNESCO heritage since 1996.

question: On a dusty plain by the Irrawaddy River in Myanmar, more than 2,000 brick Buddhist temples and stupas dot the landscape — built between the 11th and 13th centuries. The plain is:
context: Capital of the Pagan Empire, Bagan once held over 10,000 temples. It became a UNESCO heritage site in 2019.

question: A small Cambodian town serves as the gateway to a vast complex of Khmer ruins including the largest religious monument on Earth. The town is:
context: Siem Reap means 'Siam Defeated' — a reference to the Khmer kingdom's wars with neighboring Thailand.

question: Inside the walls of Bangkok's Grand Palace sits the most sacred Buddha image in Thailand — carved from a single block of green jade. It is called:
context: The 66-cm-tall figure has been in Bangkok since 1784. It is dressed in seasonal gold robes changed by the king three times a year.

question: Most of modern Singapore's land area — including Changi Airport and Marina Bay — sits on ground that did not exist in 1960. The new land was made by:
context: Singapore has grown 25% in land area since independence. Sand is imported from neighbors; some have banned the trade.

question: On a hill in Kathmandu, Nepal, an ancient Buddhist stupa is painted with the all-seeing eyes of the Buddha and surrounded by long-tailed macaques. It is called:
context: At least 1,500 years old; locally called the Monkey Temple. The eyes look out in four directions to symbolize the Buddha's all-seeing wisdom.

question: Opened in 1883, the first steel-wire suspension bridge crossed the East River in New York. It is called:
context: Designed by John A. Roebling, who died from injuries during surveys; his son Washington finished it after caisson disease confined him to bed for a decade.

question: New York's Central Park is not a leftover wilderness — every hill and pond was designed. The lead designer was:
context: Olmsted and Calvert Vaux won the 1858 design competition. The park took 20 years to complete; nearly 1,600 residents were displaced for it.

question: After fire destroyed much of Chicago in 1871, architects there pioneered a new kind of tall building using a steel skeleton frame. The first such building was completed in:
context: William Le Baron Jenney's Home Insurance Building (1885) is often called the first skyscraper. Earlier tall buildings used load-bearing walls; steel frames let walls become non-structural curtains.

question: Mexico City sinks several centimeters a year because it sits on the drained bed of a former Aztec lake. That lake was called:
context: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was built on an island in Lake Texcoco. The Spanish drained the lake; modern Mexico City sinks unevenly into the lakebed clay.

question: The Quechua name for the former Inca capital in the Peruvian Andes means 'navel of the world.' That city is:
context: Cusco was the imperial capital from the 13th century until the Spanish conquest in 1533. Inca stonework still anchors the colonial cathedrals.

question: In the Bolivian Andes, a single cone-shaped red mountain produced so much silver for the Spanish Empire that it made the city beneath it briefly one of the richest on Earth. The mountain is:
context: Cerro Rico means 'Rich Mountain' in Spanish. Potosí mined silver from 1545; perhaps 8 million indigenous and African workers died in its mines and mercury mills.

question: Atop the 700-meter Corcovado peak overlooking Rio de Janeiro stands a 30-meter Art Deco statue of Christ with arms outstretched. It was completed in:
context: Designed by Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa and French sculptor Paul Landowski. The face was sculpted by Romanian Gheorghe Leonida.

question: In the colorful dockside neighborhood of La Boca in Buenos Aires in the 1880s and 1890s, a sensual partner dance emerged blending European, African, and gaucho music. That dance is:
context: Tango arose in working-class immigrant neighborhoods. Carlos Gardel made it a global craze in the 1920s.

question: On the Argentine side of Tierra del Fuego, a town of about 80,000 calls itself the southernmost city in the world. It is:
context: Latitude 54°S. Many Antarctic expeditions depart from Ushuaia's port. Puerto Williams in Chile is smaller but slightly further south.

question: On Chile's Pacific coast, a port city draped over 42 steep hills is famous for its colorful houses and a network of old cable-car lifts. It is:
context: Fifteen funiculars (ascensores) still climb the hills, some dating to the 1880s. UNESCO inscribed the city in 2003.

question: New Zealand's largest city, Auckland, is built on top of about 50 small volcanoes. The field is:
context: The Auckland Volcanic Field has erupted as recently as 600 years ago (Rangitoto Island); future eruptions are expected somewhere in the field.

question: On New Zealand's North Island, a town sits in a caldera where geysers shoot, mud pools bubble, and the air smells of sulfur. It is a major center of Māori culture. The town is:
context: Rotorua means 'second lake' in Māori. The Pohutu Geyser erupts up to 20 times a day, reaching 30 m.

question: Rapa Nui, with its giant stone heads, lies in the Pacific over 2,000 km from the nearest inhabited island. It belongs politically to:
context: Annexed by Chile in 1888. The nearest inhabited island is Pitcairn, 2,075 km away; the nearest continent is South America, 3,500 km east.

question: The Scottish capital is split between a medieval Old Town built along a volcanic ridge and a planned Georgian New Town below it. That capital is:
context: Both districts are UNESCO heritage. Edinburgh Castle perches atop Castle Rock, a 350-million-year-old volcanic plug.

question: The Florentine palace built in 1560 as government offices for the Medici grand duke later became one of the world's first public art museums. It is called:
context: 'Uffizi' means 'offices' in Italian. Designed by Vasari; opened to public visitors in 1769. Holds Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Primavera.

question: Outside the ancient walls of Rome, multi-level underground burial galleries hold the tombs of early Christians, including saints and popes. These galleries are called:
context: Christian burial in Rome had to be outside the city walls. The catacombs of San Callisto, San Sebastiano, and Priscilla together hold over a million graves.

question: Moscow's Red Square gets its name from the Russian word 'krasnaya' which originally meant:
context: The Russian word 'krasnaya' meant 'beautiful' in old usage; the modern meaning 'red' came later. The square has been called this since at least the 17th century.

question: Moscow's Metro stations from the 1930s-1950s were built as 'palaces for the people' with marble, mosaics, and chandeliers. The line opened in:
context: Stalin commissioned the Metro as a showpiece of socialist achievement. The first line opened on 15 May 1935 between Sokolniki and Park Kultury.

question: On Estonia's Baltic coast sits one of Europe's best-preserved medieval old towns, with intact city walls and Hanseatic merchant houses. That capital is:
context: Tallinn's old town was a Hanseatic League trading hub. Most of the 14th-century walls and 26 of the original 46 towers still stand.

question: On a limestone hill overlooking the Vistula River in Krakow, Poland, the royal castle of the medieval Polish kings sits above a cave where, legend says, a dragon once lived. That castle is:
context: Wawel was the royal seat from 1038 to 1596. The cave (Dragon's Den) is a real karst cavern at the foot of the hill.

question: Russia's former imperial capital sits at 60°N, where for several weeks in June the sun barely sets. The locals call this phenomenon:
context: St. Petersburg's White Nights run roughly 11 June to 2 July. The bridges over the Neva are raised for shipping in the small hours.

question: In central Greece, six Eastern Orthodox monasteries perch atop dramatic sandstone pillars rising from a plain. The site is called:
context: 'Meteora' means 'suspended in air' in Greek. The first hermits arrived in the 9th century; the monasteries were built from the 14th century onward.

question: On the slopes of Mount Parnassus in Greece sat the most famous oracle of the ancient world, where a priestess delivered cryptic prophecies. The site was at:
context: The Greeks considered Delphi the navel (omphalos) of the world. The Pythia spoke for Apollo, breathing vapors from a chasm beneath the temple.

question: The medieval Flemish city of Bruges, Belgium, has a 13th-century belfry whose 47-bell carillon can be heard across the old town. The belfry stands in:
context: Bruges' belfry climbs 83 m via 366 steps. The carillon is played by hand on a wooden keyboard from a chamber high inside.

question: Atop a rocky hill overlooking Salzburg looms a vast white medieval fortress, one of the largest in Europe never to have been conquered. It is called:
context: Begun in 1077 by Prince-Archbishop Gebhard; expanded by 1500. A funicular built in 1892 climbs to the gate.

question: Across the Gulf of Finland, two capitals lie only 80 km apart by ferry. They are:
context: Helsinki-Tallinn ferries take about 2 hours. The two share a Finnic linguistic heritage, though Finnish and Estonian are distinct languages.

question: On Norway's western fjord coast, a row of brightly painted wooden Hanseatic warehouses lines the harbor of a medieval trading town. That town is:
context: Bergen was a Hanseatic League trading post from 1360 to 1754. The Bryggen warehouses have burned and been rebuilt repeatedly; they are UNESCO heritage.

question: The capital of Lithuania holds one of Europe's largest medieval baroque old towns, with more than 1,500 buildings packed into the historic core. That capital is:
context: Vilnius' old town spans 359 hectares. It was a center of Jewish learning before WWII, nicknamed 'the Jerusalem of the North.'

question: On a hillside in Afghanistan's capital lies a terraced 16th-century garden built by the founder of the Mughal dynasty, who is buried there. The garden is:
context: Babur conquered Kabul in 1504 and India in 1526; he asked to be buried in his Kabul garden, not in India. 'Bagh-e Babur' means 'Babur's Gardens.'

question: In Lahore, Pakistan, stands a red-sandstone Mughal mosque built in 1673 — at the time the largest mosque in the world. It is called:
context: Commissioned by Aurangzeb. Its courtyard could hold 95,000 worshippers; for over 300 years it was the world's largest mosque.

question: A 73-meter red-sandstone victory tower built starting in 1192 stands in southern Delhi. It is called:
context: Built by Qutb al-Din Aibak to mark the start of Muslim rule in northern India. It is the tallest brick minaret in the world.

question: In Jaipur, India, an 18th-century maharaja built a complex of enormous stone instruments to measure time, the sun's position, and the heavens. It is called:
context: Built by Sawai Jai Singh II from 1727 to 1734. Its 27-meter sundial is the largest in the world, accurate to two seconds.

question: Mumbai's main railway station, completed in 1887, is a Victorian Gothic-Indian hybrid carved with monkeys and peacocks. It was renamed in 1996 for which Indian king?
context: Originally Victoria Terminus, renamed for the 17th-century Maratha warrior-king Shivaji Bhonsle. Designed by F. W. Stevens; UNESCO heritage since 2004.

question: In the hill capital of central Sri Lanka, a Buddhist temple complex houses what is believed to be a tooth relic of the Buddha himself. That city is:
context: The Sri Dalada Maligawa was built in the 16th-17th centuries. An annual procession, the Esala Perahera, parades a replica of the relic on elephants.

question: In Shanxi province, China, a small city retains its complete Ming-dynasty city walls, courtyard houses, and street plan. It is called:
context: Pingyao's 6-km wall from 1370 has 72 watchtowers. The city was a Qing-era banking center; UNESCO heritage since 1997.

question: The granite peaks, twisted pines, and seas of cloud of one Chinese mountain range have inspired ink painters for over a thousand years. It is called:
context: 'Huangshan' means 'Yellow Mountain.' It rises in Anhui province; its 'Welcoming Guests' pine, perhaps 1,500 years old, has appeared in countless paintings.

question: The main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty in Seoul, burned during Japanese invasions and rebuilt, sits beneath Bukhansan Mountain. It is called:
context: Built in 1395, destroyed in 1592, rebuilt in 1867, partly torn down by Japanese rulers in 1915, and now being restored. The throne hall, Geunjeongjeon, is among Korea's national treasures.

question: The Imperial Palace in central Tokyo sits inside the moats and walls of the former castle of the Tokugawa shoguns. That castle was:
context: Edo Castle's outer moat once enclosed much of central Tokyo. The current palace was rebuilt in 1968 after WWII bombing.

question: A massive 1583 castle in Osaka, Japan — central tower rebuilt in concrete after WWII — features gleaming gold-leaf decoration. It was built by:
context: Hideyoshi unified Japan in the late 16th century; his castle was destroyed in 1615, rebuilt in 1620, burned by lightning in 1665, and reconstructed in 1931.

question: In central Vietnam, the walled imperial citadel of the Nguyen emperors (1802-1945) lies on the north bank of the Perfume River. That city is:
context: Huế was Vietnam's capital from 1802 to 1945. The citadel, modeled on Beijing's Forbidden City, was heavily damaged in the 1968 Tet Offensive.

question: On Vietnam's central coast, a UNESCO-listed old port town fills its streets with colorful silk lanterns each month on the full moon. That town is:
context: Hội An was a trading port from the 15th-19th centuries with Japanese, Chinese, and Dutch quarters. The Japanese Covered Bridge (1593) still stands.

question: At a ruined temple in the former Siamese capital, the head of a stone Buddha statue rests cradled by the roots of a strangler-fig tree. The ruined capital is:
context: Ayutthaya was sacked by Burma in 1767; the temple ruins were swallowed by jungle. The Buddha head at Wat Mahathat is a famous photograph.

question: Each dawn in this former royal capital of Laos, saffron-robed monks walk silently along the streets receiving food from kneeling residents. That ceremony, and the town, are:
context: Luang Prabang has dozens of temples; the alms-giving ceremony has gone on continuously for centuries. UNESCO heritage since 1995.

question: Northern Thailand's largest city has a square moated and walled old center founded in 1296 by King Mengrai. It is:
context: Chiang Mai was the capital of the Lan Na kingdom. The old city is a 1.5-km square with corner bastions and four gates.

question: In Yangon, Myanmar, an enormous Buddhist stupa rises 99 m above the city. Its dome covering is:
answer: Solid gold plates, capped with diamonds
choices: Solid gold plates, capped with diamonds
Painted yellow stucco with brass studs
Gilded wood carvings on copper sheets
context: The Shwedagon Pagoda's tip carries a 76-carat diamond. Devout Burmese add gold leaf to its base; tens of tons of gold cover the structure.

question: From 1998 to 2004, the world's tallest buildings were twin towers connected by a sky bridge in the capital of Malaysia. They are:
context: 452 meters tall. Designed by Argentine-American architect César Pelli; the floor plan is based on Islamic geometric patterns.

question: On Bali's southwestern tip, a Hindu temple perches on a 70-meter sea cliff above the Indian Ocean, watched over by mischievous macaques. It is:
context: Built in the 11th century by the Javanese priest Empu Kuturan; one of Bali's six 'sea temples' guarding the island.

question: On Casablanca's Atlantic shore stands one of the largest mosques in the world, built partly on a platform over the ocean. Its minaret is:
answer: 210 meters tall, with a laser pointing toward Mecca
choices: 210 meters tall, with a laser pointing toward Mecca
75 meters tall, finished in red sandstone
120 meters tall, plated in gold leaf
300 meters tall, modeled on a lighthouse
context: Completed in 1993. The minaret is the world's tallest religious minaret; a green laser at the top points toward Mecca.

question: Founded in 670 AD by Arab armies, the first major Islamic city in North Africa lies in central Tunisia and houses the Great Mosque of Uqba. That city is:
context: Kairouan was a major center of Islamic learning. Its Great Mosque, rebuilt in 836, is considered the fourth holiest in Sunni Islam after Mecca, Medina, and Jerusalem.

question: The ancient northern Ethiopian kingdom of Aksum erected giant single-block stone obelisks (steles) to mark royal tombs. The tallest fell long ago but its replica stands. The tallest standing one is:
context: Aksum's largest obelisk fell during erection around 350 AD. The 24-m King Ezana's stele still stands; Italy looted another in 1937 and returned it in 2008.

question: In eastern Ethiopia, a small walled medieval Muslim city of 368 alleys and 82 mosques is famous for its hyenas being hand-fed at dusk. It is:
context: Harar Jugol is considered the fourth holiest city in Islam by some traditions. The hyena feeders have done so for over a century.

question: Just off Senegal's capital lies a small island whose 'House of Slaves' with its 'Door of No Return' is a memorial to the transatlantic slave trade. The capital is:
context: Gorée Island was used by European traders from the 15th-19th centuries. The House of Slaves was built in 1776 by the Dutch.

question: On a Tanzanian island in the Indian Ocean, a coral-stone old town of Arab merchants made fortunes from cloves and slaves. That town is:
context: Stone Town was the capital of the Sultanate of Zanzibar (1856-1964). Freddie Mercury was born there in 1946.

question: Madagascar's capital sits at 1,280 m in the central highlands, surrounded by terraced rice paddies. Its name in Malagasy means 'city of the thousand,' and the city is:
context: The 'thousand' refers to the warriors of King Andrianjaka who garrisoned the hill in 1610. Locals call it 'Tana.'

question: Walking through Boston, a 4-km red brick line in the sidewalk links 16 historic sites of the American Revolution. The line is called:
context: Created in 1951. Stops include Paul Revere's house, the Old North Church, the Bunker Hill monument, and the USS Constitution.

question: The red-brick Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia is where both the Declaration of Independence (1776) and the U.S. Constitution (1787) were debated and signed. It is now called:
context: Built 1732-1753. UNESCO heritage since 1979 — the only such site in the U.S. east of Yellowstone.

question: Atop Mount Hollywood in Los Angeles sits a free public observatory donated by a mining magnate in 1935. It is called:
context: Built with funds from Griffith J. Griffith, who also donated the surrounding park. It has hosted millions of visitors and appeared in films from 'Rebel Without a Cause' to 'La La Land.'

question: In San Francisco Bay, a small rocky island held a federal maximum-security prison from 1934 to 1963. It is called:
context: Spanish for 'pelican.' Famous inmates included Al Capone and the Birdman of Alcatraz. Closed because rusting salt-air infrastructure made it too costly.

question: On a peninsula jutting from downtown Vancouver, a 405-hectare public park preserves temperate rainforest with cedars over 800 years old. The park is:
context: Designated a park in 1888. Larger than New York's Central Park and almost entirely native forest, ringed by a 10-km seawall.

question: The only walled city in North America north of Mexico stands on a cliff over the St. Lawrence River. It is:
context: Founded by Samuel de Champlain in 1608. The 4.6-km walls were built and rebuilt by French, British, and Canadian governments. UNESCO heritage since 1985.

question: On Colombia's Caribbean coast, a walled colonial port city built by the Spanish to defend treasure shipments houses fortresses, plazas, and pastel houses. It is:
context: Founded in 1533. The 11-km walls and the Castillo San Felipe de Barajas fortress (1657) made it one of the most heavily fortified cities in the Americas.

question: Ecuador's capital sits at 2,850 m elevation in an Andean valley and has one of the largest, best-preserved colonial old towns in the Americas. It is:
context: Quito was the first city to be inscribed on the UNESCO list (1978, along with Krakow). The equator runs just north of the city.

question: On the world's highest navigable lake, the Uros people live on islands they build themselves from a buoyant lake reed. The lake is:
context: Lake Titicaca sits at 3,812 m between Peru and Bolivia. Totora reeds form the islands' foundation; the Uros replenish the surface as it rots.

question: Deep in the Brazilian Amazon, a Belle Époque opera house with European materials and a glazed-tile dome was built during the late 19th-century rubber boom. The city is:
context: The Teatro Amazonas opened in 1896. Manaus is over 1,500 km from the Atlantic but reachable by ocean ships up the Amazon River.

question: Chile's capital sits in a long central valley with the snow-capped Andes rising sharply on its eastern edge. The eastern range tops out near the city at:
context: El Plomo is the high peak visible from downtown Santiago. Aconcagua (the western hemisphere's highest peak) is across the border in Argentina.

question: Ushuaia means 'bay penetrating westward' in the language of the original inhabitants. They were the:
context: The Yámana lived around the Beagle Channel. The neighboring Selk'nam inhabited the larger island; both groups were devastated by European contact in the late 19th century.

question: New Zealand's capital sits on a harbor between hills in Cook Strait and is often called the windiest capital city in the world. It is:
context: Wellington averages over 170 days a year with winds above 60 km/h. The 'Roaring Forties' funnel through Cook Strait between the North and South Islands.

question: Melbourne's grid of central streets is laced with narrow lanes once neglected and now lined with cafés, bars, and street art. These passageways are called:
context: Melbourne's laneway revival started in the 1990s; the city now claims the world's strongest coffee culture, descended from Italian immigrants.

question: On New Zealand's South Island, a town on Lake Wakatipu pioneered commercial bungee jumping in 1988 from a 43-meter bridge. It is:
context: A. J. Hackett opened the Kawarau Bridge Bungy after testing the cord by jumping from the Eiffel Tower. Bungee jumping itself comes from Vanuatu's Pentecost Island land-diving.

question: Sydney's steel-arch bridge of 1932, nicknamed 'the coathanger' for its silhouette, was at the time the world's:
context: Designed by John Bradfield; the arch spans 503 m. Climbers can now walk to the top, 134 m above the water.

question: Georgia's capital sits in a Caucasus valley and is named for the hot sulfur springs that still feed its 17th-century brick-domed bathhouses. That capital is:
context: 'Tbili' is Georgian for 'warm.' King Vakhtang Gorgasali founded the city around 458 AD after his hawk fell into a hot spring.

question: Armenia's capital sits in a plain with a clear view of a snow-capped twin-peaked mountain across the Turkish border. That mountain is:
context: Ararat is the national symbol of Armenia though it lies in Turkey today. The biblical tradition says Noah's Ark landed there after the Flood.

question: Berlin's neoclassical city gate, modeled on the Athenian Propylaea, was completed in 1791. After the Wall fell, it became a symbol of reunification. It is called:
context: Designed by Carl Gotthard Langhans. The bronze quadriga atop it was looted by Napoleon and recovered after Waterloo.

question: In central Helsinki, a Lutheran church carved directly into a granite outcrop with a copper dome roof was completed in 1969. It is called:
context: Designed by brothers Timo and Tuomo Suomalainen. Locally called the 'Rock Church.' The rough granite walls give remarkable acoustics; concerts are held there regularly.

question: On a rock at Copenhagen's harbor entrance sits a small bronze statue of a Hans Christian Andersen character, unveiled in 1913. The character is:
context: Sculpted by Edvard Eriksen, paid for by Carlsberg's son. She has been vandalized many times — decapitated twice — and replaced each time.

question: St. Petersburg's enormous green-and-white art museum spans five buildings including the former Winter Palace of the tsars. It is called:
context: Founded in 1764 by Catherine the Great with 225 paintings. It now holds over 3 million items; the Winter Palace alone has 1,500 rooms.

question: Bosnia's capital hosted the Winter Olympics in 1984 — eight years before becoming the site of the longest siege of a capital city in modern history. That city is:
context: Sarajevo was besieged from April 1992 to February 1996. The Olympic bobsled track on Mount Trebević still stands, bullet-pocked, in the forest above the city.

question: An elegant 16th-century Ottoman stone arch bridge in Bosnia spans the green Neretva River and was destroyed in 1993, then rebuilt in 2004. It is:
answer: The Stari Most (Old Bridge) of Mostar
choices: The Stari Most (Old Bridge) of Mostar
context: Built by Ottoman architect Mimar Hayruddin in 1566. The bridge is the namesake of the city — 'Mostar' comes from 'mostari,' the bridge keepers.

question: One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World stood at the entrance to Alexandria's harbor in Egypt and gave its name to the kind of structure built since. It was:
context: Built around 280 BC on the island of Pharos. Likely 100+ m tall; brought down by earthquakes between 956 and 1323 AD.

question: On the east bank of the Nile in southern Egypt lies the largest ancient religious complex ever constructed — pharaohs added to it for 2,000 years. It is at:
context: Karnak lies just north of Luxor. The Great Hypostyle Hall has 134 columns, the largest 21 m tall. The complex covers about 100 hectares.

question: In central Taipei stands a vast white-walled, blue-tiled memorial hall to the founder of the Republic of China on Taiwan. He was:
context: Completed in 1980. Chiang led the Nationalist government from mainland China to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the civil war to Mao's communists.

question: Until 2018, Tokyo's main wholesale fish auction took place at a giant market that has traded individual tuna for millions of dollars. The market site was at:
context: Tsukiji opened in 1935. The wholesale auction moved to Toyosu in 2018; the outer Tsukiji market of restaurants and shops still operates at the original site.

question: On the northwest edge of Kyoto, a path winds through a green forest of bamboo so dense it almost blocks the sky. The district is:
context: Arashiyama means 'Storm Mountain.' The bamboo grove is part of a larger temple complex and was a favored aristocratic retreat in the Heian period.

question: Havana's 8-km seafront promenade and seawall, built starting in 1901, draws strollers, lovers, and fishermen each evening. It is called:
context: The Malecón is battered by Atlantic waves crashing over the wall in winter storms. Lined with Spanish colonial and Art Deco buildings, slowly being restored.

question: In southern Peru, a colonial city below volcanoes is built almost entirely of a white volcanic stone called sillar. It is:
context: Arequipa sits at 2,335 m below the snow-capped El Misti volcano. The Santa Catalina Monastery is a small painted city within the city.

question: In Paris, glass-roofed shopping arcades from the early 19th century survive as gaslit passages — precursors to the modern shopping mall. They are called:
context: About 20 passages survive of the 150+ that existed in 1850. The Passage des Panoramas (1799) is the oldest still operating.

question: Paris's largest cemetery, on a hill in the 20th arrondissement, holds the graves of Chopin, Wilde, Proust, Édith Piaf, and Jim Morrison. It is called:
context: Père Lachaise opened in 1804. Napoleon needed a cemetery outside the central city; transferring Molière's remains in 1817 made it fashionable.

question: Roman concrete used a volcanic ash that made the mix harden underwater and grow stronger over centuries. That ash came from:
choices: Cumae on the Bay of Naples
context: 'Pozzolana' is named for Pozzuoli, where Romans quarried it. Recent research shows lime clasts in the concrete self-heal cracks by reacting with water.

question: From 1891 to 1938, the founder of psychoanalysis lived and saw patients at Berggasse 19 in Vienna. He was:
context: Freud fled the Nazis in 1938 for London, where he died in 1939. His Vienna apartment is now a museum.

question: Sigmund Freud worked at Berggasse 19 in Vienna from 1891 until fleeing the Nazis. The famous psychoanalyst's couch from that consulting room is now displayed in:
answer: London (the Freud Museum at his final home)
choices: London (the Freud Museum at his final home)
context: Freud took the couch with him when he escaped to London in 1938. The Vienna apartment displays a replica.

question: On the Zambia-Zimbabwe border, the Zambezi River plunges 108 meters into a narrow gorge, raising a mist visible 40 km away. The local name means:
context: 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' in Lozi. David Livingstone reached it in 1855 and named it for Queen Victoria. It is the world's largest sheet of falling water.

question: Of the three falls at Niagara, the largest by volume is the curved one on the Canadian side. It is called:
context: About 90% of the Niagara River's flow goes over Horseshoe Falls. Its crest is 670 m wide and 51 m high.

question: The world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall plunges 979 meters from the top of a flat-topped sandstone mountain in Venezuela. It is named for:
context: Angel Falls (Kerepakupai Merú in Pemon) drops from Auyán-tepui. American aviator Jimmie Angel landed his plane there in 1937 and got it stuck on top.

question: By volume of water discharged, the world's largest river is in South America. It carries about what fraction of all river water reaching the sea?
context: The Amazon discharges about 209,000 cubic meters per second — more than the next seven largest rivers combined.

question: At Manaus, Brazil, two great Amazon tributaries flow side by side for kilometers without mixing — one dark, one tan. They are:
answer: The Rio Negro and the Solimões
choices: The Rio Negro and the Solimões
context: The Negro is acidic blackwater stained by leaf litter; the Solimões is silty whitewater from the Andes. Different temperature, density, and speed keep them separate.

question: The Nile is unusual among great rivers because it flows:
answer: South to north, from East Africa to the Mediterranean
choices: South to north, from East Africa to the Mediterranean
West to east, from West Africa to the Red Sea
North to south, from Sudan into Lake Victoria
Inland into the Sahara, never reaching any sea
context: The Nile runs 6,650 km north from sources in Burundi, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, and Ethiopia. The Blue Nile (Ethiopia) and White Nile (Lake Victoria) meet in Khartoum.

question: China's longest river drops through three steep gorges in the central reaches where the world's largest dam now stands. The river is:
context: The Yangtze is 6,300 km long, third in the world. The Three Gorges Dam reservoir displaced about 1.3 million people.

question: The lower Mississippi River winds through such tight curves that it occasionally cuts off loops, leaving crescent-shaped lakes behind. These lakes are called:
context: The Mississippi has thousands of oxbow lakes along its lower course. Riverboat pilots learned that any loop they passed today might be cut off by tomorrow.

question: Europe's second-longest river flows from the Black Forest to the Black Sea, passing through more countries than any other in the world. That number is:
context: The Danube touches Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova, and Ukraine. It passes four capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, Belgrade.

question: A great river of South Asia begins on the Tibetan plateau as the Yarlung Tsangpo, makes a stunning U-turn around the Himalayas, and flows southwest into Bangladesh. It is the:
context: The Great Bend of the Tsangpo is one of the deepest gorges on Earth. After the U-turn, the river is called the Brahmaputra in Assam and the Jamuna in Bangladesh.

question: In southern Siberia, a crescent-shaped lake between mountain ranges holds about one-fifth of all unfrozen freshwater on Earth. It is also the world's:
context: Lake Baikal is roughly 25-30 million years old and 1,642 m deep. It holds more water than all five North American Great Lakes combined.

question: By surface area, the largest freshwater lake on Earth lies on the U.S.-Canada border. It is:
context: Lake Superior covers 82,100 km² — larger than Austria. Its volume is exceeded by Baikal and Tanganyika, but its area is the world's largest for freshwater.

question: Straddling the Peru-Bolivia border at 3,812 meters elevation lies a 190-km-long lake big enough for steamboats. It is:
context: Lake Titicaca is the highest navigable lake in the world. The Inca creation myth says the sun, moon, and the first humans rose from its waters.

question: The second-deepest lake in the world is a long narrow rift lake in East Africa, bordered by four countries and home to hundreds of unique cichlid fish. It is:
context: Tanganyika reaches 1,470 m deep and stretches 670 km. Burundi, DR Congo, Tanzania, and Zambia share its shores.

question: Africa's largest lake by surface area straddles Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania, and is the source of the White Nile. It is:
context: Lake Victoria is 68,800 km² — roughly the size of Ireland. John Hanning Speke named it for Queen Victoria in 1858 when he identified the Nile source.

question: On the southern edge of the Sahara, a once-huge lake straddling four countries has shrunk by about 90% since 1960. It is:
context: Lake Chad lost most of its area through a combination of drought and upstream irrigation. About 30 million people depend on its basin.

question: Between Israel and Jordan, a salt lake sits in the deepest land depression on Earth, where the salinity is so high humans float without effort. The shore lies at:
context: The Dead Sea surface is the lowest dry land on Earth. Its salinity (about 34%) is roughly ten times that of ordinary seawater.

question: The largest inland body of water on Earth, sometimes classified as a lake and sometimes as a sea, lies between Russia, Iran, and several other countries. It is the:
context: The Caspian is 371,000 km², larger than Germany. Slightly salty (about 1.2%). Five countries share its shores: Russia, Iran, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan.

question: Once the fourth-largest lake on Earth, this Central Asian sea was reduced to a fraction of its former size after Soviet irrigation diverted its rivers for cotton fields. It is:
context: The Amu Darya and Syr Darya were diverted starting in the 1960s. By 2014 the southern Aral had largely dried up, leaving a salt desert with stranded ships.

question: In Oregon, an intense deep-blue lake fills a 600-meter-deep caldera formed by an ancient eruption that destroyed Mount Mazama. It is:
context: Mazama erupted about 7,700 years ago. Crater Lake has no inlets or outlets; its blue color comes from extreme water clarity scattering blue light.

question: In southwestern Bolivia, the world's largest salt flat — 10,500 square kilometers of bright white crust — becomes a mirror reflecting the sky when a thin film of rain pools on it. It is:
context: The Salar holds an estimated 21 billion tons of salt and one of the world's largest lithium reserves. It sits at 3,656 m elevation.

question: A shallow alkaline lake in northern Tanzania can turn deep red and is so chemically harsh that animals that die there are sometimes calcified. It is:
context: Natron's water carries sodium carbonate from volcanic sources; pH up to 10.5. Lesser flamingos breed there in millions — they tolerate the chemistry.

question: The first confirmed ascent of Mount Everest was made on 29 May 1953 by:
context: Mallory and Irvine disappeared near the summit in 1924; Mallory's body was found in 1999, but whether he reached the top is still debated.

question: Africa's highest mountain rises freestanding from the Tanzanian plains and is made up of three volcanic cones: Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira. It is:
context: Kibo (the highest) is dormant; Mawenzi and Shira are extinct. The summit Uhuru Peak is 5,895 m. The summit glaciers have shrunk by ~85% since 1912.

question: North America's highest peak, 6,190 m tall, was renamed in 2015 from McKinley to its older indigenous name. It is:
context: 'Denali' means 'the high one' in Koyukon Athabascan. The peak's prominence above the surrounding plains is greater than Everest's.

question: The highest mountain outside Asia stands in western Argentina at 6,961 m. It is:
context: Aconcagua is the highest peak in the western and southern hemispheres. Its name probably means 'stone sentinel' in Quechua.

question: A near-perfect pyramid of rock on the Swiss-Italian border has four distinct faces, each carved by a different glacier. It is:
context: The Matterhorn (4,478 m) was first climbed in 1865 by Edward Whymper's party; four men died on the descent. Its silhouette adorns Toblerone chocolate.

question: In western Tibet rises a black pyramid mountain considered sacred by four religions and never climbed by humans. It is:
context: Sacred in Hinduism (Shiva's home), Buddhism (Demchok), Jainism (Rishabhanatha's nirvana), and Bön. China has refused all climbing permits out of respect for the religions.

question: The Himalayas are still rising, by several millimeters a year, because two plates of the Earth's crust continue to collide. They are:
answer: The Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate
choices: The Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate
The Pacific Plate and the North American Plate
The Nazca Plate and the South American Plate
The African Plate and the Arabian Plate
context: The collision began about 50 million years ago. India still drives northward at about 5 cm a year, fueling earthquakes and uplift.

question: The world's longest continental mountain range runs the length of South America for about:
context: The Andes stretch from Venezuela through Argentina. Volcanic, tectonically active; they rose as the Nazca Plate dives beneath the South American Plate.

question: Eastern North America's mountains were once as tall as the Himalayas but have eroded for hundreds of millions of years. They are the:
context: The Appalachians formed about 480 million years ago. The Scottish Highlands, the Atlas Mountains, and the Norwegian fjords were once part of the same range before Pangaea broke up.

question: Southern Africa's tallest mountain range — a great basalt escarpment of cliffs and rolling plateaus — forms the eastern wall of Lesotho. It is the:
context: 'Dragon Mountains' in Afrikaans. The escarpment is the eroded eastern edge of the African Plateau, capped with lava 180 million years old.

question: The conventional dividing line between Europe and Asia is a low north-south mountain range in Russia. It is the:
context: The Urals run 2,500 km from the Arctic Ocean to Kazakhstan. The highest peak, Mount Narodnaya, is only 1,895 m.

question: The world's largest hot desert covers about 9 million square kilometers of North Africa. Rock paintings show it was last green about:
context: Earth's axial wobble shifts monsoon rainfall north and south; the 'African Humid Period' ended ~5,500 years ago. Tassili n'Ajjer rock art depicts cattle herders, hippos, and swimmers in the Sahara.

question: In northern Chile lies the driest non-polar desert on Earth, where some weather stations have never recorded rain. It is the:
context: The Atacama lies in a double rain shadow between the Andes and coastal range, with cold Humboldt Current air offshore. NASA tests Mars rovers there.

question: Along southwestern Africa's Atlantic coast stretches a desert thought to be the oldest on Earth — at least 55 million years dry. It is the:
context: The Namib runs 2,000 km along the coast. Its name means 'vast place' in Khoekhoegowab; it gave Namibia its name.

question: On Namibia's foggy Atlantic shore, where the desert meets the cold ocean, the remains of dozens of shipwrecks lie partly buried in sand. The locals call it:
context: Cold Benguela Current air meets hot desert air, creating fog. The fog and currents drove ships ashore; many crews died crossing the desert toward help.

question: The vast arid interior of Australia is colored a distinctive red by iron oxide weathering. The classic image of this region's heart is:
context: Uluru is a 348-m sandstone monolith sacred to the Anangu people. Its color comes from oxidized iron in the rock.

question: The northern lights — green, red, purple curtains in high-latitude skies — are caused by:
answer: Solar wind particles striking the upper atmosphere
choices: Solar wind particles striking the upper atmosphere
Methane plumes burning in cold air
context: Charged solar particles funnel along Earth's magnetic field to the poles and excite atmospheric oxygen (green/red) and nitrogen (blue/purple) atoms.

question: On the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard, a vault carved into permafrost holds backup samples of crop seeds from around the world. It is called:
context: Opened in 2008 at Longyearbyen. The vault holds over a million seed samples; depositors include nearly every country with crop breeding.

question: In southern Argentina, a 250-square-kilometer glacier ends in a 70-meter-tall ice wall that calves icebergs into a lake with thunderous cracks. It is:
context: One of few glaciers in the world not retreating. It periodically advances across Lake Argentino, forming an ice dam that eventually bursts.

question: The tallest trees on Earth grow along a narrow strip of coastal northern California. They are:
context: The tallest known living tree, 'Hyperion,' is 115.9 m. Coast redwoods rely on Pacific fog for summer moisture.

question: The largest living tree on Earth by volume is a giant sequoia in California's Sierra Nevada, named for a Civil War general. It is:
context: General Sherman is in Sequoia National Park, ~84 m tall and 11 m wide at the base. Estimated 2,200-2,700 years old.

question: In Utah, a single quaking aspen organism shares one root system across about 43 hectares and 47,000 stems. It is named:
context: 'Pando' means 'I spread' in Latin. It may be one of the heaviest organisms on Earth, ~6,000 tonnes. Its age is debated — possibly 14,000 years or older.

question: On Madagascar's western coast, a dirt road runs between rows of massive bottle-shaped trees up to 30 meters tall. They are:
context: The Avenue of the Baobabs near Morondava has about 20 Adansonia grandidieri trees, 800+ years old. Six baobab species are endemic to Madagascar.

question: On a Yemeni island in the Indian Ocean grow umbrella-shaped trees whose red sap was once used as a dye and medicine. They are:
context: Socotra Island has many endemic plants. The dragon's blood tree (Dracaena cinnabari) gets its name from the crimson resin that drips from cuts in its bark.

question: In Japan, the pink flowers of cherry trees bloom for only about a week each spring. The intense national celebration of viewing them is called:
context: Hanami means 'flower viewing.' The Japan Meteorological Agency tracks the cherry-blossom front (sakura zensen) as it moves north each spring.

question: Off the California and Pacific coasts grow underwater forests of giant brown seaweed that can extend 60 meters from seafloor to surface. They are:
context: Giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) grows up to 60 cm a day, among the fastest growth on Earth. Sea otters keep kelp forests healthy by eating sea urchins.

question: The deepest point in the world's oceans lies in the western Pacific in a U-shaped trench reaching almost:
context: The Challenger Deep is about 10,935 m down. Pressure there is over 1,000 times atmospheric. Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh first descended in 1960.

question: The Pacific Ocean is so large that its surface area is greater than:
answer: All the dry land on Earth combined
choices: All the dry land on Earth combined
The Atlantic and Indian oceans combined
All the freshwater on Earth combined
All other oceans plus the polar caps
context: The Pacific covers about 165 million km²; Earth's total land is about 149 million km². Magellan named it 'pacific' (peaceful) after a calm crossing.

question: Western Europe's mild climate compared with other places at the same latitude is partly explained by an Atlantic ocean current. It is:
context: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Caribbean northeast across the Atlantic. Without it, London (at the latitude of Calgary) would be much colder.

question: The largest structure built by living organisms on Earth stretches 2,300 km along Australia's northeast coast. It is:
context: The Great Barrier Reef is made of corals — colonies of tiny polyps. Its scale is so large that it is visible from space.

question: On the Canadian east coast, the highest tides on Earth — over 16 meters between low and high — wash the shores of:
context: The Bay of Fundy lies between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Its funnel shape and resonant period amplify ordinary tides into a wall of water.

question: In the middle of the North Atlantic, currents enclose a calm warm sea bounded not by land but by water, with floating mats of brown seaweed. It is:
context: Sargassum seaweed gives the sea its name. The Sargasso is the only sea on Earth with no land coast. American and European eels travel thousands of kilometers to breed there.

question: Hot calcium-rich water flows over a Turkish hillside, depositing dazzling-white terraces and pools. It is called:
context: 'Pamukkale' means 'cotton castle' in Turkish. The Roman city Hierapolis was built on top, drawn by the thermal waters.

question: On Northern Ireland's Antrim coast, 40,000 columns of black basalt fit together in mostly hexagonal patterns — the leftovers of an ancient lava flow. It is:
context: The columns formed 50-60 million years ago when lava cooled and contracted. Legend says the giant Finn MacCool built a stone path across to Scotland.

question: On the Scottish island of Staffa, a sea cave with the same hexagonal basalt columns as the Giant's Causeway inspired Felix Mendelssohn's overture of 1830. The cave is:
context: Mendelssohn visited Staffa in 1829. The basalt columns were once part of the same flow as those at Giant's Causeway, 130 km away.

question: In northeastern Wyoming, a 264-meter steep-sided butte of vertical columns rises from the prairie. It became the first U.S. National Monument in 1906. It is:
context: Devils Tower is an igneous intrusion (cooled magma) exposed by erosion. The Lakota call it Mato Tipila ('Bear Lodge'). Featured in 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind.'

question: On the Philippine island of Bohol, over 1,200 grass-covered cone-shaped limestone hills cover an area of 50 square kilometers. They turn brown in the dry season, giving them their name. They are:
context: The hills are 30-50 m high. Their origin is debated — likely uplifted marine limestone weathered by rain and groundwater over millions of years.

question: A flat-topped sandstone mountain at the corner of Venezuela, Brazil, and Guyana sits above the surrounding jungle like an island in the sky. It is:
context: Roraima is a tepui (Pemon for 'house of the gods'). Conan Doyle's 'The Lost World' was inspired by it. The summit hosts unique plants and frogs found nowhere else.

question: Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni, beyond being a striking salt flat, also holds one of the world's largest reserves of an element used in modern batteries. That element is:
context: Estimates put 21+ million tonnes of lithium in the Salar's brines. Extraction is contested between economic gain and protecting the visual wonder.

question: When you see a double rainbow, the dark band of sky between the two bows has a name and is real. It is called:
context: Named after Alexander of Aphrodisias, who described it around 200 AD. The secondary rainbow has reversed color order because light bounces twice inside the raindrops.

question: Two bright spots flanking the sun on cold mornings, often with prismatic color, are caused by sunlight refracted through ice crystals. They are called:
context: Also called parhelia. They sit 22° on either side of the sun, formed when sunlight passes through hexagonal ice crystals oriented horizontally in cold air.

question: The reliable easterly winds blowing toward the equator from each hemisphere are named for their use by sailing ships. They are called:
context: Caribbean sugar and slave ships rode the trades to and from the Old World. The word 'trade' comes from Middle English 'trade' meaning 'a track' — winds that 'blow trade,' i.e., on a steady track.

question: On the eastern slope of the Rockies, a warm dry wind can melt deep snow in hours by descending and compressing. Locals call it:
context: Chinook winds can raise temperatures by 30°C in an hour. Similar winds elsewhere: Föhn in the Alps, Zonda in Argentina.

question: From December to March, a dry dusty wind blows from the Sahara across West Africa, sometimes carrying sand as far as the Caribbean. It is called:
context: Visibility can drop to a few hundred meters in the Harmattan. The same dust feeds nutrients to the Amazon rainforest after crossing the Atlantic.

question: An Egyptian hot dry south wind that blows in spring is named for the approximate number of days it lasts each year. That number is:
context: 'Khamsin' comes from the Arabic 'khamsīn,' meaning fifty. The wind can lift temperatures by 20°C in hours and carry choking sand. Compare the Sirocco (Italy), Ghibli (Libya).

question: On the Hvítá River in southwest Iceland, a famous two-tiered waterfall plunges 32 meters into a deep canyon, often crowned by rainbows. It is called:
context: 'Gullfoss' means 'golden falls.' Part of Iceland's 'Golden Circle' tourist route. The 'gull' refers to brown river sediments that glint like gold in the sun.

question: By volume of water plunging over its edge, Europe's most powerful waterfall is in northeast Iceland. It is:
context: Dettifoss is 100 m wide and drops 44 m, with an average flow of 193 m³/s. Featured in the opening scene of the film 'Prometheus.'

question: In central Croatia, 16 turquoise lakes stair-step through forested limestone, connected by countless small waterfalls. The lakes are:
context: Travertine dams between the lakes grow about 1 cm a year as calcium carbonate precipitates from the water. UNESCO heritage since 1979.

question: Deep in the Grand Canyon, a tributary plunges over red cliffs into vivid turquoise pools. The waterfall is on the:
context: Havasu Falls drops 30 m. The blue-green color comes from dissolved limestone minerals scattering blue light, just like a tropical lagoon.

question: Two great rivers flowing from eastern Turkey through Iraq enclose the plain where the first cities appeared more than 5,000 years ago. They are the:
context: 'Mesopotamia' means 'between the rivers' in Greek. Sumer, Akkad, Babylon, and Assyria all rose in this fertile plain.

question: The Indus River in Pakistan is home to a rare blind freshwater dolphin that uses echolocation to hunt in murky water. The dolphin is:
context: About 2,000 Indus river dolphins remain. They are functionally blind; the silty Indus made eyes useless, so they 'see' with sound.

question: Across western North America runs a high ridge separating waters flowing to the Pacific from waters flowing to the Atlantic or Arctic. It is called:
context: The Continental Divide follows the Rockies for most of its length. A raindrop falling on one side will reach a different ocean from one falling on the other.

question: Some inland basins have no river outlet to the sea — water flows in and only escapes by evaporation. A classic example is:
context: Such basins are called 'endorheic.' The Caspian Sea, Aral Sea, Great Salt Lake, and Dead Sea all sit in endorheic basins, where salts concentrate over time.

question: Norway's western coast is cut by deep glacier-carved inlets where the sea reaches inland for up to 200 km between cliff walls. These are called:
context: Glaciers carved U-shaped valleys during the ice ages; when seas rose, the sea filled them. Sognefjord runs 205 km inland and reaches 1,308 m deep.

question: Discovered in 1991 in central Vietnam, the world's largest known cave by cross-section contains its own jungle, river, and clouds. It is:
context: Son Doong's main passage is up to 200 m tall and 150 m wide. Sunlight enters through ceiling collapses ('dolines') and sustains the inner forest.

question: Above the Arctic Circle, around the summer solstice, the sun does not set for at least 24 hours. The most northerly inhabited town with this phenomenon is:
context: Longyearbyen has continuous daylight from late April to late August. The corresponding winter polar night lasts from October to February.

question: On certain beaches and bays — in Puerto Rico, the Maldives, parts of Jamaica — the water glows blue when disturbed at night. The light comes from:
context: Pyrodinium and Noctiluca dinoflagellates flash chemically when jolted, perhaps to startle predators. Concentrations of millions per liter can light a bay.

question: In a cave on New Zealand's North Island, the ceiling glows with thousands of greenish lights from the larvae of a fungus gnat — endemic to New Zealand. The caves are:
context: Arachnocampa luminosa larvae hang sticky silk threads to trap prey, attracting insects with their light. Waitomo means 'water passing through a hole.'

question: In central Australia, a single red sandstone monolith 348 meters high and 9.4 km around rises from the desert plain. It is:
context: Uluru is sacred to the Anangu Aboriginal people, who tell its stories in the Tjukurpa creation tradition. Climbing was permitted until 2019; it is now banned.

question: On the Utah-Arizona border, isolated red sandstone buttes rise from a flat desert floor. The valley sits within the Navajo Nation and is famous as the setting of countless Western films. It is:
context: John Ford's 'Stagecoach' (1939) and 'The Searchers' (1956) made the valley iconic. The buttes are remnants of an eroded sandstone plateau.

question: In Western Australia, a granite outcrop curves outward in a perfect 15-meter wave shape. It is called:
context: Wave Rock formed 2.7 billion years ago. The 'wave' was carved when groundwater chemically weathered the rock at ground level; later erosion exposed the curved cliff.

question: Some 50 km from Uluru rise 36 weathered red domes sacred to the Anangu and dramatic at sunset. They are called:
context: 'Kata Tjuta' means 'many heads' in Pitjantjatjara. Mount Olga (Kata Tjuta's highest dome) is 546 m above the plain — taller than Uluru.

question: On Navajo land in Arizona, a narrow slot canyon carved through red sandstone by flash floods is famous for shafts of light beaming down at midday. It is:
context: Antelope Canyon is in two sections, Upper and Lower. The walls are smoothed by water; visitors must enter with Navajo guides only.

question: The iceberg that sank the Titanic in 1912 calved from a glacier in:
context: Most North Atlantic icebergs come from Greenland's tidewater glaciers, especially the Jakobshavn (Sermeq Kujalleq) Glacier. The International Ice Patrol was founded in 1914 in response.

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing. It was built as the tomb of:
context: Khufu's pyramid was built around 2560 BC. At 146.6 m tall, it was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years.

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza is precisely aligned to the four cardinal directions to within a small fraction of a degree. The Egyptians achieved this using:
answer: Stellar observations of the north star region
choices: Stellar observations of the north star region
context: Egypt had no compass; alignment used circumpolar stars. The pyramid's sides face north, south, east, west with an error of about 0.05 degrees.

question: The Great Sphinx at Giza is the largest monolithic statue on Earth and dates from roughly:
context: Most scholars date the Sphinx to the reign of Pharaoh Khafre (~2558-2532 BC). It is 73 m long and was carved from a single outcrop of limestone.

question: In November 1922 in Egypt's Valley of the Kings, archaeologist Howard Carter peered through a hole and saw 'wonderful things.' The tomb he had found belonged to:
context: Tutankhamun, a minor pharaoh who died around 1323 BC at age 18, had been all but forgotten. His tomb was found nearly intact — over 5,000 objects packed into four small rooms.

question: At Persepolis in southern Iran, two grand stone staircases of the Apadana audience hall are carved with reliefs of tribute-bearers from 23 nations. The empire that built them was:
context: Begun by Darius I around 518 BC. The reliefs depict Medes, Lydians, Bactrians, Ethiopians, Indians, and others bringing gifts to the Persian king.

question: The blue-glazed-tile Ishtar Gate, decorated with bulls and dragons, once stood as an entrance to ancient Babylon. The reconstructed gate now stands in a museum in:
context: German archaeologists excavated and reconstructed the gate in the 1930s. The original glazed bricks were dated to about 575 BC, under Nebuchadnezzar II.

question: In southern Iraq stand the partly reconstructed remains of an enormous stepped temple-platform built by the Sumerians around 2100 BC. The city was:
context: The Great Ziggurat of Ur was built for the moon god Nanna by King Ur-Nammu. Abraham, in the biblical tradition, came from this city.

question: On Crete stand the remains of a 1500 BC palace covering 20,000 square meters, decorated with frescoes of leaping bulls. The civilization is the:
context: British archaeologist Arthur Evans excavated Knossos starting in 1900 and named the civilization for the legendary King Minos.

question: The ancient Greeks considered the temple at Delphi the navel of the world. Their word for that center-stone was:
context: A carved stone at Delphi marked the spot. According to myth, Zeus released two eagles from opposite ends of the world; they met at Delphi.

question: At Olympia in Greece stood a 12-meter-tall ivory-and-gold statue of Zeus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Its sculptor was:
context: The statue (c. 435 BC) was destroyed in late antiquity. Phidias also designed the Parthenon's chryselephantine Athena statue in Athens.

question: The Roman city of Pompeii, near modern Naples, was buried by an eruption of Mount Vesuvius in:
context: Pliny the Younger described the eruption in a letter to Tacitus. Pyroclastic flows killed an estimated 2,000 people in Pompeii alone; ash preserved the city.

question: The Colosseum in Rome could be flooded for mock naval battles called:
context: The arena floor was wooden and could be removed; pumps filled the space. The practice was discontinued when the basement (hypogeum) was added under it.

question: Rome's Pantheon, rebuilt by the emperor Hadrian around 126 AD, holds a record it has kept for almost 1,900 years. Its dome is:
answer: The largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth
choices: The largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth
The oldest building still in active use
The first building made of iron beams
The tallest classical column in Italy
context: The dome is 43.3 m in diameter and 43.3 m high. Modern engineers find it hard to replicate; Roman concrete used pozzolana volcanic ash for strength.

question: Roman aqueducts brought clean water to cities over long distances using a remarkable feat of engineering: maintained gradient. The Pont du Gard in southern France drops by:
answer: About 1 cm per 100 m over its full length
choices: About 1 cm per 100 m over its full length
About 1 m per 10 m (a steep slope)
About 1 km over its 50 km length
context: The Pont du Gard is the tallest surviving Roman aqueduct (49 m). The full aqueduct ran 50 km from Uzès to Nîmes with a 17-m total drop.

question: The Roman road system began in 312 BC with a single highway running south from Rome. It was named for the official who built it:
context: The Via Appia eventually reached Brindisi, 540 km from Rome. Romans called it 'queen of the long roads.' Sections are still walkable as cobbled paths.

question: The Great Library of Alexandria in Egypt may have held over 400,000 papyrus scrolls at its peak under the Ptolemies. The library mostly perished by:
answer: A combination of fires, decay, and budget collapse over centuries
choices: A combination of fires, decay, and budget collapse over centuries
A single fire under Julius Caesar in 48 BC
Looting during the Arab conquest of 642 AD
Christian destruction in the 4th century AD
context: Modern scholarship sees the library's loss as gradual, not a single catastrophic event. Caesar's accidental fire, Aurelian's war, Theophilus' decree, and the Arab conquest all played parts.

question: On the Maltese island of Gozo stand stone temples older than the Egyptian pyramids — among the oldest free-standing monumental structures on Earth. They are:
context: Built around 3600-3200 BC. Their name comes from the Maltese for 'giants' — locals thought such large stones could only be lifted by giants.

question: The smaller 'bluestones' of Stonehenge, in southern England, were quarried and brought from a distant region. That region is:
answer: The Preseli Hills of Wales (about 240 km away)
choices: The Preseli Hills of Wales (about 240 km away)
context: The 80 bluestones each weigh 2-4 tonnes. The journey from Wales to Salisbury Plain by sled, river, and sea is one of the great mysteries of Neolithic Britain.

question: Stonehenge is precisely aligned with one celestial event each year. On that day, the sun rises directly over the Heel Stone, framed by the trilithons. The event is:
context: Sunrise on the summer solstice is the most-photographed view at Stonehenge. The site may also have been used for winter-solstice ceremonies looking the opposite way.

question: In Ireland's Boyne Valley, a Neolithic passage tomb older than the Egyptian pyramids fills its inner chamber with sunlight for 17 minutes on a single date each year. That date is the:
context: Newgrange (~3200 BC) has a roof-box aligned to winter sunrise. Lights enter through it, slowly illuminating a corbelled chamber 19 m inside.

question: On the coast of Brittany in northwestern France stand over 3,000 prehistoric standing stones in long rows. The site is:
context: The Carnac stones (~4500-3300 BC) form three groups of parallel rows. They predate Stonehenge and may align with sunrise points over the year.

question: In southwestern France lies a cave whose walls and ceilings are painted with 600 vivid Paleolithic animal images — horses, bulls, deer. The cave is:
context: Discovered in 1940 by four teenagers. Lascaux's paintings date to about 17,000 years ago. The cave is closed to visitors; a perfect replica nearby is open.

question: In southern France, a cave discovered in 1994 contains some of the oldest known cave paintings — about 36,000 years old. It is:
context: Chauvet's paintings include rhinos, mammoths, panthers — animals rare elsewhere. The cave is closed to the public; Werner Herzog's 'Cave of Forgotten Dreams' filmed inside it.

question: On Scotland's Orkney Islands, a Neolithic stone village older than the Egyptian pyramids was preserved beneath the sand. It is:
context: Skara Brae (~3180-2500 BC) has eight stone houses with built-in stone beds, dressers, and storage. A 19th-century storm uncovered it.

question: Near Angkor Wat in Cambodia stands a smaller walled royal city whose central temple has 54 towers carved with about 200 enigmatic giant stone faces. The city is:
context: Built by Jayavarman VII around 1200 AD. The Bayon's faces are thought to represent the king himself or the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara.

question: In Sri Lanka, a 200-meter granite rock rises from the jungle, holding the ruins of a 5th-century royal palace and frescoes of bare-breasted celestial maidens. It is:
context: Sigiriya means 'lion rock.' King Kashyapa built his palace atop it around 477 AD. The entrance once passed between the paws of a giant lion sculpture; only the paws survive.

question: In Maharashtra, India, 30 Buddhist cave temples carved into a horseshoe cliff hold vivid frescoes from the 2nd century BC to the 6th century AD. They are the:
context: Ajanta was abandoned and forgotten until 1819, when a British hunter spotted a cave entrance. The frescoes show the Jataka tales — stories of the Buddha's past lives.

question: On a hilltop in southeastern Turkey, a circle of carved 5.5-meter T-shaped pillars dates to about 9500 BC — older than agriculture, older than pottery, older than the wheel. It is:
context: Discovered in 1994. Göbekli Tepe forces a rethink of prehistory: hunter-gatherers built monumental ritual sites before farming, not after.

question: Beijing's Forbidden City, the largest palace complex on Earth, has how many rooms (counting bays)?
context: The Forbidden City has approximately 9,000 bays of rooms across 980 buildings. Begun in 1406 and completed in 1420 under the Yongle Emperor.

question: At Nara, Japan stand what are considered the oldest surviving wooden buildings on Earth, built in the early 7th century AD. The temple is:
context: Hōryū-ji's pagoda and main hall date to roughly 670 AD. Each piece of timber has been periodically replaced, but the design is unchanged in 1,300+ years.

question: Near modern Mexico City rises one of the largest pyramids in the world by volume, taller than any building the Aztecs ever built. The city around it is called:
context: Teotihuacan ('place where gods were born' in Nahuatl) reached 125,000 people by 500 AD. The Aztecs found it already in ruins and gave it that name.

question: Through Teotihuacan in Mexico runs a 2.5-km ceremonial avenue lined with hundreds of small platform mounds. The Aztecs later called it:
context: The Aztecs thought the mounds were tombs. They are actually platforms for temples. The avenue ends at the Pyramid of the Moon.

question: In the jungles of Chiapas, Mexico, a Maya stepped pyramid was found in 1952 to contain the unlooted tomb of a king who ruled 615-683 AD. He was:
context: Alberto Ruz Lhuillier excavated Pakal's tomb at Palenque's Temple of the Inscriptions. The jade-mask-covered sarcophagus lid is among the masterpieces of Maya art.

question: Rising above the Guatemalan rainforest are the limestone pyramids of a great Maya city abandoned around 900 AD. It is:
context: Tikal was a Maya superpower (~200-900 AD). Its tallest pyramid, Temple IV, reaches 70 m and features in the original 'Star Wars' as a rebel base.

question: Deep in the Guatemalan jungle hides a Preclassic Maya city older than Tikal, with a pyramid named La Danta that may be the largest by volume in the world. The city is:
context: El Mirador peaked around 200 BC and was abandoned by 100 AD. La Danta is 72 m tall and contains an estimated 2.8 million cubic meters of stone.

question: At Chichén Itzá in Mexico, on the spring and autumn equinoxes, sunlight casts a shadow on the stepped pyramid that appears as a long serpent descending. The pyramid is dedicated to:
context: Built around 1000 AD by the Maya-Toltec. The pyramid has 91 steps on each of four sides plus the top platform — exactly 365, matching the solar year.

question: Above the city of Oaxaca, Mexico, the Zapotec people leveled a mountain top around 500 BC and built a city of pyramids and plazas there. It is:
context: Monte Albán means 'White Mountain.' It was the Zapotec capital for over 1,000 years and one of the first major urban centers in the Americas.

question: Across the Mississippi River from St. Louis, the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico flourished from about 1050 to 1350 AD. It is:
context: Cahokia held about 20,000 people at its peak. Monks Mound, its largest earthwork, is the largest pre-Columbian earthen mound in North America.

question: On Peru's dry coast lies a city of stone pyramids and circular plazas that flourished around 2600 BC — making it the oldest known city in the Americas. It is:
context: Caral was contemporary with the early Egyptian pyramids. It had no defensive walls or weapons; the inhabitants seem to have lived peacefully for centuries.

question: In 1911, Yale lecturer Hiram Bingham was led to a 15th-century Inca site high in the Peruvian cloud forest. That site is now called:
context: Locals knew of the site; it had never been forgotten. The Spanish never found Machu Picchu, and it was abandoned in the 16th century — perhaps because its priests fled the conquest.

question: Above Cusco in Peru stands an Inca fortress whose enormous stones — some weighing over 100 tonnes — fit together without mortar so precisely that a knife blade cannot slide between them. The site is:
context: Some Sacsayhuamán blocks weigh over 200 tonnes. The Inca shaped each stone individually, so no two are alike — a method that survives earthquakes well.

question: On a desert plateau in southern Peru, ancient people scraped giant images — a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider — into the ground, visible only from the air. They are the:
context: Made by the Nazca culture (~500 BC-500 AD). The lines survived because the desert essentially never rains. Their purpose may have been ritual paths for walking to water-related rites.

question: On Rapa Nui (Easter Island), the giant stone heads (moai) once stood atop ceremonial stone platforms facing inland toward villages. Those platforms are called:
context: About 900 moai are known, on 313 ahu around the island. They were toppled by islanders themselves between 1700 and 1838; many have been re-erected.

question: Sudan actually has more ancient pyramids than Egypt — around 200 of them — at the site of:
context: Built by the Kushite kings (~720 BC - 300 AD). Meroë's pyramids are smaller, steeper, and have flat tops or chapels at their bases.

question: The Aksumite kingdom of northern Ethiopia (1st-7th centuries AD) erected giant carved single-block granite monuments to mark royal tombs. They are called:
context: Stelae are essentially obelisks. Aksum's tallest erected stele stands 24 m. The largest, which collapsed during erection (~33 m, 520 tonnes), would have been the largest single stone ever quarried by ancient peoples.

question: In southern Africa, the ruined capital of a 13th-15th century kingdom features dry-stone walls up to 11 m tall built without mortar from granite blocks. It is:
context: Great Zimbabwe gave modern Zimbabwe its name ('great houses of stone' in Shona). The Great Enclosure has the longest dry-stone wall in pre-colonial Africa.

question: On an island off the Tanzanian coast lie the medieval ruins of a wealthy Swahili trading city that handled gold from Great Zimbabwe and ivory from the interior. It is:
context: Kilwa peaked in the 13th-15th centuries. The Husuni Kubwa palace was the largest stone building in sub-Saharan Africa when built (~1310 AD).

question: In Mali, the largest mud-brick building in the world is replastered every spring in a community festival. It is the:
context: The current building is from 1907 — a reconstruction of a 13th-century original. The plaster sticks (toron) projecting from the walls are scaffolding for annual replastering.

question: Off the island of Pohnpei in Micronesia, a complex of about 100 artificial islands built of basalt 'logs' served as the capital of an ancient kingdom. It is:
context: Nan Madol was the capital of the Saudeleur dynasty (~1200-1500 AD). The columnar basalt was quarried elsewhere on Pohnpei and floated over — by what means, no one is sure.

question: In the dockside neighborhood of La Boca in Buenos Aires in the 1880s, immigrant workers gave birth to a partner dance that became Argentina's signature. It is:
context: Tango drew on African candombe, Spanish habanera, and Italian melodies. Carlos Gardel made it a global craze in the 1920s.
