context: If you spent one minute viewing each work, the visit would take eleven years. The Hermitage cats — an official staff of about fifty — descend from cats brought by Empress Elizabeth in 1745 to control rats.

question: Because St Petersburg sits at 60 degrees north, the sun barely sets between mid-June and early July. The city stays in a long blue-pink twilight all night; cafes stay open, the drawbridges over the Neva rise at 1:25 in the morning to let cargo ships through. What is this season called locally?
context: True white nights — astronomical twilight all night — happen only between May 25 and July 16 at St Petersburg's latitude. Locals walk along the embankments to watch the bridges lift; tourists try the rooftop bars in the Petrogradsky district.

question: On the slopes of Mount Parnassus, a Pythia — a priestess of Apollo seated on a tripod above a fissure in the rock — gave cryptic answers to questions from kings and commoners alike. The Greeks called this sanctuary the navel of the world; a carved stone (the omphalos) marked the exact spot. What is this sanctuary called?
context: Croesus of Lydia asked the oracle whether to attack Persia. The answer — 'you will destroy a great empire' — proved true; he destroyed his own. Modern geologists in 2001 found two intersecting fault lines beneath the temple releasing ethylene gas.

question: Underneath central Istanbul lies an underground hall built in 532 AD by Emperor Justinian to store water for the imperial palace. Three hundred and thirty-six marble columns — many of them spolia from older temples — hold up a vaulted brick ceiling above 9,800 square metres of black water. Two columns rest on upside-down Medusa heads. What is this cistern called?
context: Forgotten for centuries, it was rediscovered when a Western traveller noticed locals lowering buckets through holes in basements and pulling up fish. The Medusa heads' orientation — sideways and upside-down — is debated; one theory is they were placed by Christian builders to neutralise pagan power.

question: Istanbul is the only major city in the world to straddle two continents. The narrow strait that divides them runs about 32 km from the Black Sea down to the Sea of Marmara, with strong currents and dangerous bends; suspension bridges and an undersea metro tunnel cross it. What is this strait called?
context: About 50,000 ships pass through the Bosphorus each year, including a third of the world's grain ships and a quarter of its oil tankers. The 1936 Montreux Convention governs traffic; Russia, Turkey, and shipping firms argue over it constantly.

question: On the Dalmatian coast, a walled city built largely of limestone juts out into the Adriatic. Its 1,940-metre defensive walls, mostly intact since the 13th-16th centuries, contain narrow streets paved in marble polished smooth by centuries of feet. Damaged by shelling during the 1991-1992 siege, the city was carefully restored. What is it called?
context: From the 14th-19th century this was the maritime Republic of Ragusa — a small but wily rival of Venice. The walls, with thicknesses up to 6 metres on the landward side, are walkable around the entire circuit.

question: At Giza, a desert plateau on the western edge of Cairo, three colossal pyramids stand in line — the largest built around 2560 BC by Pharaoh Khufu, with about 2.3 million limestone blocks averaging 2.5 tons each. For 3,800 years it was the tallest human-made structure on Earth. About how tall is the Great Pyramid today?
context: Erosion and loss of the outer casing stones brought the pyramid down by about 8 metres. Lincoln Cathedral's spire (1311) finally surpassed it. Each side aligns with the cardinal directions to within a tenth of a degree.

question: On a small island in the harbour of Alexandria, Egypt, a 100-metre lighthouse stood for over a thousand years, its mirror-reflected fire visible up to 50 km out at sea. Built around 280 BC under the Ptolemies, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. What island was it built on?
context: The Greek word 'pharos' (island name) became the word for 'lighthouse' in many languages — phare in French, faro in Spanish and Italian. A series of earthquakes between 956 and 1323 finally toppled it; its blocks were used to build the Qaitbay Fortress on the same site.

question: On the east bank of the Nile at modern Luxor lies the largest religious site of the ancient world, built and rebuilt over 2,000 years by some thirty pharaohs. Its central Hypostyle Hall holds 134 sandstone columns up to 21 metres tall and 3.5 metres thick, originally painted in vivid colours. What is this temple complex called?
context: The complex covers about 200 hectares. Senemmut, Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, and Ramesses II all added buildings. The central hall would fit Notre Dame and St Peter's inside with room to spare; how the largest column drums were stacked is still debated.

question: On the Atlantic coast of Casablanca stands one of the largest mosques in the world, its 210-metre minaret topped by a laser that projects a beam 30 km out toward Mecca. The mosque accommodates 25,000 worshippers inside and 80,000 in its plazas. Completed in 1993, it was largely built over the Atlantic — a third of its footprint sits on a platform above the ocean. After whom is it named?
context: Hassan II commissioned the mosque for his 60th birthday. The platform-over-the-ocean siting fulfils the Quranic verse 'God's throne was on the water'. Six thousand traditional Moroccan artisans worked on the cedar carving, zellige tile, and stucco for six years.

question: In Mali sits the largest mud-brick building in the world, a vast 1907 reconstruction of an earlier 13th-century mosque. Wooden palm beams stick out of its walls — these are scaffolding bracing points that allow the entire town to participate in an annual replastering ceremony. What is this town and mosque called?
context: The annual Crepissage festival (April) is a town-wide event: men climb the protruding beams to spread fresh banco (mud + rice husk) on the walls, women carry water, children carry mud. The mosque is part of the UNESCO old town of Djenne.

question: On Tanzania's Indian Ocean coast lies a former clove-trading capital where Swahili, Arab, Indian, and European cultures fused. Its old quarter is built from coral rag with massive carved teak doors — many studded with brass spikes once meant to repel war elephants. Freddie Mercury was born here in 1946. What is this old quarter called?
context: Stone Town was a major slave-trading port until 1873; the Anglican Cathedral was built directly over the old slave market as deliberate memorial. The Sultans of Zanzibar were ethnically Omani; the dialect of Swahili here is laced with Arabic loanwords.

question: At the centre of the Great Mosque in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, stands a 15-metre cubic structure draped in a black silk cloth embroidered with verses from the Quran. Muslims worldwide face it in daily prayer; over two million circumambulate it each year during the annual pilgrimage. What is this cube called?
context: The Kaaba's black cloth — the kiswah — is renewed annually before the Hajj. The interior is empty except for hanging lamps and inscriptions. The Black Stone (Hajar al-Aswad) set in one corner is believed by tradition to date from Adam; geologists who have examined fragments suggest meteorite or volcanic origin.

question: At the heart of Uzbek Samarkand lies a great public square framed on three sides by 15th-17th-century madrasas — Islamic schools whose blue-and-gold tile facades face inward and meet at the corners. Two minarets at one corner lean noticeably from earthquake damage. What is this square called?
context: The three madrasas — Ulugh Beg (1420), Sher-Dor (1636), and Tilya-Kori (1660) — span more than two centuries of Timurid and post-Timurid architecture. The Sher-Dor's facade unusually shows tigers (or lions) chasing deer, breaking the Islamic prohibition on animal images on religious buildings.

question: Samarkand sits on the main overland route between China and the Mediterranean, the so-called Silk Road. In the late 14th century it became the capital of a Turkic-Mongol empire stretching from Anatolia to India. Whose capital was it then?
context: Timur (Tamerlane) is reportedly buried under a slab of jade at the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum; his tomb carries an inscription warning 'whoever opens my grave will be defeated by an enemy more terrible than I'. The Soviet anthropologist Gerasimov opened it on 19 June 1941 — Operation Barbarossa began on 22 June.

question: In the old town of Bukhara, Uzbekistan, a 47-metre brick minaret has stood since 1127 — Genghis Khan reportedly spared it because its top was higher than his head when he tilted back to look. Its sixteen bands of carved-brick patterning have never been repaired. What is it called?
context: The minaret functioned not only as a call to prayer but as a lighthouse for desert caravans approaching Bukhara from the Kyzylkum desert. It is also notoriously called the 'Tower of Death' from the Bukharan emirs' practice of executing criminals by throwing them from the top.

question: On the southern edge of Delhi rises a 73-metre red-sandstone-and-marble tower built in 1192-1220 as part of the city's first Islamic complex — and the tallest brick minaret in the world. It is fluted with five storeys, each marked by a balcony, and carved with Arabic inscriptions. What is it called?
context: Just inside the same complex stands the older Iron Pillar of Delhi (~400 AD), a 7-metre wrought-iron column that has not rusted in 1,600 years — a metallurgical mystery long debated.

question: On the bank of the Yamuna river in Agra rises a white-marble mausoleum, perfectly symmetrical, with four minarets at the corners, a central onion-shaped dome, and a long reflecting pool in front. It was built between 1632 and 1648 by emperor Shah Jahan in grief for his second wife, who died in childbirth. Who was she?
context: Mumtaz means 'Chosen One of the Palace'. The Taj's white Makrana marble subtly changes colour from pinkish dawn to pearly noon to golden evening to silvery moonlit night. The minarets lean slightly outward — designed that way to fall away from the main building in earthquake.

question: About 40 km from Agra stands a complete late-16th-century planned city built by emperor Akbar in red sandstone — courtyards, halls of public and private audience, a vast mosque, and a tomb of a Sufi saint. Akbar abandoned it in 1585, about fifteen years after building it. The main suspected reason is what?
answer: Water shortage — the city's lake dried up
choices: Water shortage — the city's lake dried up
context: The artificial lake at Fatehpur Sikri did indeed dry up; the city's stone water lifts and reservoirs proved insufficient. Akbar then moved north to Lahore. The city was never reoccupied and survives as one of the best-preserved Mughal complexes anywhere.

question: The capital of Rajasthan was the first planned city in modern India, laid out in 1727 in a nine-block grid by Sawai Jai Singh II. In 1876 the entire old city was painted a distinctive colour to welcome the Prince of Wales (later Edward VII). What colour was used?
context: The pink colour symbolised hospitality (Hindu tradition associates pink with welcome). The city's old core remains painted that colour to this day — a city ordinance requires it. The Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II was also an astronomer who built five observatories across north India.

question: On a hill in the Tibetan capital rises a vast white-and-red palace, thirteen storeys, a thousand rooms — the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas from 1649 until 1959. Built atop a 7th-century fortress, its layered terraces stack up the slope of Red Mountain (Marpori). What is this palace called?
context: The fifth Dalai Lama began the present building in 1645; it took 45 years. The Potala sits at 3,700 metres — one of the highest palaces ever built. The 14th Dalai Lama fled into exile in 1959; the palace is now a state museum.

question: Xi'an was the eastern terminus of the trade network that connected Tang-dynasty China to Persia, Byzantium, and Rome. At the city's height around 700 AD it held about a million people inside its walls — the largest city in the world at the time. What was Xi'an called when it was the Tang capital?
context: Chang'an's foreign quarter held Persian Zoroastrians, Nestorian Christians, Manichaeans, and Sogdian merchants. The 8th-century Nestorian Stele — recording a Christian church and its monks in Chang'an — still survives in Xi'an's Beilin Museum.

question: At the heart of Beijing lies a vast rectangular palace complex begun in 1406 — 980 buildings on 72 hectares, enclosed by 8-metre walls and a 52-metre moat. From inside, Ming and Qing emperors ruled China for nearly five centuries. The yellow glazed roof tiles signal imperial use. What is its English nickname?
context: In Chinese it is Zijincheng ('Purple Forbidden City'). Common subjects entering without permission faced death. The complex now operates as the Palace Museum (Gugong); its art collection rivals the Louvre's, much of it moved to Taipei during the civil war.

question: South of central Beijing sits a vast Ming-dynasty altar complex where the Son of Heaven (the emperor) personally led an annual prayer for good harvests, on a triple-tiered white marble round altar. Three round buildings — designed without nails in 1420 — sit on the same axis. What is this complex called?
context: The Imperial Vault has the Echo Wall: whispers against the circular wall travel around to be heard at the opposite side. The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests has 28 columns: 4 central for the seasons, 12 for the months, 12 for the two-hour periods of the day.

question: Across the Huangpu river from old Shanghai sits a district that was paddy fields and warehouses in 1990. By 2015 it held three of the world's tallest buildings, an international financial centre, and the world's first commercial maglev train running from the airport. What is this district called?
context: Pudong's transformation is the fastest mass urbanisation of any major city district in history. The maglev tops out at 431 km/h — the world's fastest commercial passenger train — between Longyang Road station and Pudong airport.

question: In southern Anhui province in eastern China rises a range of granite peaks where weather-twisted Huangshan pines cling to vertical cliff faces and lone trees stick out of summits — the inspiration for a thousand years of Chinese landscape painting. Morning seas of cloud (yunhai) settle below the peaks. What is this range called in English?
context: Huangshan ('Yellow Mountain') was renamed in 747 AD by Emperor Xuanzong, who believed it was the place where the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) attained immortality. UNESCO Mixed Site (cultural and natural). Famed views include Welcoming-Guest Pine, Lotus Peak, and Cloud-Dispelling Pavilion.

question: At the north end of central Seoul stands a Joseon-dynasty palace founded in 1395 — its name means 'palace of shining happiness'. Burned to the ground in the 1592 Imjin War, rebuilt in the 1860s, partly demolished by Japanese occupation forces, it has now been largely restored. What is this palace called?
context: King Sejong the Great — inventor of the Hangul alphabet — lived here in the 1440s. The palace's Gwanghwamun gate fronts a vast plaza along Sejong-daero, where Seoul's protest movements regularly gather.

question: In the parks of Nara, about 1,200 sika deer wander freely among the temples, shrines, and tourists. They are considered messengers of the Shinto gods and have been protected for centuries. They bow back to humans — a learned behaviour tied to what?
answer: Receiving shika senbei (deer rice crackers) from vendors
choices: Receiving shika senbei (deer rice crackers) from vendors
An imperial decree from the 8th century
context: The bowing is a learned response. Nara's deer are wild — not fed by the city — but tame around humans. Until 1637 killing a deer was a capital offence in Nara; the deer's protected status survived the Meiji secularisation of Shinto shrines.

question: In central Osaka rises an eight-storey reconstructed castle keep on a base of vast Sengoku-era stone walls. Built originally in 1583 by warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi, it was the most lavishly gilded fortress of its day and was meant to overawe rival warlords. The keep was destroyed by fire and lightning and rebuilt to its current form in concrete in 1931. Who built the original?
context: Hideyoshi's stones included some of the largest single blocks ever used in Japanese castle construction — Tako-ishi ('octopus stone') in the inner moat measures about 6 by 12 metres. Tokugawa Ieyasu's siege of 1614-1615 destroyed Toyotomi power and the original keep.

question: Hanoi's old quarter is organised — uniquely — around its medieval guild trades. Streets bear names like 'Silver Street', 'Silk Street', 'Cotton Street', 'Coffin Street', and 'Grilled Fish Street'; merchants of each trade once clustered there and many still do. Roughly how many such streets make up the network?
context: The number 36 is symbolic and approximate; the streets were laid out beginning in the 13th century. Hanoi means 'inside the river' — the city sits in the bend of the Red River.

question: On the east bank of Bangkok's Chao Phraya river sprawls a glittering palace complex — its multi-tiered orange-and-green roofs, gold-leaf chedis, and mirror-tile chofa spires forming what the writer S.J. Perelman called 'a delirium'. Built in 1782 by King Rama I after he founded the Chakri dynasty. What is the principal shrine inside?
context: The Emerald Buddha is actually carved from green jasper, only 66 cm tall. The current king himself changes its three sets of gold robes — for the hot, cool, and rainy seasons — in a public ceremony three times a year.

question: Near the Grand Palace in Bangkok sits a Buddhist temple complex whose central building contains a 46-metre-long, 15-metre-high reclining Buddha statue covered in gold leaf. The soles of its feet, inlaid with mother-of-pearl, depict 108 auspicious symbols of the Buddha. What temple is this?
context: Wat Pho was the first home of formal Thai massage training; the technique is still taught here on a covered platform. Coins fall continuously into 108 bronze bowls along the wall behind the statue as visitors drop them in for merit.

question: In the former Siamese capital north of Bangkok lie the ruins of a 14th-18th-century royal city sacked by the Burmese in 1767. Among the crumbled brick prangs and decapitated Buddha statues, one stone Buddha head has been engulfed by the roots of a strangler fig that grew up around it. What is this city called?
context: Ayutthaya was named for Ayodhya, Rama's city in the Indian Ramayana. At its peak it was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps a million people. Western traders described its temple spires, jewelled facades, and royal elephants in detail.

question: In northern Thailand sits a former independent kingdom capital, the seat of the Lan Na dynasty from 1296. Its old town is a perfect 1.5-km square surrounded by a 14th-century brick wall and moat — four corner bastions still mostly intact. What is this city called?
context: The Lan Na kingdom was an independent state from 1296 to 1558. The Tha Phae Gate on the eastern side of the moat is the busiest entrance to the old city; Sunday Walking Street markets stretch into it.

question: On a flat plain along the Irrawaddy river in central Myanmar sits an archaeological zone covering more than 100 square kilometres — once site of over 10,000 Buddhist temples, stupas, and monasteries built between the 9th and 13th centuries. About 2,200 brick monuments still stand. What is this place called?
context: Bagan was the capital of the first unified Burmese kingdom from 1044 to 1297. A devastating earthquake in 1975 (and another in 2016) brought many temples down; the military government's amateur reconstructions in the 1990s caused UNESCO to refuse World Heritage listing until 2019, when the bar was relaxed.

question: Above central Kuala Lumpur rise twin slender 88-storey towers connected at floors 41-42 by a sky-bridge. Completed in 1998, they were briefly the tallest buildings in the world (until 2004) and remain the tallest twin towers. What are they called?
context: The towers' design — eight-pointed star floor plans — references Islamic geometric motifs. Argentine-American architect Cesar Pelli won the commission; the two towers were built by different contractors racing each other, with the south tower (built by a South Korean firm) being faster.

question: On the southwest coast of peninsular Malaysia sits a strategic Strait port that has changed hands among Malay sultans (15th c.), Portuguese (1511), Dutch (1641), and British (1824). The old centre still has Dutch-red painted buildings around a town square — the Stadthuys and Christ Church — and Portuguese ruined fortifications above. What is this town called?
context: Malacca controlled the Strait of Malacca, one of the world's most strategic maritime chokepoints — about a quarter of all global shipping passes through it. UNESCO listed both Malacca and Penang (George Town) jointly in 2008 for their melange of cultures.

question: Spanning the East River between Manhattan and Brooklyn in New York is a 1,825-metre suspension bridge that opened in 1883. Its main span of 486 metres was, for two decades, the world's longest. Its designer was crippled in an early accident, and his son spent fifteen years overseeing construction from a bed using a telescope and his wife as messenger. Who was the designer?
context: John A. Roebling died of tetanus from a foot crushed in a survey accident. His son Washington Roebling suffered the bends from work in the underwater caissons. His wife Emily Warren Roebling effectively ran the project; she was the first person to cross the bridge when it opened.

question: In central Boston, a 2.5-mile red-painted (or in some places red-brick) line on the pavement winds past sixteen Revolutionary War sites — the Granary Burying Ground, the Old North Church, the site of the Boston Massacre, Paul Revere's house, the USS Constitution. Inaugurated in 1951 as a way to organise tourist exploration. What is this trail called?
context: The Old North Church (1723) is where Robert Newman hung lanterns to signal British troop movements ('one if by land, two if by sea') as Paul Revere set off on his 1775 ride. The Granary Burying Ground holds the graves of Samuel Adams, John Hancock, and Paul Revere himself.

question: In the windy mid-American city on the south shore of Lake Michigan, the world's first true skyscraper — a building supported by a steel frame rather than load-bearing masonry — went up in 1885. Ten storeys tall. Its successors quickly grew far taller and reshaped global cities. What is this city?
context: The Home Insurance Building (1885, demolished 1931) by William Le Baron Jenney is generally credited as the first steel-frame skyscraper. Chicago's 1871 Great Fire had cleared a vast site for experiment; the city now hosts the Willis (former Sears) Tower and many other supertall buildings.

question: Spanning the entrance to San Francisco Bay is a 1937 suspension bridge whose two main towers were the tallest above water when built (227 metres). The bridge is painted a distinctive vermillion-orange colour, not gold. What is this bridge's signature shade officially called?
context: The colour was chosen by consulting architect Irving Morrow, who liked the way the lead-based primer looked. International Orange complements the surroundings and is highly visible in fog. The bridge is repainted continuously — never end to end, but always somewhere.

question: On a cliff above the Saint Lawrence River sits the only walled city north of Mexico in the Americas. Its 4.6-km ramparts were begun by the French in the 17th century and completed by the British in the 19th. The old town clusters around Chateau Frontenac — the most photographed hotel in the world. What is this city?
context: Quebec City was founded in 1608 by Samuel de Champlain. The Plains of Abraham, just outside the old walls, were the site of the 1759 British-French battle that decided the colonial fate of Canada. UNESCO World Heritage since 1985.

question: Behind central Montreal rises a small hill of igneous rock that gives the city its name. The American landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted, who designed New York's Central Park, also designed the park covering this hill (opened 1876). What is this hill called?
context: Jacques Cartier named the hill in 1535. Mount Royal is a Monteregian Hill — an exposed igneous plug from ancient volcanic activity. Olmsted insisted on minimising designed features and letting the existing forest dominate; the result is a park beloved by locals for its naturalness.

question: Cuba's capital old town, declared UNESCO World Heritage in 1982, is a square kilometre of pastel Spanish colonial buildings around four old plazas, surrounded by 16th-century walls long since dismantled. Convertible-roof 1950s American cars trundle the cobbled streets — a fleet preserved by the U.S. embargo. What is the district called in Spanish?
context: Havana was founded in 1519 as Spain's main fortified harbour in the Caribbean. The 1762 British occupation lasted a year; Spain swapped Florida to get Havana back. The Capitolio Nacional in central Havana is almost a copy of the U.S. Capitol — built 1929.

question: On the highest navigable lake in the world (at 3,812 metres on the Peru-Bolivia border), an indigenous people live on floating islands of layered totora reeds — about 40 of them, anchored to the lakebed. The islands have been their refuge since pre-Inca times. Who are these people?
context: The Uros built the floating islands originally to flee Inca subjugation, retreating onto the lake. The reeds are also eaten, made into boats, and used in cooking. Each island is rebuilt by piling fresh reeds on top as the lower layers rot away; total lifespan is about 30 years per island.

question: In the 16th-17th centuries, this Bolivian city at 4,090 metres was one of the largest and richest in the world — bigger than London or Paris — because of the silver streaming out of the mountain looming above it. Some 60% of the silver mined in the world from 1546 to 1825 came from here. What is this mountain called?
context: The Spanish phrase 'vale un Potosi' ('worth a Potosi') entered the language as a comparison for vast wealth. Possibly 8 million African and Andean slaves and forced labourers died in the mines over three centuries. The mountain is still partly mined today, mostly for tin.

question: Above the city of Rio de Janeiro, on the 710-metre Corcovado peak, stands a 38-metre soapstone statue of Christ with outstretched arms, completed in 1931. The statue's arms — meant to embrace the city below — span 28 metres. From whose design was the statue built?
answer: Heitor da Silva Costa with Paul Landowski
choices: Heitor da Silva Costa with Paul Landowski
context: The face was sculpted by Romanian-Polish artist Gheorghe Leonida. The statue's outer surface is mosaic soapstone (millions of small tiles) over a reinforced concrete frame. It was struck by lightning in 2014 and a thumb was damaged.

question: On the border of Argentina and Brazil, the Iguazu River drops over 275 separate cataracts across a 2.7-km cliff edge, with the central horseshoe — a roaring U-shaped chasm 80 metres deep — getting most of the flow. The water levels typically swell during the South American summer rains. What is the central horseshoe called?
context: Eleanor Roosevelt, visiting Iguazu in 1944, supposedly exclaimed 'Poor Niagara'. The falls are higher than Niagara and wider than Victoria — though smaller than Victoria by water volume. The Brazilian side gives the panoramic view; the Argentinian side gives close-up boardwalks.

question: Rio's most famous shorter beach is a 4-km curve of fine white sand between Sugarloaf and Two Brothers mountains, hosting Rio's New Year's Eve fireworks viewed by about two million people on a single night. The beach's western end gave its name to a famous bossa nova song in 1962. What is this beach called?
context: 'The Girl from Ipanema' (1962) was written by Antonio Carlos Jobim and Vinicius de Moraes about a teenager they had watched walking past Ipanema's Veloso bar. The real girl, Heloisa Pinheiro, was 17 then. Copacabana itself was named after a chapel of Our Lady of Copacabana.

question: The capital of Brazil from 1960 has been a planned modernist city laid out in the shape of an airplane (or a bow and arrow, in alternate readings). Each of the 'wings' holds residential super-blocks; the fuselage holds ministries; the cockpit holds the legislature and supreme court. Who designed the master plan?
context: Lucio Costa won the open competition for the master plan. Oscar Niemeyer designed most of the major buildings — including the National Congress with its twin office towers and the dome-and-bowl of the senate and chamber of deputies. UNESCO World Heritage since 1987 — the youngest city ever listed.

question: On the Beagle Channel at the southern tip of Tierra del Fuego, this Argentine port (population about 80,000) calls itself the southernmost city in the world. It serves as the main base for tourist and scientific ships heading to the Antarctic. About how far is it from the South Pole?
context: Puerto Williams in Chile (population about 2,800) is technically further south but is a village rather than a city. Ushuaia means 'bay penetrating westward' in the indigenous Yaghan language. Sunset in mid-summer here is at about 10:15 PM; in mid-winter at about 5 PM.

question: Across Sydney Harbour from the Opera House arches a 1932 steel through-arch bridge that locals call 'the coathanger'. The bridge carries eight lanes of road and two rail lines. A famous activity now lets paying visitors climb across the upper arch — 134 metres above the harbour, harnessed to a continuous safety line. What is this climb called?
context: BridgeClimb started in 1998 and has taken over 4 million climbers to date. The bridge took 1,400 workers eight years to build. The first car across opened it in 1932; the chief engineer's wife drove. Heritage rivets have to be hand-replaced regularly as they age.

question: New Zealand's largest city, on the North Island, sits atop an active volcanic field of about 53 dormant volcanic features (cones, craters, lava flows, and tuff rings) scattered across the city. The most recent eruption was about 600 years ago. Some cones are now public parks, some are quarried away, some are pa sites. What is the field called?
context: Mount Eden (Maungawhau), Mount Victoria (Takarunga), and One Tree Hill (Maungakiekie) are the three largest cones, all within Auckland proper. Volcanologists put the chance of a new eruption in the field at small but non-zero; it would almost certainly come from a brand-new vent.

question: New Zealand's capital, on the southern tip of the North Island, sits in a tight bowl between hills, opening onto Cook Strait. The strait funnels and accelerates winds blowing through it. The city averages more than 170 days per year with gusts over 60 km/h. What is this strait's English name?
context: Cook Strait is named for the British navigator James Cook; the Maori name is Te Moana-o-Raukawa. The Roaring Forties — westerly winds in the Southern Ocean — funnel through it. Most flights to and from Wellington have to descend through gusts that would close other airports.

question: On the shore of a glacial lake in New Zealand's South Island sits a small town that has commercialised more 'adventure sports' than any other location in the world — bungy jumping, jet boating, paragliding, river surfing, and many more. Bungy jumping in its modern commercial form was invented here. Who started it and when?
context: Hackett had taken inspiration from Vanuatu's land-divers, who tie vines to their ankles and leap from wooden platforms. His 1987 jump off the Eiffel Tower was an attention-grabber; his Kawarau Bridge operation, the world's first, opened in November 1988.

question: Iguazu Falls on the Brazil-Argentina border thunders down a 2.7-km cliff edge in 275 separate cataracts. About half the river's total volume pours through one U-shaped chasm in the middle, surrounded on three sides by walls of falling water and constant rainbow-laden mist. What is this U-shaped chasm called?
context: The Garganta drops 80 metres into a chasm so deep the bottom cannot be seen for the mist. Visitors reach a boardwalk over the lip from the Argentine side. The falls form along an ancient basalt cliff, the eastern edge of the Parana plateau.

question: On the U.S.-Canada border between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, Niagara Falls is actually three separate waterfalls — the American, Bridal Veil, and Horseshoe. The Horseshoe carries about 90% of the river's flow over a curved 670-metre lip. How fast is the Horseshoe Falls eroding upstream toward Lake Erie?
answer: About 30 cm per year (down from 1 m before flow diversions)
choices: About 30 cm per year (down from 1 m before flow diversions)
Not eroding — held in place by hard rock
context: Niagara's recession has been slowed by upstream hydroelectric diversions taking about half the river's water. At the current rate, the falls would reach Lake Erie in about 50,000 years and drain the upper Great Lakes.

question: On the Zambia-Zimbabwe border, the Zambezi river drops 108 metres into a narrow basalt slot — twice the height of Niagara, taller and wider than Niagara at peak flow. The local Tonga name means 'the smoke that thunders' for the column of spray that rises hundreds of metres and is visible from 50 km away. What is the Tonga name?
context: David Livingstone renamed it Victoria Falls in 1855 for his queen; Zambia and Zimbabwe both officially use Mosi-oa-Tunya alongside the colonial name. Devil's Pool — a natural rock pool at the cliff edge during low water — lets bathers swim within metres of the drop.

question: On a tepui (table mountain) in southeast Venezuela, the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall drops 807 metres in a single plume off the side of Auyan-tepui. The plume is sometimes pushed sideways into mist before it reaches the bottom. What is the falls' Pemon Indian name?
context: Discovered by Western pilot Jimmie Angel in 1933, the falls were renamed after him. President Hugo Chavez officially renamed them Kerepakupai Vena in 2009. The total drop including base cascades is 979 metres.

question: Deep in the rainforest of central Guyana, the Potaro river plunges off a sandstone-conglomerate plateau in a single 226-metre drop — about five times the height of Niagara and about twice as high as Victoria Falls. The remote falls receive perhaps 2,000 tourist visitors a year. What is the falls' name?
context: Visitors are usually flown in by small plane; an alternative is a two-day hike. Kaieteur is the longest single-drop waterfall by volume in the world; Angel Falls is taller but much thinner. The plateau is part of the same Guiana Shield as Mount Roraima.

question: The Amazon River carries about one-fifth of all the river water on Earth — about as much as the next seven largest rivers combined. At its mouth, the river is 240 km wide (some say wider — defining 'mouth' is contested). About how much of Earth's freshwater (by river volume) does the Amazon carry?
answer: About 20% of all river water by volume
choices: About 20% of all river water by volume
About 50% of all river water by volume
About 80% of all river water by volume
About 5% of all river water by volume
context: The river's drainage basin is 7 million square kilometres — about the size of Australia. Pororoca, the tidal bore that runs hundreds of km upstream during spring tides, makes waves up to 4 metres high — surfable for half an hour at a stretch.

question: Near Manaus, the warm, dark Rio Negro meets the cooler, lighter, sediment-laden Solimoes river. The two flow side by side for about six kilometres without mixing — a visible boundary between black and brown water that tourists are taken to see by boat. Why don't they mix immediately?
answer: Different temperature, density, and flow speed delay mixing
choices: Different temperature, density, and flow speed delay mixing
A submerged ridge between the rivers prevents contact
Differing pH values create a chemical barrier
Salt content differences keep them stratified
context: The Rio Negro is acidic and stained with decayed plant matter; the Solimoes is sediment-laden. The contrast is most visible from above. After about 6 km the rivers fully merge to form the lower Amazon proper.

question: The Yangtze (Chang Jiang) is the third-longest river in the world at about 6,300 km — the longest entirely within one country. Between Chongqing and Yichang, it cuts through three steep limestone gorges that have long been a Chinese cultural symbol. What major engineering project has dammed it since 2003?
context: Three Gorges Dam is the world's largest hydroelectric power station by capacity. Its reservoir submerged 13 cities, 140 towns, and 1,350 villages, displacing about 1.3 million people. The dam slowed sediment downstream; some delta erosion has resulted.

question: In southern Vietnam, the Mekong River fans out into a vast delta of distributaries and rice paddies before emptying into the South China Sea through nine main mouths. The Vietnamese call the delta the 'Nine Dragons' for these mouths — though several have silted up. What does the delta produce?
answer: About half of Vietnam's rice harvest
choices: About half of Vietnam's rice harvest
About one-third of Vietnam's industrial output
context: The Mekong drains about 800,000 sq km and originates on the Tibetan Plateau. Six countries depend on it; a series of Chinese upstream dams has been controversial for downstream water flows. Floating markets at Cai Rang and Phong Dien are tourist draws.

question: The Congo River in central Africa is the world's deepest river — over 220 metres deep in places. It is also the only major river to cross the equator twice. The river's mouth has cut a submarine canyon extending 800 km out into the Atlantic. The Congo discharges about how much water?
answer: Second only to the Amazon by volume
choices: Second only to the Amazon by volume
Largest of any river by volume
context: The Congo's volume of about 41,000 cubic metres per second is second only to the Amazon's roughly 200,000. Inga Falls, 40 km from the mouth, has more hydroelectric potential than anywhere on Earth — but political instability has kept it largely undeveloped.

question: The Danube River flows 2,860 km from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea coast, passing through more countries than any other river on Earth — ten in total. Which 10 are they?
answer: Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, Moldova, Ukraine
choices: Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, Moldova, Ukraine
Germany, Austria, Czechia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Greece, Turkey, Moldova, Ukraine
Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Slovenia, Italy, Romania, Ukraine, Poland
Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova, Ukraine
context: The Danube is the only major European river to flow west-to-east. Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade are all national capitals on its banks. The Iron Gates gorge between Serbia and Romania holds two huge dams.

question: Along a particularly narrow, treacherous bend of the German Rhine river south of Koblenz rises a 132-metre slate cliff. German legend says a beautiful blonde woman sat on the cliff and lured sailors to their deaths with her song. The 1824 ballad by Heinrich Heine sealed the legend. What is the cliff called?
context: The dangerous current at the Loreley bend, together with the cliff's echo of voices and boat-noises, gave the myth a physical basis. The cliff is UNESCO World Heritage as part of the Upper Middle Rhine Valley. A bronze statue at the foot now interprets the legend.

question: Paris was founded around 250 BC by a Gallic tribe on a fishhook-shaped island in the Seine, where the river curves sharply south. The Romans captured it in 52 BC and called it Lutetia; the medieval city grew outward from the original island. What is this central island called?
context: The Parisii tribe gave the city its later name. The cathedral of Notre Dame (12th c.), the Sainte-Chapelle (13th c.), and the Conciergerie all sit on Ile de la Cite. The smaller Ile Saint-Louis next door was developed as a single planned project in the 1620s.

question: Between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in modern Iraq lies a flat alluvial plain where, around 4000 BC, the world's first cities began to appear. The ancient name for this region was 'between the rivers' in Greek. What is the modern English name for it?
context: Sumerian Uruk (around 3500 BC) is the oldest known city. Mesopotamia hosted the Sumerian, Akkadian, Babylonian, Assyrian, and Chaldean civilisations in succession over three thousand years. The Saddam-era marshes draining of the 1990s destroyed much of the southern wetlands, since partly restored.

question: The Brahmaputra — known as the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet — flows about 1,000 km east across the Tibetan Plateau, then suddenly swings south and drops 2,300 metres in 250 km through a deep gorge before entering India. The gorge is twice as deep as the Grand Canyon — among the world's deepest. What is this bend called?
context: The Great Bend was one of the last unexplored mysteries of mainstream geography until expeditions in the 1990s mapped its full length. The river squeezes around the 7,756-metre peak of Namcha Barwa — one of the most dramatic geographic features on Earth.

question: In southern Siberia, a crescent-shaped lake sits in a tectonic rift between mountain ranges. It is the deepest lake in the world (1,642 metres), the oldest (25-30 million years), and holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen freshwater on Earth. What is it called?
context: Baikal contains more freshwater than all five North American Great Lakes combined. About 80% of its species are endemic — found nowhere else. The lake sits in an active rift; the two sides are pulling apart at about 2 cm per year. In 25 million years it may become an ocean.

question: Living in Lake Baikal at depths of 800-1,500 metres swims a translucent fish that gives live birth (rare for fish), contains 30% body fat, and dissolves into a puddle of oil if brought to the surface. What is this fish called?
context: The golomyanka is so adapted to deep cold and high pressure that surface conditions liquefy it. The fish's high fat content lets it tolerate the pressure shift in its normal vertical migrations; it cannot tolerate the full surface pressure drop or temperature increase.

question: Among the five North American Great Lakes, one stands out: the largest by surface area (82,000 sq km), the deepest (406 m), and the highest in elevation. It alone holds about 10% of Earth's surface freshwater. What is this lake called?
context: Lake Baikal is deeper, but Superior is the world's largest freshwater lake by surface area. Its temperature stays cold enough year-round that ships sunk in it (notably the Edmund Fitzgerald in 1975) are extraordinarily well preserved.

question: On the Peru-Bolivia border in the Andes sits the highest commercially navigable lake in the world — at 3,812 metres elevation. The Inca considered it sacred; its waters are said to be the birthplace of the Sun and the founders of the dynasty. What is the lake's local meaning?
answer: Roughly 'Stone Puma' or 'Grey Puma' in Aymara
choices: Roughly 'Stone Puma' or 'Grey Puma' in Aymara
context: The exact meaning is disputed; 'titi' is puma or wildcat in Aymara, 'kaka' might mean 'grey' or 'stone'. The lake covers 8,372 sq km and is shared roughly equally between Peru and Bolivia. The Uros people live on floating reed islands on the Peruvian side.

question: In central Africa, a long narrow lake sits in a Rift Valley graben — second only to Baikal in depth (1,470 m), second only to Baikal in volume, and the world's longest freshwater lake at 676 km. Four countries share its shores. What is this lake?
context: Tanganyika holds about 16% of the world's available freshwater. It is shared by DR Congo, Tanzania, Burundi, and Zambia. The lake is in the Western branch of the East African Rift — actively tearing apart, like Baikal. Stanley met Livingstone at Ujiji on its eastern shore in 1871.

question: Africa's largest lake by surface area (the second-largest freshwater lake by surface area in the world) is also the source of one of the world's longest rivers. The lake straddles the equator. What river begins at this lake's northern outlet?
context: Lake Victoria was named by British explorer John Hanning Speke in 1858 for his queen. The lake covers 68,800 sq km — second only to Lake Superior in surface area among freshwater lakes. The lake is shockingly shallow (max 80 m); evaporation roughly equals river inflow.

question: In south-east Africa, a long narrow Rift Valley lake holds more species of fish than any other lake on Earth — at least 1,000, of which about 99% are cichlids that have radiated from a few founder species over the past 1-2 million years. Many are popular in aquariums. What is this lake?
context: Each cichlid genus has specialised to a particular niche — algae-grazers on rocks, sand-sifters, fish-eaters, scale-eaters, and so on. The radiation is one of evolutionary biology's most-studied recent speciation events; some species have arisen in only a few thousand years.

question: Between Israel, the West Bank, and Jordan, a saline lake sits at the lowest point on Earth's land surface — 430 metres below sea level. Its water is about 34% salt (about ten times normal seawater), so dense that swimmers float on the surface. What gives the lake its English name?
answer: Almost no aquatic life can survive in the extreme salinity
choices: Almost no aquatic life can survive in the extreme salinity
A 4th-century AD plague that killed thousands of locals
An ancient Roman battle in which thousands of soldiers died
Its location below sea level — 'dead' as in beneath
context: The lake is shrinking by about a metre per year due to upstream water diversions from the Jordan River. The shoreline keeps receding; new sinkholes regularly appear in the abandoned former lakebed.

question: The world's largest inland body of water — about 371,000 sq km, larger than Germany — is surrounded by five countries. It is technically a lake by enclosure but is called a 'sea' for its size and saline water. Which five countries border it?
context: Whether the Caspian is legally a sea or a lake matters: under the law of the sea, all five countries share. Under lake-law, it would be divided into 5 zones. After decades of dispute they signed a 2018 convention treating it as 'special' — neither sea nor lake.

question: In Central Asia, the world's fourth-largest lake at the beginning of the 1960s had shrunk by 2010 to about 10% of its original area. The cause was Soviet diversion of its two feeder rivers (Amu Darya and Syr Darya) for cotton irrigation in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. What was this lake called?
context: The northern (Kazakh) part has been partially restored by a Kazakh-built dam (2005) holding back what flow remains. The southern (Uzbek) part is mostly desert — the Aralkum, the youngest desert on Earth. Salt and pesticide-laden dust storms from the dried lakebed are a regional health hazard.

question: In northern Tanzania, an alkaline lake with a pH up to 10.5 and surface temperatures up to 60°C deposits salt and natron (sodium carbonate) on the carcasses of dead birds and bats, preserving them as eerie calcified statues. The lake is red from haloarchaea and cyanobacteria. What is this lake called?
context: Lake Natron is the major breeding ground for East African flamingos — they tolerate the high alkalinity that few other species can. The 'petrified' bird photos by Nick Brandt in 2013 sparked widespread fascination; the bodies are calcified, not literally turned to stone, but the effect is striking.

question: On the summit of Mount Everest, climbers walk over yellowish limestone bedrock — the Yellow Band of the upper mountain. The rock contains trilobite and crinoid fossils from a tropical ancient seabed. What does this tell us about Everest?
answer: It was once a tropical sea floor before being thrust skyward
choices: It was once a tropical sea floor before being thrust skyward
It was once a tropical mountain peak before being eroded down
It was once a polar glacier carrying tropical sediments
The fossils were carried up by climbers and frozen in place
context: About 60 million years ago, the Indian tectonic plate slammed into Eurasia at about 15 cm per year (now slowed to about 5 cm). The ancient Tethys Ocean's sediments were folded and lifted; what was seabed is now summit. The Himalayas are still rising about 4 mm per year.

question: On 29 May 1953, two men became the first confirmed climbers to reach the summit of Mount Everest. The expedition was led by John Hunt; the climbers stayed only fifteen minutes on the summit. Who were they?
context: Hillary, a New Zealand beekeeper, and Tenzing Norgay, a Nepalese Sherpa, refused to say who stepped on the summit first. Sherpa tradition has Tenzing slightly behind Hillary; the British party agreed they reached the summit together. Mallory and Irvine had died on the mountain in 1924 — whether they summited remains unknown.

question: The world's second-highest mountain at 8,611 metres has a fatality rate among summit attempters of about 13% — much higher than Everest's roughly 3%. Climbers call it 'the savage mountain'. It sits in the Karakoram Range on the Pakistan-China border. What is it called?
context: K2 was first climbed by the Italian expedition of Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli in 1954. Its name comes from a 19th-century survey numbering; the K stood for Karakoram. Of 14 eight-thousanders, K2 has the highest fatality rate after Annapurna.

question: On the Tanzania-Kenya border rises the highest free-standing mountain in the world — a 5,895-metre volcano whose summit holds glaciers at the equator. The mountain has three distinct volcanic cones; the highest, Kibo, is dormant but not extinct. What are the three cones called?
context: Shira is the oldest and most eroded; Mawenzi is rugged and peaked; Kibo is the youngest and tallest. The summit glaciers — climate-changed and shrinking rapidly since the 19th century — are predicted by some scientists to disappear by mid-century.

question: In western Argentina near the Chilean border rises the highest peak in the Western Hemisphere — and the highest mountain outside Asia — at 6,961 metres. It is unique among the world's high peaks in being climbable by a 'walk-up' route requiring no technical climbing. What is its name?
context: Aconcagua means 'sentinel of stone' in Quechua. The non-technical Normal Route on the north face still requires acclimatisation; the Polish Glacier route on the east is challenging. About 35% of attempts succeed.

question: The highest peak in Europe sits in southern Russia on the boundary between Europe and Asia — a 5,642-metre dormant volcano in the Caucasus range. Whether it counts as Europe's top depends on where Europe's boundary is drawn; under most definitions it does. What is its name?
context: Mont Blanc (4,810 m) is sometimes called Europe's highest if the Caucasus is excluded as Asian. Elbrus has two summits — both dormant volcanic peaks. The Soviets built a cable car system on the south side; Elbrus is one of the easier 'Seven Summits'.

question: The highest peak in the Alps rises 4,810 metres on the France-Italy border. It was first climbed in 1786 by Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard — a feat that launched modern mountaineering. Whose financial reward made this climb attractive?
context: Saussure, a Swiss geologist, had offered a reward to the first man to reach the top in 1760. Twenty-six years later Balmat and Paccard succeeded; Saussure himself climbed it the following year. The pioneers of Alpine climbing were as much scientists as adventurers.

question: On the Swiss-Italian border rises a 4,478-metre peak with an iconic pyramid silhouette — one of the most photographed mountains on Earth. The first ascent was a triumph and a disaster: four members of the seven-man party died on the descent when a rope broke. Who led the successful 1865 climb?
context: The seven climbed up the Hornli ridge from Zermatt on 14 July 1865 — beating an Italian team to the summit by hours. Descending, Douglas Hadow slipped; Whymper and the two Taugwalders survived because the rope between them and Hadow's group broke. The Matterhorn now sees about 3,000 ascents a year.

question: In western Tibet rises a 6,638-metre mountain considered sacred by four religions — Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and the Bon — and is therefore not climbed; no one has officially summited it. Pilgrims walk a clockwise 52-km circuit at its base. What is the mountain called?
context: Hindus consider Kailash the home of Shiva. Buddhists consider it the seat of Demchok. Jains consider it where Rishabhanatha attained enlightenment. The Bon consider it the seat of their sky goddess Sipaimen. Reinhold Messner declined an offer to climb it out of religious respect.

question: Down the western coast of South America runs the longest continental mountain range on Earth, about 7,000 km from Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego, passing through seven countries. The range was raised by the subduction of one ocean plate beneath the South American plate. Which subducting plate?
context: The Andes are still rising as the Nazca plate continues to subduct at about 6-7 cm per year. The range is the world's second-highest (after the Himalayas). Volcanoes line its length: Cotopaxi, Chimborazo, Aconcagua, Ojos del Salado, and many others.

question: The Karakoram Range, on the borders of Pakistan, China, and India, holds an unusually dense concentration of the world's highest peaks. Four of the fourteen 8,000-metre peaks sit in the Karakoram, in a remarkably small area. They are K2, Gasherbrum I, Gasherbrum II, and which other?
context: All four sit within a 20-km cluster around the Baltoro Glacier. The 62-km Baltoro Glacier flows past their bases — one of the few places on Earth where four eight-thousanders are visible simultaneously from one viewpoint (Concordia).

question: The Pamir Mountains of Tajikistan are often called 'the Roof of the World'. The range is a knot where the Himalaya, Karakoram, Hindu Kush, and Tian Shan mountain ranges all converge. What city near the southern edge of the Pamirs is the capital of Tajikistan?
context: The Pamir Highway (M41) — the second-highest international road on Earth — runs north-south through the range, climbing to 4,655 metres at the Ak-Baital Pass. The Pamir Knot is geologically the most extreme uplift on Earth outside the main Himalayan crest.

question: Stretching about 2,500 km across Central Asia, the 'Celestial Mountains' separate the basins of Central Asia from the steppes of Kazakhstan and the Tarim Basin of China. Khan Tengri (7,010 m, the world's northernmost 7,000-er) is its iconic pyramid peak. What four countries does the range run through?
context: 'Tian Shan' is Chinese for 'celestial mountain'; the Russian name is similar. Kyrgyzstan is dominated by the Tian Shan — much of the country lies above 2,500 metres. Issyk-Kul, the world's second-largest mountain lake, sits in the eastern Tian Shan.

question: Down western North America runs a long ridge of mountains called the Rocky Mountains, which marks the continent's hydrological divide. Streams east of this divide flow toward the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico; streams west of it flow toward the Pacific. What is this divide called?
answer: The Continental Divide of the Americas
choices: The Continental Divide of the Americas
The Great Divide of the Americas
context: The Continental Divide actually runs the length of both Americas; in the Rocky Mountains it tracks the highest crests. At Triple Divide Peak in Glacier National Park, water from three sides of one mountain flows to three different oceans (Pacific, Gulf, Hudson Bay).

question: The Appalachian Mountains in eastern North America were once a massive range — taller than the modern Himalayas — formed about 480 million years ago. They have eroded for hundreds of millions of years to their present modest height. They are sometimes the oldest mountain range in North America. What range across the Atlantic was once part of the same mountain belt?
context: Pangaea reconstructions show the Appalachian and Caledonian ranges as continuous; Pangaea's breakup tore them apart. The Atlas Mountains may also have been continuous with the Appalachians via the African plate, though that connection is less direct.

question: Stretching about 2,500 km across northwest Africa, this range separates the Mediterranean coast and Sahara Desert. Its highest peak, Toubkal in Morocco, rises 4,167 metres — high enough to hold snow most of the year despite the African latitude. The Berber name for these mountains involves a Greek myth. What is the link?
answer: Greek myth: the Titan Atlas held up the sky here
choices: Greek myth: the Titan Atlas held up the sky here
Greek myth: Hercules killed the Nemean lion here
Greek myth: Perseus turned Atlas to stone here
Greek myth: Prometheus was chained here
context: Both Greek versions are sometimes told: the Titan Atlas held up the heavens, or Perseus showed him the Gorgon's head and turned him to stone (becoming the mountains). The Atlas range provides the orographic lift that creates Morocco's relatively wet northwest — without it, the Sahara would extend to the Mediterranean.

question: In South Africa and Lesotho rises a steep basalt escarpment about 1,000 km long, with peaks over 3,400 metres and waterfalls in the wet season. The Zulu name means 'barrier of upward-pointing spears'. What is the modern English name?
context: The Drakensberg sandstone caves hold the largest concentration of San (Bushman) rock paintings in the world — over 35,000 individual images in about 600 sites, painted from perhaps 8,000 years ago into the 19th century. UNESCO World Heritage 2000.

question: The Southern Alps run 500 km down New Zealand's South Island. On the wet western flank, glaciers descend to within 250 metres of the sea — among the lowest temperate latitudes that any glacier reaches. The most famous fjord on the western coast was carved by these glaciers. What is it called?
context: Mitre Peak rises 1,692 metres straight from Milford Sound's water — one of the highest cliff-to-fjord drops anywhere. Westland gets over 6,000 mm of rain a year; this is what feeds the Franz Josef and Fox glaciers down to 250 m elevation. The Tasman Sea cooled by the West Coast Current contributes.

question: The largest hot desert on Earth covers about 9 million square kilometres of North Africa. Cave paintings and dry riverbeds show that 6,000 years ago this region was savanna with lakes, hippos, and human pastoralists. The same change — wet to dry — happens cyclically on roughly which time scale?
choices: About every 1 million years (long-term climate cycle)
Never — the Sahara has always been dry
context: Earth's axial precession (the wobble of the spin axis) shifts which hemisphere gets the strongest summer sun, in turn shifting the rains. In about 13,000 years, the Sahara may again be savanna. The 'African Humid Period' (15,000-5,000 years ago) was the last green phase.

question: In southeastern Morocco, the Sahara forms a region of golden sand dunes up to 150 metres tall. The dunes are alive — they migrate slowly with the wind. Camel caravans take tourists through them. What is this dune field called?
context: An 'erg' is an Arabic word for a sand-sea — a continuous mass of sand dunes. Most of the Sahara is actually rocky 'hamada' or gravel plain ('reg'); only about 20% is sand erg. Erg Chebbi is photogenic precisely because it is unusually concentrated and tall.

question: In central Asia stretches a cold desert of about 1.3 million square kilometres across northern China and southern Mongolia. Winters drop to -40°C; summers reach +40°C. The native two-humped, woolly camel (about 1,000 left in the wild) is endemic. What is it called?
context: All domestic two-humped camels are Bactrian; the wild Bactrian is a separate species (Camelus ferus) only recently recognised, living in a protected reserve in the Gobi. The Gobi is the largest desert in Asia and the fifth-largest in the world.

question: In western China's Tarim Basin lies one of the largest sand deserts in the world — its name is variously translated 'place of no return' or 'desert of death'. The Silk Road split into northern and southern routes to skirt it; almost no travellers crossed straight through. What is the desert called?
context: The Taklamakan has produced some of the world's best-preserved mummies — the Tarim mummies, some 4,000 years old, with intact red and blond hair and woolen tartans (looking Caucasian, raising questions about ancient migration). The Taklamakan crossings remain rare today; the Silk Road oasis cities still ring its edges.

question: In the southern Arabian Peninsula lies the largest continuous sand desert in the world — about 650,000 sq km of dunes, with no permanent rivers, lakes, or settlements. Wilfred Thesiger crossed it twice in 1946-1948 by camel. What is it called?
context: The Rub' al Khali sits inside Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Oman, and Yemen. Dunes here reach 250 metres. Underneath lies one of the world's largest oil reserves — Saudi Aramco's Shaybah, Empty Quarter field. The 1971 Apollo lunar landing site selection committee studied the Empty Quarter as a Moon-like training ground.

question: Along the Atlantic coast of Namibia stretches a desert that may be the oldest on Earth — arid for at least 55 million years. Massive dunes (some 380 metres tall) reach right down to the ocean; cold ocean currents prevent rain from forming. What current is responsible?
context: The Benguela Current upwells cold water along Namibia's coast, cooling the air and preventing the rising-air rainfall typical of warm coasts. Fog from the cold ocean meets warm desert air daily; species like the Welwitschia plant and the fog-basking beetle drink the fog water.

question: The northern Namibian coast, where the Namib Desert meets the cold Benguela Current, is one of the world's most dangerous shorelines for ships. Hundreds of wrecks rust in the surf; the only land animals that can survive the area are desert-adapted elephants and lions. What is this coast called?
context: Fog combined with offshore shoals and powerful surf has wrecked ships from Portuguese vessels in the 1500s to fishing boats today. Whale bones once mantled the beach, giving the coast its English name; the Khoisan name was 'The Land God Made in Anger'.

question: On the Pacific coast of Chile and Peru sits the driest non-polar desert on Earth — some weather stations have never recorded a measurable rainfall in over 50 years of records. The desert is so arid that NASA uses it to test Mars rovers. What rain shadow effect plus what current cause the dryness?
answer: Andes rain shadow plus Humboldt cold current
choices: Andes rain shadow plus Humboldt cold current
Atlas rain shadow plus Canary cold current
Sierra Madre rain shadow plus California current
Drakensberg rain shadow plus Benguela current
context: The Andes block moisture from the Atlantic; the Humboldt Current cools coastal air so it cannot rise to make rain. Some places — Calama, Arica — average under 1 mm of rain per year. The Atacama also has the world's clearest skies; the ALMA observatory operates there.

question: South of latitude 38, the Andes' rain shadow makes eastern Argentina a vast cold desert — strong winds, sparse vegetation, sheep ranches and oil derricks. The region runs to Tierra del Fuego. What is this Argentine region called?
context: The name 'Patagonia' was bestowed by Ferdinand Magellan in 1520 — supposedly from a giant-like figure called Patagon in a Spanish novel he had read. The native Tehuelche were tall by Spanish standards, hence the comparison. Patagonia includes both the Argentine east and a thin strip of Chile.

question: In the southwestern United States lies the smallest North American desert (about 124,000 sq km). Its signature plant is a spiky tree-yucca that Mormon settlers thought resembled the prophet Joshua raising his arms to the sky. What is this desert called?
context: Joshua trees only grow in the Mojave and its borders. The desert sits between the Sierra Nevada and Colorado Plateau; Death Valley is its most extreme corner. Las Vegas is the largest city in the Mojave; the Mojave Air & Space Port is where SpaceShipOne was built.

question: Most of the interior of Australia is dry, hot, and sparsely populated — a region that English-speaking Australians call by an evocative two-word name. The legendary 'red centre' lies at the heart of it. What is this region called?
context: Coober Pedy, in the South Australian Outback, is the world's largest opal-mining town — most residents live in 'dugout' houses excavated underground to escape the heat. Most of the Outback receives less than 250 mm of rain per year; some places only briefly turn green after rare floods.

question: In southeastern Iran, this desert holds the record for the highest ground-surface temperature ever measured by satellite — 80.8°C (177°F), set in 2018. Inland from the dunes are vast Yardang plateaus carved by wind erosion. What is the desert called?
context: Air temperature there is more moderate (still very high). The Lut's salt-flats reach over 70°C surface temperature several months a year. The Kaluts — vast wind-carved ridges in the desert — are some of Earth's most striking aeolian landscapes.

question: Antarctica is roughly the size of the United States and Mexico combined. Its ice sheet — some 4.5 km thick at its thickest — holds about what percentage of all freshwater on Earth?
context: If all the ice melted, sea level would rise by about 58 metres globally. Antarctica's ice has been there for at least 30 million years. The continent is covered by ice 98%; only mountain peaks and the Antarctic Peninsula coast are ice-free.

question: Within Antarctica sits the largest ice-free region of the continent — three valleys near McMurdo Sound where strong katabatic winds prevent snow from settling. NASA tests Mars probes here. Some of the rocks in the Dry Valleys may not have been beneath ice or snow for millions of years. What are they called?
context: The valleys hold permanently frozen lakes whose surface ice never thaws but whose deep water is liquid (and saline) below. Algal mats grow under the ice in some lakes — alien-life analogues for Mars or Europa research.

question: Beneath about 4 km of ice in eastern Antarctica sits a freshwater lake roughly the size of Lake Ontario, sealed off from the surface for perhaps 15-25 million years. Russian drilling in 2012 reached its surface. What is this lake called?
context: Vostok is one of about 400 subglacial Antarctic lakes. Penetrating Vostok without contaminating it has been controversial — Russian drillers used kerosene-Freon antifreeze that critics worried might pollute the pristine water. Microorganisms in retrieved water are debated.

question: The smallest and shallowest of the world's five oceans is also the only one that ships cannot easily cross — surface ice has historically prevented routine navigation. Recent ice retreat has made some routes seasonally open. What is this ocean called?
context: The Arctic Ocean covers about 14 million sq km — about half the next-smallest, the Southern. Its summer minimum sea-ice extent has declined by about 13% per decade since 1979. The Northwest Passage and Northern Sea Route are now seasonally navigable.

question: Unlike Antarctica, which is a continent, the North Pole sits on drifting sea ice on the surface of an ocean. Beneath the pole the seabed is about how deep?
context: The seabed at the North Pole is part of the Lomonosov Ridge or its surroundings, dropping into the Eurasian Basin. Russia, Canada, Norway, Denmark (Greenland) all claim portions of the Arctic seabed; UN Convention on the Law of the Sea adjudicates.

question: On 14 April 1912 at 11:40 PM ship time, the RMS Titanic struck an iceberg about 400 km southeast of Newfoundland. The iceberg had drifted south from a Greenland glacier on which famous current?
context: The Labrador Current is cold and southwest-flowing along the Canadian coast; it carries thousands of icebergs each spring from Baffin Bay south into the North Atlantic shipping lanes. The 1912 disaster led to the International Ice Patrol, which monitors and warns ships to this day.

question: On the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard sits a deep-frozen vault built into a sandstone mountain — opened in 2008 to hold backup copies of crop seeds from genebanks around the world, as insurance against catastrophic loss. The vault now holds about 1.2 million seed varieties. About how cold is it kept?
context: Even if all the freezers fail, the surrounding permafrost stays well below freezing year-round. The vault has already had one withdrawal — Syria's genebank duplicates were retrieved in 2015 after the original was damaged in the civil war.

question: The Amazon Rainforest covers about 5.5 million sq km — 60% in Brazil, the rest spread across Peru, Colombia, and six other countries. Often called 'the lungs of the planet', it actually produces and consumes about the same amount of oxygen. What is the more accurate function it plays in the carbon cycle?
answer: A vast carbon sink — net absorber of CO2 (until recently)
choices: A vast carbon sink — net absorber of CO2 (until recently)
A net carbon source — always releasing more CO2 than absorbing
Climate-neutral — neither source nor sink of CO2
An oxygen-only producer with no role in CO2
context: Recent studies show parts of the Amazon, especially the southeast, have become net carbon sources because of deforestation and fires. The Amazon still functions as a carbon sink in much of its western and northern range. About 17% has been deforested since 1970; tipping-point estimates start at 20-25%.

question: Around the Arctic Circle, a belt of dense conifer forest covers about 17% of Earth's land surface — making it the largest terrestrial biome. The Russian name for the forest is widely used. What is it?
context: Taiga (Russian for 'forest') circles the northern hemisphere across Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia, and Russia. Spruce, fir, pine, and larch dominate; the soils are acidic and shallow. The taiga absorbs and stores enormous amounts of carbon — about 14% of the world's terrestrial carbon.

question: In California's Sierra Nevada, an inland cousin of the coastal redwood grows shorter but enormously thicker. The largest tree on Earth by trunk volume — 1,486 cubic metres, weighing about 1,200 tons — has a name. What is it?
context: General Sherman is about 2,200-2,700 years old. Giant sequoias only grow in about 70 isolated groves on the western Sierra Nevada slopes, mostly in Sequoia and Kings Canyon national parks. The biggest trees can sprout from a seed lighter than a grain of rice.

question: Off the southeast coast of Africa, the world's fourth-largest island has unique vegetation — about 85% of its plant species are found nowhere else. The most famous is a thick-trunked tree of which six of the eight species in the world grow only here. What tree is this?
context: Madagascar separated from mainland Africa about 165 million years ago, then from India about 88 million years ago. The 'Avenue of the Baobabs' near Morondava — a road lined with 800-year-old Adansonia grandidieri trees — is one of the most-photographed sites on the island.

question: On a remote Yemeni island in the Arabian Sea grows a bizarre umbrella-shaped tree whose red sap was used in medieval medicine and dye-making. About one-third of all plant species on the island grow nowhere else; the island has been isolated for millions of years. What is this tree called?
context: Socotra also holds the cucumber tree, the desert rose with bulbous trunk, and bizarre frankincense species. The island is sometimes called 'the Galapagos of the Indian Ocean' for its level of endemism. Recent civil war and Saudi-led conflict have made Socotra hard to visit.

question: In the western Pacific east of the Mariana Islands runs the deepest known place in the ocean. The bottom is about 10,935 metres below sea level — so deep that Everest, inverted, would still leave about 2 km of water above its peak. What is the deepest single point called?
context: Challenger Deep is named after the HMS Challenger expedition that found it in 1875. The first crewed descent (1960) was by Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in the bathyscaphe Trieste; Cameron and Bezos have also descended since. Pressure at the bottom is over 1,000 atmospheres.

question: The Pacific Ocean covers about 165 million sq km — more than all the land area of Earth combined. It is also the deepest ocean and holds about how much of all the water on Earth?
context: The Pacific's name comes from Magellan, who reached it after Atlantic storms and the Strait of Magellan and found calm seas — pacifico in Spanish. It is also slowly shrinking as Atlantic spreads and Pacific subducts under the Americas and Asia.

question: Off Japan's east coast flows a warm western-boundary current — the Pacific equivalent of the Gulf Stream. Its Japanese name means 'black current' (for the dark, clear, nutrient-poor tropical water). What is it called?
context: Kuroshio brings warm water and species north along Japan. It meets the cold Oyashio (Arctic-origin) current off northeast Japan, creating one of the most biologically productive zones on Earth — the Sanriku-Oki fishing ground.

question: Along the western coast of South America (mostly Peru and Chile) flows a cold north-flowing current that brings cold deep water to the surface (upwelling). The Humboldt feeds one of the world's most productive fisheries — accounting for nearly a fifth of all fish caught globally. What is the dominant fished species?
context: Anchoveta catch peaks at 8-10 million tons per year — among the largest single-species fisheries on Earth. Almost all becomes fishmeal for aquaculture and livestock feed. El Nino years collapse the upwelling and the anchoveta with it; the 1972 collapse triggered a global protein crisis.

question: Off the northeast coast of Australia stretches the largest living structure on Earth — a 2,300-km-long, 344,000-sq-km mosaic of about 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands, visible from space. What is it called?
context: The Great Barrier Reef hosts about 9,000 species. Coral bleaching — caused by warmer water expelling symbiotic algae — has hit it severely in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022. Roughly half of the reef's shallow-water coral cover has been lost since the mid-1990s; recovery happens between events but capacity is shrinking.

question: The largest barrier reef in the Western Hemisphere runs about 290 km off the coast of Belize. UNESCO World Heritage. Inside the reef sits a near-perfect circular sinkhole over 300 metres across — a former cave system that collapsed when sea level rose at the end of the last ice age. What is the sinkhole called?
context: The Blue Hole is 124 metres deep. Stalactites that hang from its underwater overhangs prove it was a dry cave at one point — about 14,000-153,000 years ago. Jacques Cousteau named it one of the 'top five scuba diving sites in the world' after exploring it in 1971.

question: Between Africa and Arabia stretches a narrow body of water that is widening by about 1-2 cm per year as the Arabian Plate splits from Africa. Geologists project that in some tens of millions of years it will be a full ocean. What is this body of water called?
context: The Red Sea is on a divergent boundary — same kind of boundary as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, but earlier in the process. The eponymous 'red' may come from seasonal cyanobacterial blooms or from a translation of the Greek 'Eritrean' (probably 'south', not 'red').

question: Between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in Canada lies a long narrow bay where the average tidal range is the largest on Earth — about 12 metres, with spring tides exceeding 16 metres in places. The bay's resonant frequency happens to match the tidal cycle. What is this bay called?
context: About 100 billion tons of water enter and leave the Bay of Fundy on each tide — more than all the rivers in the world combined. Reversing rapids and tidal bores happen at the heads of the bay's branches. Fundy is named for 'fondo' (Portuguese for 'deep' or 'bottom').

question: In the central North Atlantic floats the only sea on Earth with no land boundaries — instead, four ocean currents (the North Atlantic Gyre) circle around its still water. The sea is filled with floating yellow-brown algae for which it is named. What algae?
context: European and American eels both spawn somewhere in the Sargasso. The sea hosts a unique ecosystem of fish and invertebrates adapted to the floating sargassum. Recent years have seen blooms of sargassum so large they wash ashore in the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico in mats kilometres long.

question: In southeastern Utah's Arches National Park stands a 16-metre freestanding sandstone arch — appearing on the Utah license plate. It looks impossibly thin and is the symbol of Utah's red rock country. What is it called?
context: The arch has stood for at least 80,000 years. Park rangers were photographed measuring it; concerns about thinning sections caused the closure of the area beneath. Landscape Arch (88 m span) is technically the longest arch in the park; a 22-metre section of it fell off in 1991.

question: On Navajo Nation land in northeastern Arizona, a narrow sandstone canyon carved by flash floods rises 20 metres tall with walls only metres wide. Sunlight at noon falls through narrow openings as 'sunbeams' onto the canyon floor, lighting up the swirled red walls. What is this canyon called?
context: Antelope Canyon's name comes from herds of pronghorn antelope that once grazed nearby. Flash floods can be deadly even in clear weather; eleven tourists died in a 1997 flash flood here. The canyon is only accessible with Navajo tour guides.

question: About 50,000 years ago, a 50-metre-wide iron-nickel meteorite struck a flat plateau in what is now northern Arizona, creating a 1.2-km-wide, 170-metre-deep bowl. The crater is one of the best-preserved on Earth — the dry climate has barely weathered it. About how big was the impactor?
context: The impact released energy equivalent to about 10 megatons of TNT. The Apollo astronauts trained at Meteor Crater for lunar geology. Daniel Barringer bought it in 1902 expecting to mine a buried iron meteorite worth millions; he died bankrupt — the meteor had vaporised on impact.
