question: On the Bolivian altiplano at 3,656 metres lies the largest salt flat on Earth — 10,582 sq km of nearly perfectly flat white salt crust over a brine pool. In the rainy season a thin layer of water turns the entire surface into a mirror reflecting the sky. What is the salt flat called?
context: The salt is about 10 metres thick on average and overlies about 11 lakes of brine. Beneath the brine lies an estimated 70% of the world's lithium reserves. The salt was deposited by the drying of prehistoric Lake Minchin, about 40,000 years ago.

question: On the northern coast of Northern Ireland, about 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns step out into the sea — the cooled and fractured top of a Paleogene lava flow about 60 million years ago. Local legend says the giant Finn MacCool built it to fight a Scottish giant. What is the formation called?
context: The columns formed as the lava cooled and contracted, naturally fracturing in a hexagonal pattern (closest to a honeycomb of equal-sized cells). A similar feature, Fingal's Cave on the Scottish island of Staffa, was once connected to the same lava flow before the Atlantic opened up.

question: In northeastern Wyoming rises a 265-metre-tall flat-topped igneous monolith that geologists believe is the eroded core of an ancient volcanic intrusion. Lakota and Cheyenne peoples consider it sacred. It featured prominently in the 1977 film Close Encounters of the Third Kind. What is its name in English?
context: The Lakota name Mato Tipila ('Bear Lodge') reflects the legend that the tower's vertical scoring marks where a giant bear clawed it. President Theodore Roosevelt declared it the first U.S. National Monument in 1906. Climbers ascend its rock columns; a voluntary climbing ban honours indigenous spiritual practice in June.

question: In central Australia, a 348-metre-tall sandstone monolith rises sharply from the flat desert. It is the eroded tip of a much larger underground rock formation — most of the rock lies hidden below the surface. What kind of formation is it?
context: Uluru's iron content reddens at sunrise and sunset. Estimates of how much of the rock is below the surface vary — some say only about 10% is visible. Uluru and the nearby Kata Tjuta (the Olgas) are part of the same basement rock unit.

question: On the Filipino island of Bohol stand about 1,500 nearly identical conical limestone hills, about 30-50 metres tall. Their grass turns brown each dry season, giving the impression of a chocolate landscape. What kind of geological feature are they?
context: Tropical karst forms in humid climates where chemical weathering dissolves limestone faster than mechanical erosion. The Chocolate Hills are an unusual case where the hills are remarkably uniform; theories include uplifted ancient coral reefs eroded uniformly by groundwater.

question: In Western Australia, a 14-metre-tall, 100-metre-long granite outcrop forms a perfect curl like an enormous surf wave about to break. The 'wave' face has been carved over 2.7 billion years by chemical weathering followed by erosion. What is this rock called?
context: Wave Rock is part of the granite outcrop called Hyden Rock. Chemical weathering at the base of the rock, where groundwater pools, slowly hollowed out the curl shape; later erosion has revealed it as the rock emerged from soil. The streaks on the wall are mineral run-off from the weathering.

question: On the borders of Venezuela, Brazil, and Guyana rises a 2,810-metre table mountain — a tepui, the world's oldest mountain plateau, separated from surrounding lowlands by cliffs 400-1,000 metres tall. The isolated summit hosts species found nowhere else on Earth. Arthur Conan Doyle's 1912 novel borrowed its mystery for his book title. What was the book?
context: Roraima's flat summit is about 30 sq km. The tepui plateau hosts carnivorous plants and unique endemic species (a small frog, a cricket, a specialised bird). Climbers reach the summit via a 'natural staircase' on the Venezuelan side. The vegetation on top — adapted to extreme leaching of nutrients — is bizarre.

question: In southwest Iceland, a hot spring that erupts gives the entire phenomenon its name in English. Records of its eruptions go back to 1294. Its current eruptions are sporadic; nearby Strokkur is more reliable, erupting every 5-10 minutes. What is the original spring called?
context: The English word 'geyser' derives from this Icelandic spring — from Old Norse 'geysa', to gush. Geysir's eruptions stopped largely after silica was added to its plumbing in the 20th century, in unsuccessful attempts to revive eruptions. Earthquakes occasionally restart it briefly.

question: In Ethiopia's Danakil Depression — one of the lowest points on land at 125 metres below sea level — hot acidic mineral pools cluster on a sulfur-coated salt plain. Iron, salt, sulfur, and bacteria turn the pools brilliant yellow, green, orange, and white. The air temperature averages 35°C year-round, among the hottest inhabited places. What is this site called?
context: Dallol sits over a still-active volcanic complex. The Afar people mine salt here in traditional camel-caravan operations. Visitors come on guided trips with armed escort — the Eritrean border is contested and bandit attacks happen. Dallol is among the most extreme environments on Earth's surface.

question: On hot tarmac on a desert road, a shimmering 'puddle' that disappears as you approach is actually an image of the sky bent into your eyes by a layer of very hot air just above the road. What is this kind of mirage called?
context: Inferior mirages put the false image below the real object (the sky is below your eye-line in the puddle effect). Superior mirages put the image above the real object — and can produce phantom ships, distant cliffs, and the famous Fata Morgana of the Strait of Messina.

question: Sometimes after a rain shower you can see two concentric rainbows — a brighter inner one with red on top, and a fainter outer one with red on the bottom (colours reversed). Between them lies a darker band where no rainbow forms. What is the darker band called?
context: Alexander of Aphrodisias described it around 200 AD. The primary rainbow comes from one internal reflection inside each raindrop; the secondary from two reflections. The dark band is the angular gap where neither one nor two reflections puts light into your eye.

question: On full-moon nights at Victoria Falls in Africa, when mist from the falls fills the air, a rainbow forms in the moonlight — a pale arc against the dark sky. What is this phenomenon called?
context: Moonbows are physically identical to ordinary rainbows but appear much fainter because moonlight is about 400,000 times dimmer than sunlight. They appear nearly white to the naked eye; long-exposure photography reveals colour. Victoria Falls and a few other waterfall locations are reliable moonbow spots.

question: On cold winter days, two bright spots of light may appear flanking the sun at the same elevation, about 22° away on each side. Hexagonal ice crystals in high cirrus clouds act as tiny prisms refracting the light. What are these spots called?
context: Sun dogs form a triple image of the sun. The Latin name parhelion means 'beside the sun'. The same crystals can also produce a 22° halo around the sun — a faint ring at the same radius.

question: Each year in early June, a massive seasonal wind shift brings the rains that water about a fifth of the world's people in South Asia. The summer monsoon arrives first on the southwest tip of India, in the state of Kerala. What is the rough date of arrival?
context: Indian agriculture and economic life still rotates around the monsoon's onset. Failure or weakness causes drought and famine; excess causes flooding. The mechanism — solar heating of the Tibetan plateau drawing in moist air from the Indian Ocean — is a major topic in modern climate science.

question: Between the equator and about 30 degrees north and south, steady easterly winds blow from the higher pressure subtropical highs toward the equator. European sailing ships used them to cross the Atlantic toward the New World. What are these winds called?
context: Columbus rode the trades west. The name 'trade' comes from an obsolete English meaning of 'track' or 'path' — the winds blow along a regular path. The trade winds converge near the equator in the Intertropical Convergence Zone, where they spawn most of the world's tropical thunderstorms.

question: On the eastern (lee) side of the Rocky Mountains in Alberta and Montana, a warm dry wind sometimes sweeps down from the mountains in winter, raising temperatures by 20-30°C in hours and melting snow. Native peoples called it 'snow-eater'. What is the meteorological name?
context: Chinook is descended cold air that has dropped its moisture on the windward side of the mountains and adiabatically warmed as it sank. Similar warm-dry foehn winds happen on the lee of many mountain ranges worldwide; the Chinook is North America's example.

question: Surrounding each pole in the stratosphere swirls a circumpolar low-pressure system of frigid air. When it weakens or splits, lobes of Arctic air can spill far south, causing record cold in regions like the central United States or Europe. What is this called?
context: The polar vortex weakens when stratospheric warming events happen — a wave of warming travels from the tropics. Famous polar vortex breakouts hit the U.S. in January 2014 and again in February 2021, freezing Texas. Climate change appears to be making such breakouts more common, paradoxically.

question: On New Zealand's remote outer islands lives the world's largest and longest-lived parrot — a nocturnal, flightless, ground-dwelling species that smells strongly of honey and moss. It evolved in the absence of mammals; introduced rats and possums nearly drove it extinct. How many remain (as of 2024)?
context: The kakapo population has been growing slowly under intensive conservation management. Each bird has a name and is tracked individually. They live on predator-free offshore islands. The species breeds only when certain native trees mast — every 2-4 years.

question: Across the plains of Tanzania and Kenya, about 1.5 million wildebeest, 200,000 zebras, and 500,000 Thomson's gazelles move in an annual cycle following seasonal rains and grass. The herd crosses the Grumeti and Mara rivers — where huge Nile crocodiles wait. What is this cycle called?
context: The migration's exact timing varies — it tracks rainfall, not the calendar. About 250,000 wildebeest die each year during the cycle from drowning, predation, or exhaustion. The Serengeti National Park and Maasai Mara National Reserve combine to protect the entire migration route.

question: In certain bays in Puerto Rico, the Maldives, and Jamaica, swimmers stir the water at night and the wake glows brilliant blue-green. Microscopic single-celled algae produce light when disturbed — a defensive response thought to startle predators or attract bigger fish to eat them. What are these organisms?
context: Bahia Bioluminiscente in Vieques, Puerto Rico, holds the highest concentration ever measured — about 700,000 dinoflagellates per gallon. The reaction uses luciferin and luciferase, the same enzyme family that lights up fireflies. Light pollution reduces the visible effect; the brightest experiences are away from cities.

question: In the Western Caucasus of Abkhazia, a cave descends 2,212 metres below its entrance — the deepest known cave on Earth, surpassed in 2018 by another cave just down the mountain. Climbing down takes weeks; cavers camp in the cave for the descent. What is the cave called?
context: Cave depth is measured from highest entrance to lowest passage point. Krubera-Voronya was the world's deepest from 2001 to 2018; Veryovkina now holds the record at 2,212 m. Both lie in the Arabika Massif of Abkhazia.

question: In central Vietnam, a single cave passage measures 9 km long, with one section over 200 metres high and 150 metres wide — large enough that a Boeing 747 could fly through it. A jungle grows on the floor where sinkhole roofs have collapsed. What is the cave called?
context: Son Doong was only discovered by science in 1991 and first explored in 2009. The British Cave Research Association mapped it; tours started in 2013, limited to about 1,000 visitors per year. The cave has its own ecosystem of bats, river fish, and even monkeys living in the open sections.

question: Along tropical coastlines, salt-tolerant trees grow with their roots partly submerged in salty tidal water. Their tangled aerial root systems trap sediment, build land, and buffer storm surges. What is this kind of forest called?
context: Bangladesh's Sundarbans — the largest mangrove forest in the world — buffers Bangladesh from cyclonic surges. Mangrove loss accelerates storm damage; the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed disproportionately more people where mangroves had been cleared for shrimp farming. Restoration is a major coastal-engineering tool.

question: On Sicily's east coast rises Europe's largest active volcano — about 3,330 metres tall, although its summit height changes from eruption to eruption. UNESCO World Heritage 2013. The local Sicilian name for the mountain reflects the constancy of fire activity. What is the local nickname?
context: Etna has been continuously active for about 500,000 years. The Greek myth places the workshop of Hephaestus inside it. Etna's wine industry has revived in the past two decades — vineyards on lava-rich black soils.

question: On 27 August 1883, an Indonesian island volcano erupted in one of the most powerful explosions of modern recorded history. The sound was heard about 4,800 km away in Perth and Mauritius. The tsunami killed about 36,000 people. What is the volcano's name?
context: The 1883 eruption ejected about 21 cubic km of material. A new volcano — Anak Krakatau, 'Child of Krakatoa' — has been growing in the same caldera since 1927. A 2018 partial collapse of Anak Krakatau caused another deadly tsunami.

question: Beneath Yellowstone National Park sits one of the world's largest volcanic systems — a caldera 70 km across, formed by three colossal eruptions in the past 2.1 million years. The most recent (about 631,000 years ago) ejected about 1,000 cubic km of material. What kind of volcano is this?
context: Yellowstone's three giant eruptions came roughly 2.1, 1.3, and 0.63 million years ago — a rough 700,000-year interval. Whether the next one is geologically imminent or millions of years away is debated. The current state — geothermal features, slow uplift — is interpreted as 'active and restless'.

question: Around the Pacific Ocean basin runs a 40,000-km horseshoe-shaped belt that contains about 75% of the world's active and dormant volcanoes and about 90% of its earthquakes. The activity is driven by subduction at the basin's edges. What is this belt called?
context: Major Ring of Fire countries include Chile, Peru, Mexico, the U.S. (West Coast), Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia, and New Zealand. Mount St Helens, Mount Pinatubo, Krakatoa, Tambora, Fuji, Mount Cotopaxi, and Popocatepetl are all on the ring.

question: Off the coasts of California, Chile, South Africa, and New Zealand, fast-growing brown algae form underwater 'forests' up to 50 metres tall. The species can grow 60 cm a day. Diverse species — sea otters, abalones, sheephead, leopard sharks — depend on them. What is the canopy-forming species along the U.S. West Coast?
context: Giant kelp anchors to rock with a holdfast, builds a stalk via internal gas-filled floats, and forms a canopy at the surface. Sea otters protect kelp forests by eating sea urchins that otherwise overgraze the kelp; their return to California since the 1970s has restored vast kelp ecosystems.

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza, completed around 2560 BC for Pharaoh Khufu, is aligned with the four cardinal directions to within about a tenth of a degree. The four sides of its base have lengths within a few centimetres of each other. About how many limestone blocks make it up?
context: Average block weight is about 2.5 tons; the largest in the King's Chamber weigh 50-80 tons. How they were moved and stacked is still debated; recently a papyrus of an overseer named Merer detailed limestone-block transport via canals. The pyramid's sides are oriented to within 3 arc minutes of cardinal directions.

question: Beside the Great Pyramid at Giza sits a colossal limestone statue of a recumbent lion with a human head — 73 metres long and 20 metres tall, carved from a single bedrock outcrop. The face is generally thought to portray Pharaoh Khafre (Khefren), Khufu's son. What is its English name?
context: The Sphinx has lost its nose — the popular story blaming Napoleon's troops is false; it was already gone in 18th-century drawings. Etched between its paws is the 'Dream Stele' of Thutmose IV (1400 BC), which describes a dream that led him to excavate the body from desert sand.

question: Beneath the western desert hills near Luxor lies a dry valley where most New Kingdom pharaohs (about 1500-1070 BC) were buried in rock-cut tombs. The 1922 discovery of one nearly intact royal tomb by Howard Carter (funded by Lord Carnarvon) made global headlines for years. Whose tomb was this?
context: Tutankhamun was a minor short-reigned pharaoh (1332-1323 BC), about 19 when he died. His tomb survived robbery because dust from cutting a later tomb above it concealed the entrance. Carter found over 5,000 objects, including the iconic gold death mask.

question: On the west bank of the Nile, four colossal seated statues of Pharaoh Ramesses II — each 20 metres tall — flank the entrance to a temple cut into the cliffside around 1264 BC. In the 1960s, the entire temple complex was cut into about 1,000 blocks (averaging 20 tons each) and moved to higher ground. Why?
answer: To save it from flooding by Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam
choices: To save it from flooding by Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam
To save it from earthquake damage in the Aswan area
To enable a new tourist-access tunnel for visitors
To consolidate it with the Karnak temple complex
context: The 1960-1968 rescue, funded by 50 countries through UNESCO, lifted the temple about 65 metres up and 200 metres back. Twice a year (22 February and 22 October), sunlight at dawn penetrates the inner sanctuary to illuminate the king and his deified self — the relocation preserved this within hours' difference.

question: The Nabataeans, who carved Petra into Jordanian sandstone cliffs from the 4th century BC onward, made the desert blossom by managing flash floods and rainfall. Their system of channels, cisterns, and dams stored enough water that Petra could host tens of thousands of people. What was the structure that diverted flash floods from the Siq?
choices: A buried channel from Wadi Araba
context: The flash floods in the Siq (the narrow canyon entrance) could and did kill visitors caught inside — 22 French tourists died in 1963 before the dam was repaired. The Nabataean channels around the cliffs and the dam at the canyon mouth kept the Siq dry through their 600-year occupation.

question: In central Syria stand the ruins of a Roman caravan city that briefly defied Rome under a warrior-queen in the 3rd century AD. Her armies captured Egypt and most of Anatolia before Emperor Aurelian defeated her in 272. Some of her temple and colonnade ruins were dynamited by ISIS in 2015. Who was the queen?
context: Zenobia (Septimia Bathzabbai Zenobia) claimed descent from Cleopatra. After her capture, accounts say she was paraded in golden chains through Rome, then either executed or settled to live as a Roman noblewoman. The ISIS destruction targeted the temples of Bel and Baalshamin and the Arch of Triumph.

question: In Lebanon's Bekaa Valley stand the ruins of one of the largest Roman temple complexes ever built, dedicated to Jupiter, Bacchus, and Venus in the 1st-3rd centuries AD. The Temple of Jupiter once had 54 columns; only six still stand. Foundation stones include some of the largest cut stones ever used. About how heavy is the largest?
context: The 'Stone of the Pregnant Woman' in a nearby quarry was never moved; a similar 1,650-ton stone was found there in 2014. How the Romans moved similar (smaller) stones to Baalbek's foundations is unclear. The site predates Roman use — it had been sacred for millennia.

question: About 90 km northeast of Persepolis stands the simple six-stepped limestone tomb of the founder of the Persian Empire, who died around 530 BC after building the largest empire the world had yet seen. Alexander the Great paid his respects there in 324 BC. Whose tomb is this?
context: The tomb is a 6-metre-tall house-shaped chamber on a stepped platform. Cyrus's empire stretched from Anatolia to Central Asia; he is praised in the Hebrew Bible for freeing the Jews from Babylonian captivity. The Cyrus Cylinder (a clay barrel with his proclamation) is sometimes called the first declaration of human rights.

question: In southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), one of the earliest cities of human civilisation rose around 4000 BC. By 2100 BC, King Ur-Nammu built a vast three-tier brick stepped temple platform here. The kingdom of Ur was the home of the biblical Abraham. What kind of structure is the stepped temple platform called?
context: Ziggurat means 'raised up' or 'high' in Akkadian. The Ziggurat of Ur is one of the best-preserved; American 20th-century reconstruction restored the lowest tier. Ziggurats were not tombs but temple platforms — the shrine of the god sat at the top. The biblical Tower of Babel is thought to be inspired by the Etemenanki ziggurat in Babylon.

question: The mythical site of Homer's Iliad was found in 1870-90 by the German amateur Heinrich Schliemann digging at Hisarlik in northwest Turkey. Schliemann found that the site contained multiple superimposed cities — at least nine, going back to the Bronze Age. How did Schliemann's digging methods damage the site?
answer: He dug a deep trench through to bedrock, destroying upper layers
choices: He dug a deep trench through to bedrock, destroying upper layers
He used explosives that destroyed key foundations
He removed all artefacts to Russia in unmarked boxes
He left the trenches open, exposing the ruins to weather damage
context: Schliemann's 'Troy II' (a Bronze Age city he had identified with Homer's Troy) actually predates the Trojan War by a thousand years. The true Homeric layer is now identified as Troy VIIa, which was destroyed by fire around 1180 BC — close to traditional dating.

question: On a hill in Greece's Peloponnese stand the ruins of one of the major Bronze Age citadel-cities of the Aegean. Its main entrance is topped by a massive triangular relief of two heraldic lions flanking a central column — one of the oldest sculptural monuments in Europe (around 1250 BC). What is this gate called?
context: The lions' heads are missing — they may have been made of separate inset stones. The walls of Mycenae are built of stones so large the later Greeks thought only Cyclopes could have moved them; 'Cyclopean masonry' is the technical term. Heinrich Schliemann also dug Mycenae; he found a gold death mask he called 'the mask of Agamemnon'.

question: On the island of Crete, the largest Bronze Age palace in Greece was excavated 1900-1931 by Sir Arthur Evans. He named the civilisation after the legendary king Minos. The complex's many corridors and rooms (over 1,000) probably inspired the Greek myth of a particular monster's lair. What was the monster?
context: Evans was a controversial figure; he heavily reconstructed Knossos in concrete, which most modern archaeologists consider too speculative. The Minoan script Linear A remains undeciphered; Linear B was cracked in 1952 by Michael Ventris and proved to be an early form of Greek.

question: On the Greek Peloponnese, an open-air theatre built around 340 BC seats 14,000 spectators on stone benches climbing a hillside. Its acoustics are famous: a coin dropped at the centre stage can be heard in the back row, 60 metres away. The shape and gradient are responsible. What is this theatre called?
context: Recent acoustic research credits the stone steps acting as a corrugated filter — they let high frequencies (consonants and the higher partials of vowels) through to the rear seats while dampening low background noise. The theatre is part of the Sanctuary of Asclepius, the ancient Greek god of medicine.

question: At Olympia in Greece, the ancient sanctuary of Zeus held a 12-metre seated statue of the god — gold and ivory over a wooden core, designed by Phidias around 435 BC. It was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. What happened to the statue?
answer: It was moved to Constantinople and destroyed in a fire around 475 AD
choices: It was moved to Constantinople and destroyed in a fire around 475 AD
It was buried beneath the Olympia temple ruins and never recovered
It was shipped to Rome and was lost when Vesuvius destroyed Pompeii
It still survives, in the Olympia archaeological museum
context: After Christianity replaced classical religion, the statue lost its function. Theodosius II moved it to Constantinople in the 4th century; it perished in the great Lauseion palace fire. The Olympia temple itself was destroyed by earthquakes in the 5th-6th centuries. The site hosted the ancient Olympic Games from about 776 BC.

question: On the Tyrrhenian coast south of Naples stand three nearly intact Greek temples — built around 600-450 BC by Greek colonists from Sybaris. The three are some of the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere outside Greece itself. What were these Greek colonial cities collectively called?
context: Magna Graecia covered southern Italy and Sicily. Greek colonisation in the 8th-6th centuries BC introduced the alphabet, coinage, and political ideas to the western Mediterranean. The Doric temples at Paestum (originally Greek Poseidonia) survived because the area declined and was abandoned, then forgotten in malarial swamps.

question: Across the Gardon river in southern France stands a 49-metre-tall Roman aqueduct bridge — three superimposed tiers of arches, built around 50 AD as part of a 50-km aqueduct supplying water to the city of Nimes. The whole 50-km channel descends only 17 metres in total. What is this aqueduct called?
context: Roman aqueducts moved water on a slight constant gradient using only gravity — no pumps. The Pont du Gard's middle and upper levels were built without mortar; only friction and gravity hold the limestone blocks together. About 200 cubic metres of water flowed across daily.

question: In 312 BC the Roman censor Appius Claudius Caecus began the construction of a major paved road running south from Rome — the first of the great long-distance Roman highways. The road eventually ran 580 km to Brundisium (modern Brindisi) on the Adriatic coast. Sections of the original lava-stone blocks survive. What is this road called?
context: The Appian Way was used for over two millennia. About 6,000 of Spartacus's followers were crucified along it after the failed slave revolt of 71 BC. Roman roads totalled over 400,000 km at the empire's peak; about 80,000 km were paved.

question: About a kilometre north of Angkor Wat lies the walled city of Angkor Thom, the late-12th-century capital of King Jayavarman VII. At its centre stands a Buddhist temple whose 54 towers each carry four giant carved faces — 216 faces gazing in all directions. What is this temple called?
context: The faces are usually identified as Avalokiteshvara, the Buddha of compassion, possibly with Jayavarman's features. Some scholars argue they portray the king himself. The temple sits at the geographic centre of Angkor Thom, considered the centre of the Khmer Buddhist universe.

question: About 1 km east of Angkor Thom in Cambodia, a 12th-century Buddhist temple has been deliberately left in the embrace of the jungle. Massive silk-cotton and strangler fig trees grow on, around, and through the masonry — roots gripping walls, towers held up only by the trees themselves. What is this temple called?
context: Ta Prohm was used as a location for Tomb Raider (2001), and is now sometimes called the 'Tomb Raider Temple'. Conservation policy keeps the trees where they are not too dangerous; removing them would collapse the masonry, which only the roots hold together.

question: Twenty kilometres northeast of Angkor lies a small Cambodian Hindu temple built in pink-tinted sandstone — the finest stone carving of the Khmer Empire. The reliefs are so deep, sharp, and ornate that the temple has been called 'the jewel of Khmer art'. The name means 'citadel of women'. When was it built?
answer: 967 AD (under Rajendravarman II and Jayavarman V)
choices: 967 AD (under Rajendravarman II and Jayavarman V)
context: Banteay Srei is unusual: it was not built by a king but by a court Brahmin named Yajnavaraha. Its dwarf-scale doorways and reliefs led 19th-century French scholars to mistakenly think it was a child-temple. Andre Malraux was convicted in 1923 of stealing reliefs from it; he later became a French minister of culture.

question: On the Indonesian island of Java sits the largest Buddhist monument on Earth — nine stacked terraces ascending to a central stupa, with 504 Buddha statues, 2,672 relief panels, and a total length of relief about 5 km. Walked clockwise as a pilgrimage. When was it built?
context: The structure rises 35 metres on a base 123 metres on a side. Earthquakes and volcanic ash buried Borobudur for centuries; British colonial administrator Stamford Raffles 'rediscovered' it in 1814. A massive UNESCO restoration in the 1970s dismantled and reassembled much of it to fix groundwater damage.

question: On the plains along the Irrawaddy river in central Myanmar, the medieval capital of the first unified Burmese kingdom (1044-1297) covered about 100 sq km with over 10,000 Buddhist temples and pagodas. About 2,200 brick monuments still stand. What is the city called?
context: Bagan was the centre of Theravada Buddhism in Southeast Asia for centuries. A devastating earthquake in 1975 destroyed many temples; the 2016 quake brought down more. UNESCO World Heritage 2019 — long delayed because the government's reconstructions in the 1990s were considered too speculative.

question: In the former capital of Siam, sacked by the Burmese in 1767, lies one of the most photographed Buddhist relics in Asia: a stone Buddha head fully wrapped in the roots of a Bodhi (strangler fig) tree. The head fell from a statue and the tree grew around it over the centuries. What is the city's name?
context: Ayutthaya was named after Ayodhya, Rama's city in the Indian Ramayana. Its founder, King Ramathibodi I, established it in 1351. At its peak in the 17th century it was one of the world's largest cities. UNESCO World Heritage 1991.

question: In central Sri Lanka rises a 200-metre dome of igneous rock, on top of which a 5th-century king built a fortress-palace. The entrance once passed through the open mouth of a giant carved-stone lion (only the paws survive). Wall paintings of 'cloud maidens' survive in a sheltered overhang. Who built the fortress?
context: Kassapa (Kasyapa) seized the throne in 477 AD by murdering his father and walling him into a cistern. He built Sigiriya as fortress against expected attack by his half-brother Moggallana, who eventually defeated him in 495. The fortress was abandoned and became a Buddhist monastery.

question: In western India, a single Hindu temple was carved straight downward from a basalt cliff face beginning around 760 AD — the largest monolithic excavation of stone in the world. About 200,000 tons of rock were removed from above to leave a freestanding temple in the void. What is the temple called?
context: The Kailasa Temple is dedicated to Shiva and resembles Mount Kailash, his Himalayan home. It was built top-down — carving started from the cliff top and proceeded downward. The temple is 30 metres tall; the rock removed would fill a building 40 storeys high.

question: On a steep hillside in eastern Kyoto stands a wooden Buddhist temple founded in 778 AD. Its main hall projects out from the slope on a stage of 13-metre wooden pillars assembled without a single nail. From this stage, a Japanese idiom says, 'to leap off' means to make a desperate decision. What is the temple called?
context: Kiyomizu-dera is named for the three waterfalls at its base — visitors drink from them for longevity, love, and academic success. The temple has burnt down many times; the current main hall dates from 1633 under Tokugawa Iemitsu. The Edo-era 'leap from the stage' was an actual gesture: 234 historical leaps are recorded; survival rate was about 85%.

question: On the Konya Plain in southern Turkey, archaeologists have excavated a vast Neolithic settlement of about 8,000 people living from 7400 to 6200 BC in densely packed mud-brick houses, entered through ceiling hatches because there were no streets. People walked across the rooftops. Wall paintings inside depict hunting scenes. What is this site called?
context: Catalhoyuk had no doors at ground level; houses opened only through the roof. The dead were buried under the floors, sometimes with red ochre or mounted bull skulls. The settlement abandoned domestic interior animal-skull mounting and shifted to other practices in its later phases. UNESCO World Heritage 2012.

question: The main north-south axis of the great city of Teotihuacan is a 2.5-km boulevard flanked by ceremonial buildings, ending at the Pyramid of the Moon at one end and continuing southward toward the Ciudadela complex. The Aztecs named it for what they imagined the buildings were. What did they call it?
context: The Aztecs called the flanking platforms 'tombs' (incorrectly — they were ceremonial buildings). The 'avenue' actually shifts about 15 degrees east of true north — possibly aligned with the setting Pleiades on the day of the sun's first solar passage. UNESCO World Heritage 1987.

question: In the dense jungle of northern Guatemala lie the ruins of a city that flourished from about 600 BC to 100 AD — the largest Preclassic Maya city, with the largest pyramid by total volume in the Americas. La Danta pyramid contains about 2.8 million cubic metres of fill — more than the Great Pyramid of Giza. What is this city called?
context: El Mirador peaked centuries before the Classic Maya — sometimes called the 'cradle of Maya civilization'. The city was abandoned around 150 AD, possibly due to deforestation and soil collapse from making lime plaster. The LiDAR surveys 2018-2022 have revealed enormous suburbs and causeways previously hidden under jungle.

question: On a 12-metre limestone cliff on the eastern Yucatan coast stand the ruins of a small late-Maya port (active 13th-15th centuries) — among the few Mayan cities still inhabited when the Spanish arrived. The site has white-sand beaches at its base and a temple oriented for the heliacal rising of Venus. What is this site called?
context: Tulum was originally called Zama ('city of dawn') for its east-facing position. The Templo del Dios Descendente shows a figure diving headfirst — possibly the Mayan Venus god or the bee god Ah Mucen Cab. The city traded with merchants by sea-canoe routes spanning the whole Caribbean coast.

question: Beneath modern Mexico City lie the ruins of the Aztec capital, founded around 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. When Hernan Cortes arrived in 1519, the city was probably larger than any European city of the time. About how many people lived there?
context: Tenochtitlan was reached by causeways from the mainland. The city had aqueducts, sewers, public schools, markets, and a vast central ceremonial precinct. Cortes burned it in 1521 after a brutal siege; Mexico City was built directly atop the ruins.

question: In the centre of the Aztec capital stood a double pyramid honouring two gods on its twin summits — the rain god on the north side, the war and sun god on the south. The Spanish dismantled the pyramid to build the colonial cathedral; the ruins were rediscovered in 1978 when electrical workers found a stone disc. What is this pyramid called?
context: The 1978 discovery of the Coyolxauhqui Stone (the dismembered moon goddess) led to systematic excavation. The Templo Mayor was rebuilt seven times by successive Aztec rulers; each rebuild encased the earlier structure, so the inner cores survive. The site is now a museum directly behind Mexico City's cathedral.

question: In southern Ohio runs a 411-metre earthwork in the shape of an undulating serpent, jaws open around an oval (perhaps an egg, perhaps the sun). It is the largest effigy mound in the world. Radiocarbon dates have been disputed — possibly Adena culture (300 BC) or possibly Fort Ancient (1000-1100 AD). What is it called?
context: The Serpent Mound's head aligns with the summer solstice sunset; the curves of its body may align with other astronomical events. The site was nearly lost to plowing in the 19th century before being purchased and preserved by the Peabody Museum in 1888.

question: On the desert north coast of Peru sit the ruins of the largest adobe city ever built — about 20 sq km, 30,000 buildings, 10 walled royal compounds. It was the capital of the Chimu Empire (about 900-1470 AD), defeated and absorbed by the Inca. What is this city called?
context: Chan Chan was originally elaborately decorated with painted plaster reliefs of waves, sea creatures, and geometric patterns. Heavy rainfall during El Nino events has damaged the adobe; large sections are now covered by protective roofing. UNESCO World Heritage 1986, on the in-Danger list since 1986.

question: Above Cusco rises an Inca complex of three concentric zigzag walls of huge polygonal stones — some weighing over 100 tons — fitted together so precisely that a knife blade cannot pass between them, with no mortar. The walls form the head of the puma in the Inca city plan of Cusco. What is this complex called?
context: Sacsayhuaman ('satisfied falcon' in Quechua) is among the most extraordinary masonry feats in the world. The Inca polished and shaped the stones to fit by trial fitting — Spanish chroniclers describe craftsmen sliding stones back and forth and chipping. Spaniards used the easily-removable upper stones to build colonial Cusco; only the largest base stones survive.

question: In Peru's Sacred Valley near Cusco, an Inca fortress-town descends in steep terraces from a temple plateau down to the modern town below. The site is one of the few places where the Inca defeated a Spanish military expedition (1537), under Manco Inca. Massive andesite blocks survive at the top of the temple terrace. What is the town called?
context: Manco Inca dammed the Patacancha river and flooded the Spanish cavalry; the survivors retreated to Cusco. The Inca eventually withdrew to Vilcabamba in the jungle, where they held out until 1572. Ollantaytambo's grid-pattern street plan still survives in the modern town.

question: About 65 km west of Machu Picchu in remote Peruvian jungle sits an Inca royal estate of similar size and grandeur — but accessible only via a tough two-day hike. Only about 30% of the site has been excavated. It is sometimes called 'Machu Picchu's sister'. What is its name?
context: Choquequirao is at 3,033 metres elevation. A controversial cable car proposal would make it as accessible as Machu Picchu (which now sees about 1.5 million visitors a year). The site contains a series of llama-shaped stone terraces — 24 white llamas in profile, climbing a hillside.

question: Down the Nile in modern Sudan stand the ruins of the ancient Kushite kingdom of Meroe — its royal cemetery contains more pyramids than all of Egypt combined (about 250, compared to Egypt's ~120, although smaller). The pyramids are tall and steep. They were built between roughly 800 BC and 300 AD. What is the modern country?
context: Meroe was the southern Kingdom of Kush capital. Italian doctor Giuseppe Ferlini blew open many tops in the 1830s looking for treasure, destroying the upper sections. UNESCO World Heritage 2011. The Nubian pyramids are smaller and steeper than Egyptian ones — perhaps 60-degree faces vs Egyptian 50-degree.

question: In southeastern Zimbabwe sit the dry-stone-wall ruins of a 11th-15th-century Bantu-speaking kingdom, the largest stone structures in sub-Saharan Africa before the colonial era. The 11-metre-tall walls of the Great Enclosure run 250 metres in a circle without mortar, made of perfectly fitted granite blocks. The country takes its name from these ruins. What does 'Zimbabwe' mean?
context: Cecil Rhodes and other colonial-era Europeans refused to accept African builders could have made the ruins, attributing them variously to Phoenicians, Arabs, or biblical Queen of Sheba. African scholars confirmed Bantu builders in the early 20th century; the modern Zimbabwean state took its name from the site in 1980.

question: On a small island off the coast of southern Tanzania, the ruins of a Swahili-Arab-African trading city flourished from the 9th to 16th centuries — when it controlled the gold trade from Great Zimbabwe to the Arab world. The 14th-century Great Mosque had a domed roof in the Indian Ocean style. What is the city called?
context: Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa in 1331 and described it as among the most beautiful cities in the world. The Portuguese sacked it in 1505; it never fully recovered. UNESCO World Heritage 1981, on in-Danger list 2004-2014.

question: In southeastern Algeria, in the heart of what is now Sahara, sandstone rock shelters preserve over 15,000 paintings and engravings of cattle, hippos, giraffes, dancers, and chariots — testifying that the green Sahara 6,000 years ago was a savanna. The art ranges from 12,000 to 1,000 years old. What is this region called?
context: Tassili n'Ajjer means 'plateau of rivers' in the Tuareg language — preserving the memory of the wet Sahara. The art shows the cultural shift from hunting-gathering to cattle pastoralism to camel pastoralism, tracking the gradual desertification. UNESCO World Heritage 1982.

question: In County Meath, Ireland, stands a 5,200-year-old passage tomb — older than Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids — built by Neolithic farmers around 3200 BC. A 19-metre stone passage leads to a central chamber under a corbelled stone vault. At dawn on the winter solstice, a beam of sunlight passes through a 'roof box' above the entrance and lights up the inner chamber. What is the tomb called?
context: The Newgrange solstice alignment was rediscovered in 1967 by archaeologist Michael O'Kelly. The light enters at 8:58 AM on the solstice morning and persists for about 17 minutes. A lottery selects a small number of visitors to be inside the chamber on the actual solstice morning each year.

question: On the south coast of Brittany, France, more than 3,000 standing stones (menhirs) stretch in parallel rows for about 8 km — the largest concentration of megalithic monuments in the world. They were erected between 4500 and 3300 BC by Neolithic farmers. What is their purpose generally thought to be?
answer: Unknown — astronomical, ritual, or funerary functions proposed
choices: Unknown — astronomical, ritual, or funerary functions proposed
Almost certainly defensive — they were barriers against raiders
Almost certainly agricultural — they marked field boundaries
Almost certainly commercial — they marked trade routes
context: The Carnac stones are some of the oldest megalithic monuments in the world. The Menec rows alone hold 1,099 menhirs in 11 rows. Some align with sunrise points; others may have served as ritual processional avenues. No clear consensus exists.

question: On the wall of a cave in Périgord (Dordogne), south-west France, are paintings of horses, aurochs, bison, deer, and human stick figures — about 600 figures dating to around 17,000-15,000 years ago, in the Upper Paleolithic. Four teenage boys discovered the cave in 1940 while exploring for a buried treasure. What is the cave called?
context: Lascaux was closed to visitors in 1963 because the carbon dioxide breath of tourists was damaging the paintings; a full-size replica (Lascaux II) was built nearby and opened in 1983. A second replica (Lascaux IV) opened in 2016. The cave preserved the paintings because it was sealed by a rockfall shortly after the artwork.

question: On the Orkney Islands off Scotland's north coast, a 5,000-year-old Neolithic village was uncovered when a storm in 1850 stripped sand from a coastal dune. Eight houses built of dry-stone walls, with stone furniture (beds, dressers, hearths) still in place. The village is older than the Pyramids and Stonehenge. What is it called?
context: The village was used from about 3180 to 2500 BC. The stone furniture survived because the islands have no native trees, so stone replaced wood. UNESCO World Heritage 1999 as part of 'Heart of Neolithic Orkney' that also includes Maes Howe passage grave.

question: On the Maltese island of Gozo stand two megalithic temples built between about 3600 and 3200 BC — among the oldest free-standing stone structures in the world, older than the Egyptian pyramids and Stonehenge. The local Maltese legend says they were built by a race of giants. What is this site called?
context: Ggantija means 'giant's tower' in Maltese. The complex's stones reach 5 metres tall; the largest weighs about 50 tons. The temples were used for about 1,500 years. Maltese megalithic culture vanished mysteriously around 2500 BC, replaced by Bronze Age pottery cultures.

question: On the Italian island of Sardinia stand the ruins of about 7,000 ancient stone towers — circular dry-stone keeps from the Bronze Age (1800-1100 BC), some still 25 metres tall. They were built by an iron-age civilisation that vanished without leaving a writing system. What are these towers called?
context: The Su Nuraxi at Barumini, UNESCO World Heritage, has a central tower surrounded by four corner towers. Some 7,000 nuraghi have been catalogued. The Nuragic civilisation was contemporaneous with Mycenaean Greece and traded with it; their religion and language are unknown.

question: In the central Ethiopian highlands, eleven Christian churches were carved straight down from the bedrock in the 12th-13th centuries — each church monolithic, surrounded by a trench and connected by tunnels. Bete Giyorgis (Church of Saint George), the most photographed, is carved in the shape of a Greek cross from above. Whose name does the town and complex carry?
answer: King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty
choices: King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty
context: Lalibela was a 12th-13th-century Zagwe king who is sacred in Ethiopian Orthodox tradition. Legend says angels helped his masons work at night. The complex includes drainage tunnels, courtyard chapels, and one church (Bete Maryam) preserves frescoes. Coptic-Orthodox Christians still worship in all eleven churches; the site sees roughly 100,000 pilgrims at Christmas.

question: Inside the Qutub Minar complex in Delhi stands a 7-metre iron pillar — wrought iron, weighing about 6 tons, dating to about 400 AD. It is famous for having survived 1,600 years of monsoon rains without significant rust. What is the explanation now generally accepted?
answer: High phosphorus content + a passive coat of misawite (iron oxyhydroxide)
choices: High phosphorus content + a passive coat of misawite (iron oxyhydroxide)
Constant burnishing by pilgrims over centuries
Mythical — the pillar does rust; only the lower section is clean
context: The pillar's phosphorus content (about 1%) and the local climate combine to form a thin protective film of misawite on the iron. Some rust exists at the base in damper, more touched zones; the upper sections are remarkably pristine. The pillar was likely moved from elsewhere when the Qutub complex was built around 1192.

question: When travellers emerge from the kilometre-long crack in the Jordanian sandstone called the Siq, the first sight is a 40-metre-high facade carved into a pink cliff. Greek-style Corinthian columns frame an urn at the top. The facade was reportedly used as a Bedouin shooting target. What was the function?
answer: Most likely a royal tomb (possibly King Aretas IV)
choices: Most likely a royal tomb (possibly King Aretas IV)
Most likely a temple to Dushara
Most likely a treasury (despite the modern name)
context: The Treasury (Al-Khazneh) probably housed the burial of a Nabataean king — the inside has three simple chambers, no decoration. Local Bedouin legend held that the urn contained pharaoh's treasure; bullet marks on the urn show generations of attempts to break it open.

question: In the swampy Gulf coast of Mexico, the oldest known major civilisation of Mesoamerica (1500-400 BC) carved colossal stone heads — 17 of them, up to 3.4 metres tall and 50 tons. Each head wears a distinctive helmet-like headdress, perhaps a ball-game helmet, perhaps the headgear of a specific ruler. Who were these people?
context: Olmec basalt for the heads was quarried at Cerro Cintepec, about 60 km from the carving sites. The heads weigh up to 50 tons; how the Olmecs moved them — over swamps, on logs and rafts — is one of Mesoamerica's mysteries. The Olmec are sometimes called the 'mother culture' of Mesoamerica; their iconography influenced everything that followed.

question: On the Orkney Islands off northern Scotland stands a 5,000-year-old megalithic ring of about 36 originally tall standing stones (21 still upright), 104 metres in diameter — the third-largest stone circle in Britain. Built around the same time as nearby Skara Brae. What is this circle called?
context: The Ring of Brodgar is part of the UNESCO Heart of Neolithic Orkney complex with Maes Howe (passage tomb), Stenness (older smaller stone circle), and Skara Brae. The site is on a peninsula between two lochs (Stenness and Harray). Geophysical surveys 2003-2020 have found extensive associated settlements (the Ness of Brodgar).

question: A Bronze Age script written on clay tablets from Knossos (Crete) and the Greek mainland was deciphered in 1952 by a young English amateur. The decipherment revealed the script encoded an early form of Greek. What is the script called?
context: Michael Ventris was an architect by training; he died in 1956 at age 34 in a car crash before finishing the academic edition of his work. Linear A (probably a different language) remains undeciphered. Linear B tablets are mostly bureaucratic — inventories, tax records — not literature.

question: On Easter Island (Rapa Nui), about 900 large stone moai statues were placed atop nearly 300 ceremonial platforms around the coast. The platforms — and the statues — face inward toward the island's interior. The statues represent deified ancestors. What are these platforms called?
context: Most moai were toppled face-down off their ahu by Rapa Nui themselves between 1722 (European contact) and 1864 — a period when traditional religion was abandoned and many statues were deliberately knocked over. About 50 have been re-erected by archaeologists since the 1950s.

question: Above the Treasury and the city of Petra in Jordan, a rock-cut altar on the summit of one of the surrounding sandstone mountains was used for Nabataean ritual sacrifice. A flight of more than 800 carved steps leads up to it from the canyon floor. What is this called?
context: The Nabataean altar still has carved channels for blood drainage. Two obelisks nearby may have represented the gods Dushara and Al-Uzza. The climb is steep but rewards visitors with panoramic views over the entire Petra site.

question: Outside the Temple of Luxor in Egypt once stood two 23-metre red granite obelisks erected by Pharaoh Ramesses II around 1250 BC. One remains in front of the temple. Where did the other go in 1836?
context: Muhammad Ali Pasha (ruler of Egypt 1805-1848) gave the obelisk to France in exchange for a mechanical clock now in the Cairo citadel that has never worked. Moving the 230-ton obelisk to Paris took five years. The remaining Luxor obelisk and 'Cleopatra's Needles' in London and New York all date from the Ramesside or earlier periods.

question: Among the most-visited buildings in the buried Roman city of Pompeii is a small structure with paintings on the walls of 10 specific erotic scenes above doorways to small chambers. What was this building?
context: Pompeii had at least 25 lupanari (brothels); the main Lupanar is the largest and best-preserved. Prices and services were written in graffiti on the walls. The paintings above each doorway were probably menus rather than decoration. Roman attitudes toward prostitution were complicated — legal, taxed, but socially stigmatised.

question: In the Bamiyan Valley of central Afghanistan, two colossal Buddha statues — 53 metres and 38 metres tall — were carved into a sandstone cliff in the 6th century AD when the area was a thriving Buddhist centre on the Silk Road. They were the largest standing Buddhas in the world. What happened to them?
answer: Dynamited by the Taliban in March 2001
choices: Dynamited by the Taliban in March 2001
Eroded away by 1,500 years of Afghan winters
Captured by the Soviet army in 1985 and relocated
context: Despite international protests including from Muslim authorities (the OIC, Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia all condemned the destruction), the Taliban under Mullah Omar destroyed the statues with explosives. International efforts since 2003 have considered partial reconstruction; current Afghan authorities have not endorsed any plan.

question: On a hill in Lhasa, Tibet, rises a 13-storey white-and-red palace of the Dalai Lamas, begun in 1645. It sits at 3,700 metres elevation — one of the highest palaces in the world. About how many rooms does it hold?
context: The 5th Dalai Lama built it on the site of an older 7th-century fortress of King Songtsen Gampo. The 14th Dalai Lama fled to India in 1959. The palace is now a state museum under Chinese control; the Tibetan exile government considers it the spiritual capital of Tibet.

question: The 12th-13th-century Khmer king who built much of Angkor Thom and the Bayon temple. He converted the kingdom from Hinduism to Mahayana Buddhism and built more monuments than any other Khmer king. Who was he?
context: Jayavarman VII ruled from 1181 to about 1218 AD; his reign was the high point of Khmer power. He built Ta Prohm, Preah Khan, Banteay Kdei, and the city walls of Angkor Thom. The 216 stone faces of the Bayon may portray him as the bodhisattva of compassion.

question: In the mid-1940s, mandolin player Bill Monroe and his Blue Grass Boys band (named after the Kentucky bluegrass plant) crystallised a high-energy acoustic music style using fiddle, banjo (3-finger picked in the Earl Scruggs style), mandolin, guitar, and bass. The name of the band became the name of the whole genre. What state takes credit?
context: Bluegrass features rapid tempos, instrumental virtuoso breaks, close harmony singing in the 'high lonesome' style, and a strong off-beat. The Earl Scruggs 3-finger banjo roll became the genre's signature sound. Bill Monroe is often called 'the Father of Bluegrass'.

question: In the early 1950s, a fusion of rhythm and blues, country, and gospel produced a new American teen dance music. Recordings such as Ike Turner's 'Rocket 88' (Memphis, 1951) and Bill Haley's 'Rock Around the Clock' (1954) are sometimes called the first rock and roll songs. Where did Sun Records of Sam Phillips operate?
context: Sam Phillips's Sun Records launched Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins, Roy Orbison, and Jerry Lee Lewis — all between 1953 and 1956. Chess Records in Chicago launched the electric Chicago blues and Chuck Berry. Whether 'rock and roll' was 'invented' anywhere specific is debated; Memphis and Chicago have the strongest claims.

question: In Jamaica in the late 1960s, the older ska and rocksteady styles slowed down further and developed the characteristic 'one-drop' rhythm with offbeat guitar chops (skanking) and a deep bass line. Bob Marley and the Wailers carried it globally. The genre's name is variously explained. What city was its birthplace?
context: Reggae is closely tied to Rastafari religious culture. UNESCO inscribed reggae as Intangible Heritage 2018. Trench Town in Kingston was the home neighbourhood of many genre-shaping musicians including Bob Marley, Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, and Toots Hibbert.

question: In southern Italian Apulia and Calabria, a frenetic 6/8 dance was originally believed to be the only cure for the bite of a venomous spider — sufferers would dance until exhausted, supposedly sweating out the venom. The dance and the spider share a name. What is it?
context: The tarantula is misnamed: the wolf spider native to Taranto is mostly harmless. The European black widow (latrodectus) of southern Italy delivers the real bite. The medical condition 'tarantism' — manic dancing — was almost certainly a cultural-psychological phenomenon, not actual venom response.

question: A 17th-century Polish folk dance in triple meter (3/4 or 3/8) with strong accents on the second or third beat — adopted by 19th-century Chopin into 58 piano mazurkas. The dance type is named after a region of central Poland. What region?
context: Chopin's mazurkas are among the most distinctively Polish music in the classical repertoire. He composed them throughout his career; many were published only after his death. The mazurka kept Polish folk identity alive during the 19th-century partition of Poland by Russia, Prussia, and Austria.

question: In northern India, one of the eight classical Indian dance forms uses storytelling and the rapid stamping of feet (with strings of bells), spinning, and graceful hand gestures (mudras). The form has roots in temple dance and was patronised by Mughal courts. What is it called?
context: Kathak combines Hindu and Persian-Islamic elements — the Mughal-court evolution gave it heavy use of metal-bell anklets and rhythmic precision. The three gharanas (schools) of Kathak — Lucknow, Jaipur, and Banaras — preserve different stylistic strands.

question: In Mongolia, traditional musicians play a two-stringed bowed instrument carved with a horse's head at the scroll. Mongolian legend says the instrument's first strings were made from a beloved horse's mane and tail. What is the instrument called?
context: The morin khuur is Mongolia's national instrument; UNESCO Intangible Heritage 2008. Its sound is often compared to a horse whinnying. The strings are traditionally made of bundled horsehair (the bowstring still is).Tuvan and Mongolian fiddle traditions are close cousins.

question: In late-19th and early-20th-century coastal cities of the Gold Coast (modern Ghana), African musicians took up European brass-band instruments and Caribbean dance rhythms to play in palm-wine bars and elite ballrooms. The music's name comes from the lifestyle of those who could afford to attend. What is it called?
context: Highlife came in different streams: dance-band highlife in concert halls, and palm-wine highlife on guitars in roadside bars. E.T. Mensah, Osibisa, and the Ramblers were major highlife bands. Fela Kuti grew up listening to highlife before fusing it with funk to create Afrobeat in Nigeria.

question: In 19th-century Naples, pizza was cheap fast food sold by street vendors. In 1889 a pizzaiolo named Raffaele Esposito reportedly made three pizzas for the visiting Italian queen, including one with tomato, mozzarella, and basil — bearing Italy's flag colours. The queen's name was given to that one. What was the queen's name?
context: The pizzeria Brandi still operates in central Naples. Whether the 1889 story is exact history is debated, but Neapolitan pizza is now UNESCO Intangible Heritage (2017). A Vera Pizza Napoletana association certifies authentic Naples-style pizza — defined by ingredients, dough, and oven temperature.

question: The British word 'curry' (from Tamil 'kari') generalises a huge variety of South Asian spiced dishes. In the 16th century the Portuguese brought a key New World ingredient that transformed Indian cooking — making 'spicy' Indian food possible for the first time. What ingredient was this?
context: Pre-Columbian Indian food used black pepper, ginger, mustard, and other native spices, but no chili. The chili spread within India within a century of Portuguese contact (Goa was Portuguese from 1510); Indian regional cuisines today depend on it heavily. The same is true of Sichuan Chinese, Thai, and Korean cuisines.

question: Across Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia, a heavy clay cooking pot with a tall conical lid lets steam circulate, drip back, and slowly cook ingredients in their own juices — perfect for stews of lamb, prunes, almonds, and preserved lemon. The dish takes its name from the pot. What is this called?
context: Tagines come in two varieties — cooking tagines (rougher) and serving tagines (decorated). The Berber cuisines of the Atlas Mountains use them daily. Salt, preserved lemon, olives, and dried fruit are common ingredients. Tagine the dish has become globally popular as Moroccan tourism expanded.

question: Tiny granules of durum wheat semolina, steamed multiple times, originated with the Berber peoples of the Maghreb. They are now a staple food across North Africa. Why does the wheat have to be steamed and not boiled?
answer: Boiling would dissolve the durum semolina into porridge
choices: Boiling would dissolve the durum semolina into porridge
Boiling would damage the wheat's protein content
Boiling would scorch the bottom of the pot
Boiling is impossible at high desert altitudes
context: Couscous is traditionally rolled by hand: durum semolina is moistened, rolled into beads, and steamed in a special pot (couscoussier) over a stew. UNESCO inscribed couscous as Intangible Heritage in 2020 — jointly claimed by Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, and Mauritania.

question: On the Pacific coast of Peru, ancient Andean peoples cured raw fish in fermented juice; after the Spanish brought citrus, they switched to lime or bitter orange. The dish — fish 'cooked' in acid rather than heat — is now Peru's signature culinary export. What is it called?
context: Peruvian ceviche uses lime, salt, chili, onion, and cilantro. The fish is briefly marinated (5-10 minutes, not hours). Peru has a national ceviche day (28 June). The dish is also claimed by Ecuador, Mexico, Chile, and Panama — each with its own variation.

question: Brazil's national dish — a slow-cooked stew of black beans with pork or beef, served with rice, collard greens, and orange slices. It is traditionally eaten on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Its origins lie in:
answer: Adaptations of Portuguese bean stews by enslaved Africans in Brazil
choices: Adaptations of Portuguese bean stews by enslaved Africans in Brazil
A 1930s national-identity invention by Getulio Vargas
context: Earlier scholarship attributed feijoada to enslaved Africans cooking the discarded scraps of plantation owners; this story is now considered mostly myth. Portuguese feijoada (a similar bean stew) existed before the slave trade. Brazilian feijoada is a melding of Portuguese, African, and indigenous techniques — but probably did not originate on plantations as such.

question: A traditional Beijing dish: a duck specially raised, air-pumped between skin and meat to crisp it, then hung and roasted in a closed-fire oven, brushed with maltose syrup. The meat and crispy skin are served with thin pancakes, scallions, and sweet bean sauce. Its golden-age refinement came under which dynasty?
context: Quanjude (founded 1864) and Bianyifang (1416) are the two most famous Peking duck restaurants. Bianyifang predates Quanjude by nearly 450 years and is the original closed-oven roaster; Quanjude uses an open hung oven. American president Richard Nixon's 1972 visit to Quanjude helped globalise the dish.

question: Thailand's most famous soup — hot-and-sour, with lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves, galangal, fish sauce, chili, and shrimp or chicken. The combination of distinct citrus, herbal, and chili notes is unmistakable. What does the soup's name mean roughly?
context: Tom yum is a Thai national dish and global ambassador for Thai cuisine. The shrimp version (tom yum kung) and chicken (tom kha gai, with coconut milk) are the most internationally familiar. Galangal and kaffir lime leaves are essential — substitutes are not equivalent.

question: In the Swiss-French Alpine cantons of Fribourg, Neuchatel, and Vaud, mountain herders had a traditional way to use up hardened cheese: melt it with white wine over a small flame in a heavy pot, then dip stale bread cubes in. What is this dish called?
context: Fondue means 'melted' in French. The Swiss Cheese Union promoted fondue as a national dish in the 1930s to boost dairy industry sales. The traditional pot is a caquelon — a heavy earthenware pot. Etiquette has strict rules: don't double-dip, don't lose your bread in the pot (or you pay penalties).

question: In 1832 Vienna, a 16-year-old apprentice cook had to step in for the head pastry chef who had fallen ill. He invented a dense dark chocolate cake with a thin layer of apricot jam, glazed with dark chocolate, for an aristocratic dinner. Who was the chef?
context: The original Sacher recipe is fiercely guarded by the Hotel Sacher in Vienna. The 'Sachertorte War' (1934-1962) was a long lawsuit between the Sacher Hotel and the Demel patisserie over which had the right to call their cake the 'Original Sachertorte'. Both establishments now sell their own version under slightly different names.

question: In the American South, 'barbecue' is a noun (the food, not the cooking technique). The tradition of slow-smoking large pieces of meat (usually pork shoulder, brisket, or ribs) over low fires of hardwoods has roots in indigenous, African, and European techniques. The Spanish word for it gives English the word. What is it?
context: The Taino word barbacoa described slow-cooking meat over a wooden frame above coals. The four major American regional BBQ styles are: Memphis (dry rub on pork ribs), Carolina (whole hog with vinegar sauce), Kansas City (sweet tomato sauce), and Texas (brisket with minimal sauce).

question: In rural Quebec in the late 1950s, a small restaurant served fried potatoes topped with cheese curds and brown gravy. The dish — now Quebec's national food — has spread across Canada and into the United States. What is the dish called?
context: Both Drummondville and Warwick (Quebec) claim invention of poutine around 1957. The cheese curds must be fresh — they should squeak when bitten. The gravy must be hot enough to melt the curds slightly. Restaurants like La Banquise in Montreal offer over 30 poutine varieties.

question: From the 3rd to 17th centuries, blacksmiths in Syria (and elsewhere across the Islamic world) forged sword blades with a distinctive wavy banded pattern in the steel. The blades were so sharp they reportedly could split a hair falling on the edge. The technique was lost in the 18th century. From what raw material was Damascus steel made?
context: Modern metallurgists have analysed surviving Damascus blades — the steel contains carbon nanotubes and cementite nanowires, possibly accidental products of the wootz-smelting process and the forging temperature. Reproducing authentic Damascus steel remains contested. The 'pattern-welded' steel sometimes called Damascus today is a different technique.

question: From the high-altitude goats of Ladakh and Kashmir comes a very fine wool — the soft undercoat the goats grow to survive Himalayan winters. The wool is gathered when the goats moult in spring. The finest Kashmir shawls of Mughal-era Lahore took months to weave. What is this wool called?
context: Pashmina is the same wool as cashmere — the English word comes from Kashmir. The finest pashmina has fibres about 14 microns thick (compared with about 25 for normal sheep's wool). A genuine pashmina shawl should pass through a wedding ring. Most modern 'pashmina' on global markets is blended.

question: On the Indonesian island of Java, a wax-resist textile dyeing technique has produced ornately patterned cotton fabrics for at least 1,500 years. The wax is drawn or stamped onto the cloth; the cloth is dyed; the wax is melted off; the design appears in the resisted areas. What is this technique called?
context: Indonesian batik was inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Heritage in 2009. The most prestigious traditional batik centres are Solo and Yogyakarta in central Java. The hand-drawn batik tulis (with a wax-pen tjanting) is the slowest and most prized form; stamped batik cap is faster and more common.

question: Iceland sits on the ridge where two of Earth's major tectonic plates are pulling apart at about 2 cm per year. The North American plate is on the west side, the Eurasian plate on the east. At the Thingvellir rift you can literally walk between the continents. What is this ridge called?
context: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs the entire length of the Atlantic Ocean, mostly under deep water. Iceland is the only place where it rises above sea level. The 1783 Laki eruption in Iceland — caused by the rift opening — killed about a fifth of Iceland's people and caused a famine across Europe.

question: About 75% of the world's active and dormant volcanoes — and about 90% of its earthquakes — happen along a horseshoe-shaped belt around the Pacific Ocean basin. The belt's activity is driven by subduction at the basin's edges. What is the belt called?
context: Major Ring of Fire volcanoes include Mount St Helens (USA), Popocatepetl (Mexico), Cotopaxi (Ecuador), Fuji (Japan), Pinatubo (Philippines), Krakatoa (Indonesia), and Ruapehu (New Zealand). The 2004 Sumatra earthquake and 2011 Tohoku earthquake — and resulting tsunamis — both came from Ring of Fire subduction zones.

question: In the western Pacific Ocean lies the deepest trench in the world. It is the seafloor expression of one tectonic plate subducting beneath another. Which plate dives beneath which?
answer: The Pacific Plate subducts beneath the Mariana Plate
choices: The Pacific Plate subducts beneath the Mariana Plate
The Mariana Plate subducts beneath the Pacific Plate
The Pacific Plate subducts beneath the Indo-Australian Plate
The Philippine Plate subducts beneath the Pacific Plate
context: The Pacific Plate is being subducted along the Mariana Trench. The trench is 10,935 metres deep at Challenger Deep — deeper than Everest is tall. Subduction zones generate the largest earthquakes (megathrust earthquakes). The 1960 Valdivia (Chile) earthquake — magnitude 9.5 — is the largest ever recorded; it was a megathrust event.

question: The world's tallest mountains were thrust up by the collision of two continental plates over the past 50 million years. The collision is ongoing, and the mountains are still rising at about 4-5 mm per year. Which two plates collided?
context: About 130 million years ago the Indian plate broke off Antarctica and drifted north at an unusually rapid 15 cm per year. It collided with Eurasia around 50 million years ago. The leading edge of India is still moving northward at 5 cm per year, pushing Tibet up. The Arabian plate is colliding with Eurasia to make the Zagros (Iran) mountains — much smaller-scale uplift.

question: Down the eastern side of Africa runs a vast rift system — the African continent is in the slow process of splitting apart. In about 10 million years a new ocean basin will form, separating Somalia from the rest of Africa. What is this called?
context: The East African Rift contains the great lakes (Tanganyika, Malawi, Albert, Edward) and ancient hominid sites (Olduvai, Hadar). The Afar Triangle (Ethiopia) is the closest to becoming a new ocean — already 100 metres below sea level, with active volcanic eruptions and earthquakes.

question: Along the western coast of California runs a major fault where two tectonic plates slide horizontally past each other. Los Angeles is on one side, San Francisco on the other; they are moving toward each other at about 5 cm per year. What kind of plate boundary is this?
context: Transform boundaries don't make volcanoes or trenches; they make earthquakes when locked sections of fault break. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake (magnitude 7.9) and the 1857 Fort Tejon earthquake (also 7.9) were major San Andreas events. The 'next big one' is anticipated; the southern segment near Los Angeles has not had a major event since 1857.

question: Japan sits at the meeting of four major tectonic plates — Pacific, North American (or Okhotsk), Eurasian (or Amurian), and Philippine. This is why Japan has so many active volcanoes and earthquakes. The 11 March 2011 Tohoku earthquake (magnitude 9.0-9.1) caused a 40-metre tsunami at one location. What was the tsunami's primary destructive cause?
answer: The Pacific Plate subducting under Japan jolted upward suddenly
choices: The Pacific Plate subducting under Japan jolted upward suddenly
Underwater landslides triggered by the earthquake
Volcanic eruption from Mount Fuji during the quake
Internal fluid pressure release from beneath the seabed
context: Subduction-zone megathrust earthquakes lift the seabed sharply, displacing the entire water column above it. The 2011 Tohoku event released about 600 million times the energy of the Hiroshima bomb. About 20,000 people died, most from the tsunami; the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear meltdown was triggered by the same event.

question: Beneath Yellowstone National Park sits one of the world's largest active volcanic systems — a magma chamber producing thousands of geothermal features (Old Faithful, Grand Prismatic Spring, mudpots, hot springs). The volcano has erupted three colossal times in the past 2.1 million years. About when were these eruptions?
answer: About 2.1 million, 1.3 million, and 631,000 years ago
choices: About 2.1 million, 1.3 million, and 631,000 years ago
About 100 million, 50 million, and 25 million years ago
context: Each Yellowstone supereruption was about 1,000 times larger than Mount St Helens 1980. The chamber pulses on a roughly 600,000-700,000-year rhythm; whether the next one is imminent or far off is uncertain. The Yellowstone caldera is 70 km across — Old Faithful sits inside it.

question: The Hawaiian Islands form a chain stretching nearly 6,000 km across the Pacific seafloor (most of it underwater). The islands age progressively from the active Big Island in the southeast to the eroded extinct seamounts in the northwest. This pattern indicates the plate is moving over what?
context: The Hawaii-Emperor seamount chain extends to the Kamchatka subduction zone, dating its source plume to over 80 million years. The Pacific Plate's motion changed direction about 50 million years ago, causing the chain to bend. Loihi (now Kamaehuakanaloa), the next-future Hawaiian island, is already a seamount about 35 km southeast of the Big Island.

question: On the Big Island of Hawaii rises the largest volcano on Earth by total volume — about 80,000 cubic km of basalt above and below sea level. Its height is moderate (4,170 metres above sea level) but its base extends 5 km below the sea, making it taller than Everest from base to peak. What is it called?
context: Mauna Loa means 'long mountain'. The volcano has erupted 33 times since 1843; most recently in 2022. Mauna Kea (next door) is slightly higher in elevation above sea level but smaller in total volume. Olympus Mons on Mars (about 25 km tall) dwarfs both — its volume is about 100 times Mauna Loa's.

question: On 18 May 1980 in Washington state, USA, a 5.1 magnitude earthquake triggered the collapse of the north side of a volcano, releasing pressure on the magma below. The resulting lateral blast levelled 600 sq km of forest in seconds, and an ash column rose 25 km into the sky. About how much did the eruption reduce the volcano's elevation?
context: Mount St Helens lost its top — and developed a horseshoe-shaped crater open to the north. Fifty-seven people died, including volcanologist David Johnston, who radioed 'Vancouver! Vancouver! This is it!' from his observation post before being engulfed. A dome of new lava has been growing slowly in the crater since 1980.

question: In the Khasi Hills of northeastern India sits one of the wettest inhabited places on Earth — receiving on average over 11,500 mm of rain per year, almost all in the summer monsoon. In 1861 it received 26,460 mm in a single year — a world record. What is the town called?
context: Mawsynram, a nearby village, has slightly higher recent averages and is sometimes cited as the wettest place on Earth. Both depend on the dramatic Bay of Bengal monsoon hitting the steep Khasi Hills, which produce extreme orographic lift. Local people build root-bridges from rubber trees that grow stronger over decades.

question: About 10-15 km above the Earth's surface, narrow bands of fast westerly winds run around both hemispheres at high altitudes — they are responsible for the dominant west-to-east weather pattern in mid-latitudes. The polar jet stream can exceed 400 km/h. What drives these jet streams?
answer: Strong temperature gradients between polar and tropical air masses
choices: Strong temperature gradients between polar and tropical air masses
Solar heating of the upper atmosphere
The pressure of solar wind on the upper atmosphere
context: Jet streams form where cold polar air meets warmer subtropical air at upper levels. The greater the temperature contrast, the stronger the jet stream. Aircraft fly with the jet stream to save fuel; the trans-Atlantic crossing east is typically 1-2 hours faster than westbound for this reason.

question: On a rotating Earth, moving objects appear to deflect to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere — when viewed in the rotating reference frame. The effect is what makes hurricanes spin counterclockwise (north) and clockwise (south). What is it called?
context: Named after Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis (1792-1843) who described it mathematically. The effect is not strong enough to influence water draining out of bathtubs — that's a myth (bathtub geometry dominates). But at the scale of ocean currents and weather systems, Coriolis is dominant.

question: In the central United States — Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, South Dakota — cold dry air from Canada and warm humid air from the Gulf of Mexico repeatedly collide, producing the densest cluster of tornadoes on Earth. About how many tornadoes does the U.S. experience in a typical year?
context: The 2011 'Super Outbreak' in April produced 348 confirmed tornadoes across the southeastern US over 3 days. EF5 tornadoes (the strongest category, 200+ mph winds) are rare; about one occurs in the US per year on average. The 2013 Moore, Oklahoma EF5 was a recent example.

question: When moist air blows up against a mountain range, it cools and drops its moisture as rain on the windward (upwind) side. The downwind (lee) side is much drier — sometimes a full-fledged desert. The Atacama (driest place on Earth) sits in the rain shadow of the Andes. What is this effect called?
context: Patagonia (eastern Argentina), the western US Great Basin, and Asia's Tarim Basin all sit in rain shadows. The Tibetan Plateau, in the Himalayan rain shadow from the Indian Ocean monsoon, is mostly desert despite being adjacent to the wettest region on Earth.
